#3689. If You Loved 'Carrie,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Stephen King’s Carrie is one of those endlessly rebootable stories. Way back in 1974, King zeroed in on a near-perfect horror setup that explored being othered, the emotional and mental health consequences of bullying, and just how crappy being a teen girl can be in the modern world. Those themes—and the iconic visuals King conjured with his words—are evergreen, and resonate with audiences each time the story gets rebooted. Mike Flanagan has proved himself a master of horror and a clear successor to King’s legacy in the genre, and if you thought his Carrie reboot on Prime Video was terrific (and you’ve watched all the similar series out there), you should really watch Jennifer’s Body.

Carrie and Jennifer’s Body share a lot of themes—the corrosive pressure of high school, the casual cruelty of adolescents, the explosive power of feminine anger. While Jennifer Check (Megan Fox) is superficially presented as having more power and control than Carrie White (Summer H. Howell) because she’s more self-possessed (and played by Megan Fox), underneath the hair and makeup, Jennifer is just as naive and confused as Carrie. Both girls endure horrific experiences that set them on a path to horrific violence—and those experiences are symbolic of what women everywhere have to deal with all the damn time.

Just as in Carrie, Jennifer’s Body tracks a teen girl’s descent into monstrousness—but where Carrie leans into the tragic nature of those themes, Jennifer’s Body offers a funnier, more sarcastic take buoyed by Diablo Cody’s sharp dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments. The series highlights Carrie’s suffocating home life that offers her no relief from the grinding hell of being a 16-year-old girl who doesn’t quite fit the expected physical or behavioral norms imposed on teen girls, tracing a slow boil of rage. Jennifer’s Body depicts a character who ultimately chooses the dark path, leaning into her newfound destructive power, and has more fun with it, making it the perfect complement to the series.

Although the stories take different paths to get there, they both wind up at a cathartic and bloody climax centered on a school dance, where a lot of people die and chaos reigns. The film is the perfect way to examine, from a different angle, the themes that Carrie explores. Stream Jennifer’s Body on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

Looking for more stories about angry teen girls teaching society a terrifying lesson? Here are a few more films that make a perfect pairing with Carrie.

It’s been 50 years since Brian De Palma adapted King’s novel for the first time, and it’s still worth watching today, especially if you enjoyed Flanagan’s modern take. What could have been a trashy horror movie designed to cash in on the book’s success is instead a well-crafted film that makes every character feel real and consequential, and Sissy Spacek’s performance as Carrie is screen-meltingly amazing. Few horror films have aged this well, and watching a different creator’s vision of the story will be well worth your time. Rent Carrie on Prime Video.

If Carrie’s cathartic presentation of female rage and teen angst is what hooked you, the most relevant movie to jump to is The Craft. The story of four high school girls who harness dark powers to take revenge on, well, high school life itself is anchored by four feral performances from Robin Tunney, Fairuza Balk, Neve Campbell, and Rachel True. Like Jennifer’s Body, the teen protagonists enthusiastically embrace their power in a way that Carrie White doesn’t, but it transforms (and destroys them) just the same. Rent The Craft on Prime Video.

One reason Carrie is terrifying in all its forms? The very idea of a child with an imperfect grasp of ethics and an immature emotional state having thermonuclear-level psychic powers. After all, teenage girls without powers can be terrifying when triggered. The Innocents focuses on sisters Ida (Rakel Lenora Petersen Fløttum) and Anna (Alva Brynsmo Ramstad), who meet Ben (Sam Ashraf) and Aisha (Mina Yasmin Bremseth Asheim), who both demonstrate powers including telekinesis and mind control. Their interaction soon reveals that Anna also has mental powers, and the four begin working to enhance their capabilities—but when one of them begins using their powers to hurt others and seek revenge, things take a dark turn that fans of Carrie will appreciate. Stream The Innocents on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Anyone who was ever bullied in the teen years (so ... everyone) knows that those wounds never quite heal. That’s one aspect of Carrie’s power, and it’s also what makes Sissy an ideal movie to watch when you’ve finished the series. A mental health influencer, Cecilia (Aisha Dee)—once known as “Sissy”—runs into her old best friend, Emma (Hannah Barlow) and is unexpectedly invited to Emma’s bachelorette weekend—only to run into her childhood tormentor, Alex (Emily De Margheriti). The old trauma hits Cecilia like a bomb, shattering her fragile mental balance and leading to a surprisingly funny series of murders as Sissy works through her lingering anger issues. Stream Sissy on Hoopla or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you’re a Mike Flanagan and Stephen King superfan, the obvious movie choice is their other collab, Doctor Sleep. A sequel to one of the most famous horror stories of all time (The Shining), the story finds a middle-aged Danny Torrance (Ewan McGregor) struggling to control his psychic powers, and leading the fight against an ancient group of entities that feed off of people like him. If you want more of that Flanagan/King magic, this is the right move. Rent Doctor Sleep on Prime Video.

#3688. Nier Automata’s File Size Now Reflects How Good It Is

Nier Automata is my favorite game of all time, and I've been telling everyone I know to play it for nearly a decade. On PC, however, Square Enix accidentally made that a little bit more difficult, because the game's latest patch ballooned the game's file size by more than 600%.

The update, tested by RPG Site, takes what was a pretty reasonable 50GB file size and raises it to 366GB. It appears to be incorrectly assigning a file size of more than 40GB to each piece of DLC. The patch itself was supposed to simply add three new languages to the Steam version: Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, and Korean.

"We are currently investigating the cause and working to resolve the issue. We apologize for the inconvenience," Square Enix said in a post on Steam.

Because the giant file size is linked to the different pieces of DLC, you can temporarily resolve the issue by going to "Properties" and "DLC" on Steam and unselecting them. Of course, this also means you won't be able to enjoy that DLC, so if you mostly want to fight the former CEO of Square Enix in the game, you're going to have to wait.

As for what's next for the Nier series, Square Enix and director Yoko Taro have been pretty hush-hush, but Automata has been an immense success. As of February 2026, it had sold more than 10 million units. An anime adaptation is also available now on Crunchyroll.

The huge success of Michael took me by surprise. I knew it would be popular, as I’m a child of the ‘80s and I remember just how huge Michael Jackson was. In fact, the first cassette tape I ever owned was Thriller, which I got for Christmas in 1982 or 1983. Still, I didn’t think Michael would crush the 2026 movie schedule the way it did when it rang up north of a billion dollars at the box office. As for my opinion on the movie, I think it’s…well…fine.

However, Jaafar Jackson’s performance is spectacular. I honestly think he should be nominated for an Oscar, though I’m skeptical that he will be. Obviously, I’m not alone in my praise for Michael’s nephew’s acting, singing, and dancing skills shown off in the film. His performance has been lauded by virtually everyone, even those who didn't like Michael. Another person who loved the performance is Prince Jackson, Michael’s youngest son and Jaafar’s cousin.

Prince recently spoke to The Associated Press and talked about his cousin playing his dad, and he definitely loved it. Prince said:

I’m so thankful that the world has embraced his performance and his embodiment of my father in the way in which they did. But I think that it would be incredible for him to get the acknowledgement from his peers in this field of the creative artistry, the determination and the discipline I think that went into this.

The performance by Jaafar wasn’t luck, either. He didn’t rely on his family name (Jaafar’s father is the late Jermaine Jackson) to coast through the movie. He worked his tail off to give that performance. His practice sessions have become the stuff of legend already. Prince noted this in his comments as well, saying:

He’s a little bit older than me. We grew up together, but I watched my cousin work his butt off. He locked himself in our family home in Hayvenhurst for weeks at a time. And we would see each other regularly, weekends or whatever. But, during that time when he was working, didn’t see Jaafar. [The] only time we saw him was when he was dancing or sweating or locked in his room when he was doing his character research.

Unfortunately, the Academy often seems to forget movies that are released in the first half of any year, as Michael was when it came out in April. That means that Jaafar Jackson is likely going to be overlooked come Oscar nomination morning in January. It’s also a big, splashy movie about a man, Michael, who isn’t without serious controversy. Controversy, it’s worth noting, that the movie doesn’t get into.

I don’t think that’s on Jaafar, though, and for his performance, he is worthy of great praise. It’s nice to see his cousin (and the son of the man he’s playing) lavish that upon him. Maybe it’ll bring more attention to the people who vote. In the meantime, if you want to watch the performance again, it’s available with the Starz add-on to a Prime subscription.

#3686. ‘Little Rascals’ Child Star Launches GoFundMe Ahead of Welcoming 6th Baby

Brandon “Bug” Hall is reaching out for a helping hand as he and his wife prepare to welcome their sixth baby.

The former child star, 41, launched a GoFundMe campaign on Thursday, November 5, in an attempt to raise funds to cover expenses associated with their expanding brood and to help finish setting up their new home.

Hall shared via the GoFundMe campaign that he was initially hesitant to create the fundraiser but he had reached the point where he felt it was necessary.

“It’s now six years since I self-cancelled, and I have avoided doing one of these in all that time. I always said this was my choice, and so I didn’t want to offload the glorious burden of it unless there was no other choice. Well here we are,” Hall, who is best known for his role as Alfalfa in The Little Rascals, wrote.

Hall shared that he and his family were working hard towards finding their feet in their new property in rural Arkansas but challenges had arisen.

“We’ve made it onto the new land in record time, but I’m a few materials short of having things working right, and I’ve fallen a little behind on the few bills we have (phone, propane for the camper, and an unexpected electric hookup service fee),” he explained.

Hall continued, “We’re all overjoyed to be where we are, and we’re even enjoying roughing it, but baby six is less than a month away, and I really need some help getting the last few things buttoned up beforehand.

The father-of-five said he wanted to get everything sorted before his wife gives birth and acknowledge that he isn’t the only one doing it tough at the moment.

“My hope is to finalize everything here over the next two weeks so I can take some work until the baby arrives,” he wrote. “Times are hard for everyone, and I’m no more deserving than anyone else, but I ask in your charity that you help where you can, whether monetarily, by sharing this, or by prayer and sacrifice for the Hall-Barnetts of the Holy Cross.”

The GoFundMe’s stated goal was set at $2,000. At time of publication, Hall had received more than $9,000 from 102 donations.

Hall’s campaign comes after he was arrested in Ohio in April after failing to appear in court, according to multiple reports.

The actor missed a December 31, 2024, court date tied to an October 29, 2024, traffic citation for driving without liability insurance. He was charged with failure to appear.

Hall left Hollywood behind in 2020 in a bid to embrace a self-described “radical Catholic extremist” lifestyle off-the-grid as he took a “vow of poverty,” according to the Daily Mail.

#3685. Bill Skarsgard Didn’t Need Much Convincing To Join Hideo Kojima’s Physint

Hideo Kojima's Physint has a leading man in Bill Skarsgård, and the Hollywood actor recently spoke more about his part in the game. Billed as a spiritual successor to Kojima's Metal Gear Solid franchise, Physint is an action-espionage game that features Skarsgård alongside several other actors, like Charlee Fraser, Don Lee, and Minami Hamabe. Skarsgård's love for the Metal Gear Solid franchise and a chance to work with Kojima proved to be the deciding factors in taking on the role of the unnamed Physint protagonist.

"I played every single one," Skarsgård said to Josh Horowitz on the Happy Sad Confused podcast. "Starting from the one on PlayStation One all the way to the last one. I was very enamored by him [Kojima], the mythology and the universes that he creates, but also the mystique and the allure about him, as well. He is an auteur, but he's a video game auteur. He's fluent in filmmaking, and film, and cinema."

Skarsgård believes that Kojima's cinematic video games are a new medium that he's pioneering, and with Physint, the developer is getting closer to "something that's photorealistic and also interactive," the actor said. "I think he's a pioneer, and he keeps going out to untreaded waters."

Kojima is also a fan of Skarsgård, and he recently spoke about how he was introduced to him through a mutual acquaintance, Death Stranding 2: On the Beach composer Yoann "Woodkid" Lemoine. After traveling to Sweden to meet Skarsgard and his family, Kojima pitched him the lead role in Physint, which Skarsgard accepted.

While it looks like production on Physint is starting to pick up steam, it's still early days for the project. Kojima previously revealed that the script for it is ready, but there's still work to be done on motion-capture and filming performances. Sony was originally funding development on it, but after the PlayStation company pulled support for it, Kojima found a new home at Xbox for Physint. The developer has described Physint as the "biggest-selling" game that he could possibly create, and Xbox is also funding development on his upcoming horror game, OD Knock.

#3684. Russell Brand Has Been Found Guilty. American Courts Could Learn a Lot From His Trial

Britain’s most notorious serial killers and infamous gangsters are convicted at London’s Old Bailey, under a neo-Baroque dome and gold-gilded statue of Lady Justice. But it is Southwark Crown Court, an entirely bland heap of 1980s bricks by the River Thames, where the embattled entertainers wash up.

Only recently, this is where rapper Chris Brown—who pleaded guilty to affray after striking a man in the head with a glass bottle in a nightclub—learned he would avoid prison. It is also where Russell Brand today was found guilty of one count of rape and three of sexual assault. He was found not guilty of two other counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

The week before, whilst reporting on Brand’s trial, I watched a fan in the corridor outside the courtroom admiringly accost the comedian. “I’ve been told to tell you there are many who support you,” she told him. He gave a zen reply: “I receive it, I receive it.” But by and large, English courts are not interested in fame.

In England, the court is an uncontaminated information space: There are no cameras to broadcast what happens inside, and there are strict rules to marshal what information can come in. It may be one of the few places on earth where an influencer can no longer influence; even Katy Perry, Brand’s ex-wife, had to be explained to the judge. In 2026, the closest the US has come to creating a similar environment is Taylor Swift’s wedding.

In a world of video clips, this courtroom is unclippable. What happens here is beyond the reach of rubbernecking pundits or home sleuths wanting a hot take for their socials. Unlike in modern discourse, there are rules in this court, and they are strictly enforced: Complainants in sexual cases are entitled to immediate and lifelong anonymity in the UK. Their real names and identifying details were heard in court—but mention them outside, and you risk arrest for contempt of court. Here, the defense also must ask the judge’s permission to bring up the accusers’ sexual history. When it was suspected that one blogger may have crossed the line, the judge barked at the lead prosecutor: “You’ve plenty of police officers back there…. Send one to arrest him!” They promptly did, and he was ultimately released with a caution.

Jurors, too, can never be unmasked, and their deliberations are forever secret. I sat watching them throughout the trial, but can never tell you what I observed.

From the initial charging to the conclusion of the trial, we in the British media are limited to reporting fairly and accurately only what the jury hears each day. Anyone weighing in publicly with an opinion, a prediction, or anything that could create a “substantial risk of serious prejudice or impediment” to the trial risks joining Brand in the dock of a criminal court. This meant there was no spin as Brand stepped down from the witness stand—no online reprisals against his accusers.

In court, Brand described himself as someone who had once been “staggeringly” famous. His defense argued that, in 2023, reporting from Channel 4, The Times, and The Sunday Times alleging sexual misbehavior changed that—and made everyone desert him. This, Brand said, is why only three witnesses were called to support him—two, if you exclude his wife.

“It’s not the case you’ve been completely abandoned,” wily prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones stated in cross-examination on October 28. Eight seconds of silent staring was Brand’s reply.

“You have a platform with followers in the millions, don’t you?” Silence.

“Yes,” he eventually returned, albeit quietly. Even Harold Pinter would have shouted, “Get on with it.”

Keeping up? To follow any of this is to wade through a thicket of non-sequitur arguments, florid vocabulary and, in his latest twist, the Gospels.

How has Brand’s flimflam, wrapped up in the needy personality of an entertainer who lives off clicks, landed in England’s criminal court system? Uncomfortably, I would say. Southwark is dilapidated and definitely analogue. The litigators wore robes and horsehair wigs, and the microphone on the prosecutor’s lectern was held in place with an enormous amount of yellow and black hazard duct tape. The lights went out twice because of a power cut.

If the world is now video-first, our courts are video-last. With the occasional exception of a judge’s sentencing remarks, nothing in court is photographed, filmed, or recorded for the media. Even the court artist can only take written notes, and must do their actual sketches outside.

“It’s not theater,” I heard the court clerk tell a law student who’d come to watch Brand’s trial but was annoyed to find the six public seats were full.

If this case had been undertaken in Brand’s adopted home of Florida, everyone’s evidence would have been tailored to win over cable news panel pundits. Soundbites would trump reasoned long-form arguments. The names of his accusers would likely be public—as would anything else anyone could dig up about them. Did the framers of the American Constitution really want @truecrimesleuthboy unpicking old Facebook albums of women alleging rape, or network news cameras hounding jurors on their decision?

Did you watch the Amber Heard–versus–Johnny Depp defamation trial in 2022? Were you one of the billions using #AmberTurd online as the “courtroom porn,” as Monica Lewinsky called it for Vanity Fair, was dissected, criticized, and memed? After her defeat, Heard’s lawyer spoke out in frustration: “There’s no way [the jury] couldn’t have been influenced” by the online discussion, she said. “It was horrible.”

Because of where Brand’s trial took place, his testimony could never have been turned into a similar show. In Court 3, there was no camera awaiting his reactions to what he was allegedly being subjected to. Maybe that’s why he didn’t try to pull any of that.

Brand did arrive at court with a Holy Bible bursting with index tabs. One day, when stuck in the corridor with the assembled press pack, he also uncomfortably boomed out, “This is a great day.” But for the most part, I observed him sitting tall and still and lonely in the dock. His personal bodyguard dozed in the courtroom’s family and friends section as an assistant scrolled through her phone and his father demolished a Snickers.

The only sign his group was listening to the awful things their friend/boss/son was being accused of was the very active facial expressions of Brand’s wife, Laura. “Oh, come on,” she appeared to mouth on one occasion, listening to one woman alleging rape.

There was no sign of Brand the comedian or Brand the YouTuber when the defendant took to the witness stand—though he did begin his testimony defiantly, answering the first question with a “No” so loud he seemed to shock even himself. From then on, he diminuendoed so far that the judge jumped in: “You are starting to drop your voice.”

Brand’s silences began when prosecution advocate Karmy-Jones took to her feet. A distinguished prosecutor and defender, she’s worked with and around murderers, sex offenders, and organized crooks. She’s also done time with terrible showoffs, having begun her career as a theater director. Kristin Scott Thomas or a young Lauren Bacall might play her in the film version of the trial.

Karmy-Jones was achingly polite as she unpicked what Brand called his “escalating recollection” of events. In four police interviews across 18 months, claimed Brand, he had no memory of the six women accusing him—even when given photographs, names, and some details. The British version of the Miranda warning tells suspects under caution, “You do not have to say anything. But it may harm your defense if you do not mention when questioned something which you later rely on in court.”

According to the police tapes, so-called Woman 3 did not ring a bell for him back then. But in the witness box, Brand described meeting her at a bar, recalling that a friend had said something like, “There’s a bird here who really wants to meet you.” He remembered that she had “prominent eyes,” was “lithe, elfic, pixyish,” and consented to go to the toilet for “kissing..fondling.” He was found guilty of sexually assaulting her, and acquitted on that charge of rape.

“Are you sure you aren’t piecing an account together from the evidence that was served?” Karmy-Jones asked.

Maybe the lack of spotlight and vodcaster microphone lowered his guard. This proud wordsmith did not seem ready for his words to be used against him. He wouldn’t have sexually assaulted a woman he was flirting with, Brand said. He would have been “complimentary, flirtatious, tactile.” Yet when Brand tried to drift into generalities, he was dragged back to specifics.

“Not if you met someone, Mr Brand. What was the conversation you had?” What did he mean when he said he would have been “tactile?” “Tactile means touch,” was his gently smug reply.

“Indeed it does,” Karmy-Jones returned, dragging him back to the allegation that he had grabbed the woman’s breasts.

When was the last time Brand had been spoken to like this? He did not seem to enjoy it. He even conceded there were “small details” in his evidence “that are inconsistent, and I acknowledge that.”

Perhaps you can see why Brand and his advocates didn’t attempt any “this is a deep state conspiracy sparked by my client’s vlogging about Pfizer” material on the witness stand. During the trial, he somehow managed to maneuver himself into a difficult position: insisting that despite not remembering it previously, he did have a conversation with Woman 5 about consent in which she agreed to unprotected anal sex, even though she’d just insisted their consensual vaginal sex involve a condom. “Nonsense, wasn’t it, Mr. Brand?” asked Karmy-Jones. The jury must have agreed. Brand was found guilty of this charge.

The jury was given the space to examine all this without any public discourse crowding their own thoughts out of their head. And it’s clear to the rest of us that this is preferable: A Gallup poll this year suggested just 17% of Americans have confidence in their criminal justice system. Compare that to the latest Crime Survey for England and Wales, which found 48% have confidence in how criminal justice is administered.

Our courts need physical repair, better pay, more money generally. But the fundamentals are right and working.

On one of the last days of the Brand trial, I left the court building and recognized one of the jurors standing in front of me. They had their coat on, a bag on their shoulder, and were stepping out into a cold London evening totally anonymously. A thick gaggle of paparazzi, waiting for Russell and co., were lined up at the boundary. The juror slipped through without a single flashbulb going off, without a single paparazzo glancing or realizing this person might be someone worth photographing. That is exactly how it should be.

#3683. Google's 'Health Guardian' Is Now Available for Fitbits

Google’s “Health Guardian” feature set rolled out in late September to Pixel Watches 3, 4, and 5, and is now coming to Fitbit Air users in a new update. Google says the new features include reports on your blood pressure trends and on insulin resistance, which is a big claim for a wearable. Here’s what we know about Health Guardian, including how to set it up and what to expect.

Insulin resistance is associated with type 2 diabetes, and can be an early sign that you are heading toward pre-diabetes or diabetes. When your body’s insulin receptors stop responding as strongly to insulin, you’re more likely to have higher blood glucose.

Insulin resistance is normally measured with bloodwork. For example, your fasting glucose levels and fasting insulin are combined into a score called HOMA-IR. If you’re concerned about insulin resistance or pre-diabetes, it’s best to talk to an actual healthcare professional to find out what tests they recommend, and what to do with the results.

The insulin resistance feature coming to Google Health is, Google notes, “not intended for medical purposes” and “not a pre-screener for diabetes.”

Google published a paper describing some of the testing that went into developing its insulin resistance algorithm. In the study, the researchers had people use their own Fitbits or Pixel Watches to record a variety of metrics, including heart rate, HRV, and activity. It’s not clear from this paper exactly how the algorithm works or whether it’s likely to be useful in a general population, but apparently Google is betting on it being an interesting factor to track in your Google Health app.

Google also published a paper on a blood pressure algorithm, although it is not peer-reviewed. Instead of explaining how the algorithm works, it describes how the researchers tried to figure out what their AI-based model might be looking at. According to this paper, Google's model works about as well as clinical blood pressure measurements, but it's not clear how useful it would be in the real world. For example, the study excluded people with heart disease, but I'd imagine plenty of people with heart disease would be interested in their blood pressure scores.

Google said last month in a press release that Health Guardian, which includes insulin resistance and blood pressure trends, is available for free for people who use a Pixel Watch 3, 4, or 5. Fitbit Air users, they added, would get blood pressure and insulin resistance trends “with a Google Health Premium subscription later this year.” "Later" has arrived, as the feature for Fitbit users is in Google Health 5.11, available on both Android and iOS.

So it’s free if you have a Pixel Watch, but not if you only have the Fitbit Air: Google Health Premium is $9.99/month. It’s unclear what happens if you own both devices; presumably, having a Pixel Watch will get you free access. In any case, other devices, including older Fitbits, do not seem to be included.

The Pixel Watch got Health Guardian in the 5.09 release of the Google Health app for Android. The Fitbit got Health Guardian in the 5.11 release for both Android and iOS.

You can set up your blood pressure and insulin resistance tracking as soon as you get the new version of the Google Health app. I was able to set up insulin tracking by going to the health tab and then tapping Metabolic, and I set up blood pressure under Heart. If you go to Respiratory, you can also set up sleep-breathing quality. (Some European users will get a feature that can call for help in a "breathing emergency," but that is not available in the U.S.)

Google said that the insulin and blood pressure features will give you a monthly report on the first of each month, with the first report coming Oct. 1, if you have given the watch enough data in the previous month. If you're a Fitbit user and are just setting up the feature now, you'll get your first report on Nov. 1. Here is what the app requires:

For blood pressure reports: You need to wear the watch for five consecutive days in the previous month (so, in October to get your November report). You don't have to wear the watch at night.

For insulin resistance: You need to wear the watch for seven days and nights in the previous month, but they don't need to be consecutive.

I set up both features as soon as I got the update for the Pixel Watch, but that timeline didn't allow me a full seven days and nights before the October report. That means I don't have an insulin resistance result. I do have my blood pressure trend result: "Not High." As a reminder, a watch cannot know your actual blood pressure, so the watch is making estimates based on data that may not correspond with your actual blood pressure. That said, my blood pressure tends to read in the normal range at doctors' visits, so at least this wasn't surprising.

What's more confusing is what you're actually supposed to do about the results. If your watch says your blood pressure or insulin are fine, would you delay seeking care or abandon a treatment or lifestyle change that was supposed to help you? If your watch says something is wrong, would you believe that and maybe spend unnecessary time and money getting checked out? Pixel Watch users are discussing their results online, with a variety of reactions. One redditor says: "I awoke to find out that my blood pressure is too high and apparently the insulin in my body does nothing. This despite that my most recent doctor's visit and blood work were all perfectly normal." Another said: "I got this high insulin result this morning. I have really changed my diet the last four months and I have been going to the gym regularly. I have lost about 40 pounds this year. It's a bummer to see this. I just wonder if it's accurate." I wonder that, too.

#3682. Head Of GTA 6 Owner Reveals His Advice To Be Healthy, Fit, And Live A Long Time

Strauss Zelnick, the head of Rockstar Games owner Take-Two, is known for his dedication to health and fitness. In 2018, he published a book titled Becoming Ageless: The Four Secrets To Looking and Feeling Younger Than Ever, and images of the executive looking shredded and lean at 8% body fat have circulated online. Zelnick has now spoken more about his health and fitness lifestyle, and offered some advice for people who want to get in shape and feel better.

Zelnick started off by telling Business Insider that he's good friends with Bryan Johnson, the billionaire who is trying to live forever, but Zelnick doesn't subscribe to the kinds of things Johnson is trying to do in terms of longevity in that regard.

Instead, Zelnick said he got some advice from his former doctor, the celebrity longevity doctor Peter Attia who appeared in the Epstein files, who told him he could help him with his healthspan but not his lifespan, and Zelnick was into that.

In 2016, Zelnick filmed a video for Business Insider where he showed off his workout routine--you can see it below.

Zelnick said his No. 1 piece of advice for anyone trying to improve their health is to avoid smoking altogether. "Smoking is the factor most highly correlated with a short, unhealthy, and frankly unhappy life. Don't smoke." Second, Zelnick said people should not abuse alcohol and drugs. "Those are the two most highly correlated factors with a bad old age, or no old age," he said.

After that, Zelnick said it's a good idea to get "some exercise," and that could be walking for 30 minutes four or five days a week. Zelnick said he goes way beyond this because health and fitness are his hobbies "but you really don't need to do that." Beyond exercise, Zelnick said he recommends that people eat a "responsible" diet, but it doesn't have to be "insanely healthy." The best practice for food, Zelnick said, is to simply not overdo it on unhealthy foods.

Another part of increasing your healthspan is getting enough sleep, and that should be about seven hours each night, Zelnick said. "If you're getting less than six hours of sleep a night, you're making bad decisions; that's what the math says," he said. "You are going to make bad personal decisions and bad professional decisions."

Having some kind of "emotional or spiritual life" is important, too, Zelnick said. "You have to have people you love and love you in your life, and preferably, you have to have a community around you," he said.

Also in the interview, Zelnick pushed back against taking peptides, which are popular in some fitness circles, but are largely unregulated.

"No. We have an FDA for a reason," he said. "Don't take something that is not double-blind tested. Even if it worked, do the stuff I do, forget the peptides, and you'll be in a better place."

Lastly, Zelnick said if people want to lose weight, they should consider taking some kind of GLP-1.

"Don't be grossly overweight. But in the world of GLP-1s, you have no reason to be," he said. "I am a huge advocate [for GLP-1s]. And no, there is absolutely no shame in taking them, whatsoever. If you're carrying extra weight, take a GLP-1. I happen never to have struggled with my weight, ever; I am blessed that way."

"I have this workout group, and I've had people show up who are heavyset, because we welcome everyone. So one guy shows up and he comes over and he says, 'I want you to talk to me about your diet, because I want to lost weight. I want to lose 50 pounds.' So I said, 'See, there are these things called GLP-1s. Go to my endocrinologist and get a prescription.' He said, 'Really? What about diet?' I said, 'That is literally like saying to me, I have a migraine, and I would say to you, forget about Tylenol, just meditate.' You take prescribed medications to help you live a healthier life. Of course."

Joanna Gaines knows what every fixer upper needs, and (alongside her husband Chip) has proven this episode after episode. They’re specifically credited with popularizing "farmhouse chic" in the late 2010s, which I have to admit is always a favorite of mine. However, there’s one aspect of this trend that doesn’t seem to have fallen out of favor… and honestly, I bet you can guess the one Fixer Upper thing fans bring up to Gaines every single day.

I’m not talking about clawfoot tubs or barn doors... or even the newest Fixer Upper project. I'm talking about a certain fever that continues to run hot. When Gaines stopped by Kylie Kelce’s podcast Not Gonna Lie for a quick chat about her new mansion project, the host quickly brought up the aesthetic that Gaines put on the map. (Have you guessed it yet?) That’s right. We're here to talk about shiplap. Check out the exchange below:

In case you somehow slept through an episode where she used shiplap, I’ll explain it real quick. Shiplap was originally a functional exterior siding technique (primarily for things like ships, coastal homes, or barns) before it became a popular interior design element used during the height of the farmhouse era. Although has it really subsided? Both women were quick to defend the technique, with Kelce even describing it feeling like “a warm hug.” My farm upbringing can see her point as there is something homey about the way shiplap looks.

While shiplap was already around before Fixer Upper, the use of it was definitely popularized by the mom of five. Although when they found it she admittedly didn’t know what it was called. She even referred to the siding as "boards." Still, I'm not going to hold that against her. Fast forward to today, and Gaines still can’t escape it. Once it’s a hashtag, there’s no going back. For this, she blames it on one specific factor:

I’m gonna defend myself here because every now and then I’ll see like on social, it’ll be like ‘the modern farmhouse aesthetic is over.’ Like you hear all this but it’s like in 2013 and 2014 when the modern farmhouse aesthetic was rising. It really was like people wanted the open floorplan. The hardest thing was I would do client meetings at the farm and there was shiplap on the wall so the client would say, ‘I want what your house looks like. Can I have shiplap on the walls?’ Like, everyone got shiplap.

Not sure if this counts as "one of the biggest mistakes" people make with house design, but there is an irony in Gaines’ own aesthetic rubbing off on clients. We’ve continued to see trendy design ideas since she and Chip launched the Magnolia Network, including a livable garden, and I look forward to seeing what they do with the mansion.

For those who don’t know, the couple is facing a new project in Fixer Upper: Chip Bought A Mansion. The title is a bit of a giveaway, but Chip bought an European-inspired mansion overlooking Lake Waco in Texas. Having bought it three years ago, Gaines is now stepping with her signature eye. The series lands on the 2026 TV schedule on December 27 and is expected to have six episodes. It can be watched on the Magnolia Network the day of or the next day streaming on Discovery+ and HBO Max.

However, the real question we should be asking is, will the new project have shiplap?

#3679. Ratchet & Clank Game Shutting Down Before Ever Fully Launching

Sony Interactive Entertainment and French developer Oh BiBi have announced Ratchet & Clank: Ranger Rumble, a phone and tablet game, is coming to a close before it was even released fully.

In a statement, the developers said the game's final update is coming today, November 6, and the game itself will be removed from digital stores on November 21, 2026.

No information was provided as to why Ranger Rumble is shutting down. The game soft-launched in 2025 in limited territories, and expanded to more markets, but it's no longer going ahead with a full global release.

People who already have the game installed can keep playing until May 1, 2027, which is when the game's servers permanently close. Once the servers are shut down, the game will be completely unplayable.

Ranger Rumble is described as a "fast-paced multiplayer platformer arena shooter" where you battle others on a quest to become a galactic ranger.

In-app purchases have been removed from Ranger Rumble, and if you have a balance of currency, you should spend it before May 1, 2027. Alternatively, you can seek a refund from Apple’s App Store or Google Play.

"On behalf of the dev team and everyone helping to make the game, thanks to our amazing community for all your support, especially to those who have spent time playing, sharing feedback, and helping shape Ranger Rumble throughout its development," the developer said.

The latest entry in the mainline Ratchet & Clank series was 2021's Rift Apart. Its developer, Insomniac Games, has focused on Marvel properties more recently, releasing Marvel's Spider-Man 2 in 2023 and Marvel's Wolverine this year.

#3678. My Favorite Travel Headphones Are $250 Off Right Now

As a headphone reviewer, not many headphones outside of the flagship Sony, Bose, and Apple models get me excited. However, the JBL Tour One M3 Smart Tx headphones became the exception to that rule when I started using them over my Sony 1000XM6 as my go-to headphones. And right now, the Tour One M3s are down to $199.95 (originally $449.95), their lowest price ever, according to price-tracking tools. This is a great deal for these headphones, which I deemed my favorite travel headphones in my review.

Everything from design to the features on the Tour One M3 was made with travel in mind. The headphones are very light, which, along with the comfortable soft earcups and headband, makes them great for wearing for long periods of time. I was able to wear these on a long flight without feeling any discomfort. Feeling like you're not wearing any headphones is the gold standard for comfort, and the Tour One M3 nails that aspect. The battery life is also impressive, with up to 70 hours with ANC off and 40 hours with it on.

The travel case is compact, convenient, and has extra storage for the audio transmitter, which is the best feature of the Tour One M3. This is a high-quality, low-latency audio transmitter. Anything that you can plug an AUX cable, USB, or USB-C port into can stream high-quality, 24-bit audio wirelessly to the Tour One M3. The main way most people will use these headphones is by plugging them into the in-flight entertainment, which lets you watch movies in high-quality LDAC with ANC. But I've also been able to use them to watch TV.

The Tour One M3 Smart Tx are incredible traveling headphones, especially at $199.95, and I recommend them to anyone who values comfort, battery life, simplicity, and likes the idea of the audio transmitter.

#3677. Let’s Throw “Maxxing” Into the Dustbin of History

There was a land of Usenet forums and AOL keywords, LiveJournals and Blogspots and single-topic Tumblrs. It was called the internet, and it was a patchwork quilt sewn together by delightful little freaks—a collective fabric woven from psychologically damaged but individually discernible threads.

With time, that changed. “It had also once been the place where you sounded like yourself,” Patricia Lockwood, poet laureate of the terminally online, wrote of the internet in her wonderfully bizarre 2021 novel No One Is Talking About This. “Gradually it had become the place where we sounded like each other.”

Never has that been truer than in the wee months of 2026, when everyone suddenly woke up, unlocked their glowing rectangles, and decided to start talking like supplement-addled bridge trolls. Mogging, gooning, bonesmashing, mewing: Without rhyme, reason, or the public’s consent (funny thing about that!), incel language had fully colonized our speech. And after the takeover, no neologism was more prominent than the all-purpose suffix “-maxxing.”

We were not talking about what Cher Horowitz might do with her father’s credit card. We were using a slangier term for optimization, attaching it willy-nilly to any nouns or verbs it could plausibly describe. Working out became gymmaxxing; eating too many beans became fibermaxxing; neglecting to look at your phone for eight whole hours became sleepmaxxing. Like all good colloquialisms, the word was adaptable and edgy and undeniably fun to say. It’s got those playful and lightly pornographic double x’s, the push-pull of a hard k sound—famously the most inherently funny consonant—followed by soft sibilance and a literal “zing.”

But after a full 12 months of maxxing, I am more than ready to minn. And not least because no amount of overuse can obscure the ugly origin of 2026’s favorite syntaxx.

Back in the Gamergate era, maxxing was coined by pathetic losers on websites with names like SlutHate, where they used it to describe how they were hoping to attract women: enhancing their appearances through looksmaxxing, enhancing their social status by moneymaxxing. (Perhaps they could have started by showermaxxing.)

True, innumerable everyday expressions have uncomfortable connotations. Just ask anyone who’s absentmindedly used one of them before pausing to frantically google “Is ‘gung ho’ racist?” (answer: yes, but not in the way you might think) or “butthurt word homophobic??” (fortunately, it’s actually not). But most of those questionable expressions weren’t invented five minutes ago. It’s reasonable to expect the hoi polloi not to know the roots of words that have been grandfathered into the lexicon. Maxxing’s upsetting genesis, though, is easily traceable—and anyone who’s online enough to use it is also probably well-informed enough to know better. (Incidentally, “grandfathered in”? Also racist!)

And then, of course, there’s the death knell of all slang: repetition and co-option by both corporations and figurative bad actors. The fun was over the moment the Cheesecake Factory’s official Instagram account advised its 1.1 million followers to try “brown bread-maxxing.” It was ready for last rites by the time Trump’s Department of Homeland Security tweeted about its intention to engage in “deportationmaxing.” (Yes, with one x; given who authors these posts, you’d think they could have spelled it right.) And it was really in the ground two days after that, when The Wall Street Journal’s X account published this sentence: “The era of AI ‘tokenmaxxing’ in corporate America is over. Companies are now embracing ‘thrift-maxxing.’” At this point, we are dead horse–maxxing every time we insert the term into a new sentence, even—especially—if we’re trying to use it ironically.

Language is contagious, particularly for those who live online. In No One Is Talking About This, Lockwood bemoans internet-speak’s unparalleled ability to infect its users: “It was so tiring to have to catch each new virus, produce the perfect sneeze of it, and then mutate it into something new.” But here’s the thing: Protective measures can be taken. If your phone still autocorrects this particular word to “max inc,” there is hope. The bad news, of course, is that by the time you read this, it’s entirely possible an even worse word will have clawed out of the dark web to take its place.

Warning! Spoilers ahead for Season 3, Episode 3 of Happy’s Place, “Full Gabby," which hit the 2026 TV schedule on Friday, November 6th.

Happy’s Place is back for Season 3, and the tavern just got a little bit more chaotic. After making her debut as Gabby’s narcissistic mother, Val, last season, Jane Lynch made her return in this week’s episode of the hit NBC sitcom. Not surprisingly, the actress brought even more chaos and tension, as well as entertainment. I absolutely loved the final scene in Friday's episode, and when I got the opportunity, I had to ask Lynch about those “handsome firemen.”

Despite their tense relationship, Val and Melissa Peterman’s Gabby moved in together during Season 2, and things have not been the greatest, to say the least. In Friday’s episode, “Full Gabby,” fans got a look at how they’ve been doing as roommates, and it was about what you’d expect. The two have differing opinions on renovations, and Gabby’s saging ended up causing a fire and smoke damage, so they crashed at Bobbie and Isabella’s for the night.

That situation at Gabby and Val’s winded up getting some screen time at the very end of the episode. Gabby showed off the security footage from the front porch to Bobbie and Isabella, and their opposite reactions were entertaining. Lynch gave her own rundown of the series of events to CinemaBlend, which included Val’s hilarious and relatable interaction with some handsome firemen:

Well, we're at each other's throats, blaming each other about it, and then, of course, very handsome firemen come out, and I want a selfie with them. I jump into one of their arms, and I'm all inappropriately sexual with them. And of course Gabby hates it. And then I force Gabby to take the picture. So that's how that ends up.

I personally felt the scene showed off just how different Gabby and Val are, and just what their relationship has been like since moving in together. They never really had the greatest mother-daughter bond, and being in close quarters with each other has not helped. The footage only proved that Gabby is tired of her mother’s antics, as if that wasn’t evident before, and there’s no telling what else could be in store. Lynch has portrayed a ruthless TV villain before, and Val may just be added to that list in the near future.

But also, who doesn't love a good fireman scene?

It sounds like there will be more where this came from, too. Lynch has confirmed she’s coming back to Happy’s Place, so she shouldn't have an Only Murders In The Building trajectory this time around. Fans can probably expect chaos and more intense scenes between Val and Gabby, but when asked who else on the cast she’d love to work with more, Lynch couldn’t help but point out her first real scene with Reba McEntire in this week’s episode, which really served as a turning point for Bobbie’s relationship with Gabby:

I've been lucky to have a really good scene with everybody, but in this episode I have my first with Bobbie sitting in her office, where Bobbie learns — because I pointed out to her how much she treats Gabby like I treat Gabby — and I say, ‘You're just like me.’ And she literally jumps off her seat and is like, ‘No, I'm not. I'm nothing like you.’ So that was really fun. We really enjoyed doing that scene.

Even though most of Lynch’s scenes are (of course) with Peterman, she does work with the rest of the cast every so often, like in Friday’s episode. The Glee alum recalled some other scenes she’s done, and I desperately need her to continue branching out to the rest of the cast. It just makes her episodes even better.

In the first episode, I had a great scene with Rex [Linn]. And then I had a great, great scene with Pablo [Castelblanco]. And with Belissa [Escobedo], I've had a good scene with her too. So I've been pretty lucky. I've had a really good scene with everybody, of course, including Melissa.

Happy’s Place can be unpredictable with Val around, and there’s no telling what kind of chaos she will bring during her next appearance. I’m sure she’s hoping to run into more handsome firemen, though. Fans will just have to watch new episodes on Fridays at 8 p.m. ET on NBC, streaming the next day with a Peacock subscription, to see what happens. We'll have to wait and see who else might be joining Happy's Place coming up!

#3674. You Can Get These 'Nothing' Over-Ear Headphones for $55 Right Now

Nothing, the upstart U.K. brand that makes products like phones, smartwatches, and headphones, has quickly become one of my favorite players in tech. Its products offer unique features and designs, and the prices are competitive. For example, right now, Nothing's latest budget over-ear headphones, which were released in October 2025, the CMF Headphone Pros, are just $55 (originally $99). This is a great option for anyone looking to get reasonably priced over-the-ear headphones that punch above their weight when it comes to performance.

Much like Nothing's CMF Buds Pro 2 earbuds, the CMF Headphone Pros are budget headphones that don't feel like it. There is a companion Nothing X app that allows you to customize action buttons, among other things, but the cool thing about these headphones is the control you get without needing the app.

There is a multi-function roller on one side of the headphone that you can roll to adjust volume or press to control the ANC modes, which include adaptive ANC (adjusting cancellation/transparency in real-time) and Spatial Audio (creates an immersive, 3D soundstage for music/movies). #3673. GTA+: Price, Free Games, And All The Other Perks You Get With A Membership Ahead Of GTA 6 Launch

In 2022, Rockstar Games introduced GTA+, a subscription service that provides a variety of perks and bonuses in GTA Online--and beyond.

With GTA 6's release coming up this month, we're running through everything you need to know about GTA +. Do you really need to sign up for yet another subscription service? Only you can answer that, but below you'll find a breakdown of the key facts about GTA+ to help you decide.

In This Article
  • What Is GTA+?
  • Free Games And Other Perks
  • How Much Is GTA+?
  • How To Sign Up For GTA+
  • GTA 6?
  • Take-Two "Thrilled" With GTA+

What Is GTA+?

GTA+ is a subscription service for GTA Online that originally debuted in March 2022 for PS5 and Xbox Series X|S. The subscription offering came to PC for the first time with GTA 5 Enhanced's launch in March 2025.

Free Games And Other Perks

To begin with, every GTA+ subscriber gets 500,000 worth of GTA$ deposited automatically into their in-game accounts monthly based on their billing date. Members also get a 15% bonus in GTA$ for Shark Card purchases, while they also earn GTA$ multipliers for certain GTA Online missions and modes. Subscribers also get discounts on in-game items, with discounted wares varying month by month.

GTA+ members also get access to The Vinewood Car Club where they can claim free vehicles. Also in terms of vehicles, subscribers get a 100-car garage, spread across five floors.

Members receive monthly benefits--for November 2026, Rockstar is offering the Grotti Itali RSX sports car for free, along with the new Chameleon Paints, and more items for your mansion.

You can visit this page to see the current month's special bonuses for subscribers.

Another major perk of signing up for GTA+ is getting access to the GTA+ Games Library. This is a rotating selection of classic Rockstar titles that players have access to for as long as their membership remains active. The current roster of freebies--as of November 2026--includes a range of titles for PC, console, and mobile:

  • GTA 5
  • Red Dead Redemption
  • GTA Online
  • GTA Vice City - The Definitive Edition
  • GTA III - The Definitive Edition
  • Bully
  • GTA: The Trilogy - The Definitive Edition
  • LA Noire
  • GTA: Liberty City Stories
  • GTA: Chinatown Wars

How Much Is GTA+?

GTA+ launched in 2022 priced at $6/month, but the price went up to $8/month in 2024. Memberships can be canceled at any time. There is no multi-month or annual subscription option.

How To Sign Up For GTA+

GTA+ requires a copy of GTA V or GTA Online. You can sign up on PS5 and Xbox Series X|S through those platforms' store pages or from within GTA Online. On PC, people can sign up via their preferred store or in game.

GTA 6?

Rockstar Games has not said anything yet about if GTA+ will be supported with GTA 6. Given that GTA 5's GTA Online may stick around even after GTA 6 launches, it's possible GTA+ will continue to be supported for that game at least. It's expected that GTA 6 will have a significant online mode given the huge success of GTA Online, but it remains to be seen what form it may take.

While we don't know if GTA+ will give you anything extra or new in GTA 6, Rockstar has confirmed that all preorders of GTA 6 come with a free month of GTA+. It auto-renews, so be sure to cancel if you don't want to keep it.

Take-Two "Thrilled" With GTA+

In 2022, Rockstar owner Take-Two commented on GTA+'s introduction, saying the company was "thrilled" with the response out of the gate.

"We're thrilled about how it's been rolled out so far. We're thrilled with the conversion rate," Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick said back then. "And it's clear, that consumers really like the opportunity to engage with GTA Online and they value... what we're offering through a subscription."

Take-Two hasn't said a whole lot about GTA+ in the ensuing years, but the company loves the kind of recurring revenue that a subscription service provides.

#3672. Bonfire of the Neocons: The MAGA Finger-Pointing Begins

Good afternoon from Washington, where foie gras is now illegal and the local Stasi is going door-to-door to check that every citizen has downloaded Bluesky.

The town, one of the bluest in the country, is in a state of stunned ecstasy as it struggles to process the mind-bending midterm election results. Democrats won the House, the Senate, and a majority of governorships, penetrating deep into historically red strongholds like Texas, Kansas, Mississippi, and South Carolina. During a book party for Sophia Bush at The Jefferson hotel on Wednesday night, the actor nearly cried as she delivered a toast to the results—and to her new bestseller.

On the right, the finger-pointing has already begun. In this edition of Party Animals, you can read my dispatch from a night out with the DC Republicans in mourning and the Democrats celebrating in cocktail-fueled delirium. Plus, a MAGA civil war reignites over Iran, with Vice President JD Vance already wading into the factional fight that could determine the future of the party.

Also mentioned in this issue: Marc Thiessen, Curt Mills, Darline Graham, Ken Paxton, Greg Abbott, James Talarico, Annie Andrews, Mark Mitchell, Matt Walsh, and more.

Got tips? Hit the Party Animals hotline: aidan_mclaughlin@condenast.com. Or text me—my number is 917-817-8266. Complaints will be drowned in cocktail-fueled delirium. Praise will be run as a Democrat south of the Mason-Dixon Line.

The morning after the generational Republican midterm collapse that Party Animals is dubbing Blue Tuesday, JD Vance put on his political-analyst cap. “The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in a lengthy X post. “The president himself said so last night.”

Never mind that Vance’s referenced war is one that his own administration started and is currently presiding over. Vance has often tried to cast himself as an outside observer of the Trump administration, its preeminent reply guy on social media and podcasts—a clever, if often ludicrous, pose for the vice president.

The Vance post was the highest-level opening salvo in a civil war that had been brewing for some time. It erupted into the open on Tuesday night as the results began to spell doom for Republicans and the blame started flying with velocity. The internecine battle is between the “America First” faction of the Trump movement and those who have supported the war in Iran, the latter labeled by detractors—with a sneer—as neocons.

The day before the blue tsunami, hopeful MAGA devotees attended a campaign rally in Ohio.

“The Iran War is the greatest political blunder in the last two decades at least,” wrote Matt Walsh in a post on X. “A catastrophically stupid decision. An unforgivable betrayal of America First principles.” As the dire results came down, even some on the right who had cheered on the war came to see, in the cold glow of their screens, the political devastation it had wrought. “Iran War is clearly catastrophically unpopular and has to end,” posted Will Chamberlain, who had spent the last few months loudly dismissing the war’s critics as subliterate simpletons.

On social media, MAGA luminaries shared a screenshot of an infamous op-ed written by Iran war booster Marc Thiessen, whose headline confidently claimed earlier this year: “There is no US downside to striking the Iranian regime.” Fox host Mark Levin lashed out at critics blasting his support for the war, insisting it had nothing to do with the results. Reality would seem to differ. One NBC News exit poll found that 74% of voters said Iran was a “crucial or major factor in how they voted.”

“It was the Iran war, stupid,” said Curt Mills, the executive director of The American Conservative, in an interview with Party Animals. Speaking about Thiessen and Levin, Mills was unsparing: “Professional liars. Professional liars. Not analysts, not honest people, and, honestly, not very invested in the future of the country.”

I asked Mills, who praised Vance’s statement, if it was not strange for the vice president to speak out against the administration while serving in it. “What option does he really have if he wants to keep his job, stop the war, and maybe run for president? I mean, it is strange. It is unprecedented in some ways,” he said. “Is it working? Maybe.”

In restaurants and barrooms across the capital, the ruling party’s apparatchiks watched and agonized as Democrats mounted a historic midterms rout.

The How: The Wall Street Journal’s Josh Dawsey and colleagues have the definitive account of how Trump lost the midterms for Republicans, packed with genuinely shocking reporting that reveals exactly what went wrong at each turn.

Rockstud the Vote: My colleague José Criales-Unzueta trained his gimlet eye on a photo posted by Free Press reporter Olivia Reingold from a Democratic election night party in Michigan and found some suspicious discrepancies in the leather straps of a smoking heel.

Ballroom Blues: Read Shawn McCreesh’s New York Times dispatch from Trump’s strange walk of shame around the White House ballroom construction site the morning after the midterms. “Inside his concrete chrysalis,” McCreesh writes, “everything was still beautiful.” 💔

Department of (Deeply Unpopular) War: Amid a flurry of anonymous quotes from Trump officials and allies laying blame for the midterms on Pete Hegseth, the president tells Jonathan Karl of ABC News that he’s standing by his defense secretary—for now, at least.

Of Mics and Men: In the wake of Patrick Bet-David’s election night stream, Vanity Fair’s Dan Adler has a biting eulogy for the manosphere: “Donald Trump’s 2024 tour of the Joe Rogan–dominated podcast circuit heralded the makings of a new mainstream media. But in the MAGA midterm wreckage, the idea of the manosphere as a political force has shattered.”

A Few Good Streamers: VF’s Abigail Sylvor Greenberg spoke with Hasan Piker and his lawyer, who promised that Piker’s $75 million defamation lawsuit against Scott Jennings is only the beginning.

Russell Brand trial: The star comedian turned right-wing podcast lounge lizard was found guilty in a London court of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Musk in the barrel: Elon Musk, who just torched nearly half a billion dollars in an effort to keep Republicans in power, now faces the wrath of Democrats. The New York Times has a handy guide to the coming storm. “They are going to need to plant new forests for all of the subpoenas we’ll be printing,” said Senator Ed Markey.

#3670. Mass Effect Is Getting A New Art Collection At A Difficult Time For Its Fans

This year's annual Mass Effect Day looks to be somber in light of the studio behind the games, BioWare, being shut down last month. But while no new Mass Effect games are currently on the horizon, you can celebrate its legacy through some classy art prints that are going up for sale ahead of N7 Day. Preorders for the Mass Effect Collection will begin on Friday, November 6, at 10 AM PT / 1 PM ET / 6 PM BST on the Moor-Art website.

The Mass Effect Collection

Moor-Art says it began collaborating with BioWare over a year ago to release a new selection of limited-edition posters. "What began as a celebration of an ongoing saga now feels like the bastion in the continuation of a studio's legacy," the studio said in a press release.

The collection from Moor-Art is inspired by the characters and worlds of Mass Effect, with the original artwork being produced by acclaimed artists and Mass Effect die-hard fans Matt Essom and Dan Mumford. The designs will also be available as T-shirts. The first one is by Essom, and Moor-Art says this illustration captures the spirit and emotional depth of the series, as well as the bonds forged on the Normandy as her crew traveled to unknown worlds. This will be limited to 200 hand-numbered prints worldwide, plus 30 Giclée prints with a certificate of authenticity signed by the artist.

Mumford's "Mass Effect 2" poster aims to capture the sci-fi horror elements of the confrontations against the Reapers, and it features a full ensemble of crew members. As an added touch, it'll be available in two distinct editions: one with the Normandy crew being led by the version of Commander Shepard, while the other one swaps him out for FemShep. Only 150 hand-numbered prints for each variant will be produced, alongside 30 Giclée prints of each Shepard variant, with a certificate of authenticity signed by the artist. If you miss out on both of these prints, you can grab them as T-shirts, either to wear or to frame--or both!

Meanwhile, EA announced a new sale on various items from the BioWare Gear store, which has not gone over well with the studio's fandom. While Moor-Art's collaboration was months in the making and is launching with some terrible timing behind it, EA's approach has been called out for being tone-deaf, considering that it made the call to shut down BioWare after it was acquired by an investor consortium led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund. Efforts are underway to try and save the studio, and while a Change.org petition likely won't change EA's mind no matter how many signatures are attached to it, Canadian fans are attempting to convince lawmakers that the developer is worth rescuing.

#3667. Bob Dylan Meets Pope Leo in a Black Hoodie and Polka-Dot Tie

Yes, I was there. Not at his meeting with the pope, of course, but at the controversial Bob Dylan concert held at the Unipol Dome in Milan.

The legendary singer-songwriter has a discography that stands the test of time, but his recent decision to perform in near darkness hasn’t exactly been celebrated. With a black hood pulled up that almost completely conceals his face and only a few dim lights illuminating the stage, the impact of seeing one of the greatest artists of the 20th century was greatly diminished. From the stands, I couldn’t even zoom in on my phone because it was sealed in a bag at the entrance.

Eventually, I accepted it. Dylan intentionally created this experience, expressing his desire to distance himself from the audience. Far from a technology-forward performance, the Nobel Prize laureate, whose face has become a central figure in modern history, sang nonstop from under a hood for more than an hour and a half.

Dylan has worn the hood for at least the last two years, likely because he wants the audience to focus on his music rather than on him as a public figure. But does it have the same effect when meeting with the pope, especially when he isn’t performing?

The singer was received by Pope Leo XIV at the Apostolic Palace, dressed as if it were a stop on his tour: black sweatshirt, hood up, black gloves, black pants, and a loosely tied polka-dot tie. The ensemble was completed by an umbrella—also black—being used as a cane.

Andrea Monda, editor in chief of the Vatican newspaper L’Osservatore Romano, and Reverend Antonio Spadaro, an official from the Vatican’s Ministry of Culture, which sponsored this meeting, as it had done in July with Patti Smith, escorted Dylan. The two Americans came together in a tableau that is destined to become iconic.

The contrast bordered on the surreal: The Pope's characteristic white robes and Dylan's reclusive black hood. As always, the memes were quick to follow. Some compared Dylan to Palpatine from Star Wars, while others saw a parallel to the final encounter in the game Assassin’s Creed II.

It’s amusing to see them visually contrasted, because their personalities overlap in many ways (and not just because of their American origins). Pope Leo wrote the foreword to a book on disarmament, quoting a 1963 protest song by Dylan titled “Go Away You Bomb.” As for Dylan, he has embarked on a spiritual journey over the years that has brought him closer to the Christian faith.

Pope Leo XIV meets Bob Dylan on November 4, 2026, in Vatican City, Vatican.

“I’m a religious person,” he said in an interview with the Wall Street Journal—“I read the scriptures a lot, meditate and pray, light candles in church. I believe in damnation and salvation, as well as predestination. The Five Books of Moses, Pauline Epistles, Invocation of the Saints, all of it.”

So, is wearing a hood in the presence of the Pope a provocation? Probably not: If anything, it’s consistent with how he has made his recent public appearances.

The brief, 10-minute meeting was private, during which the two exchanged gifts. The Pope gave Dylan a rosary. The musician reciprocated with a signed copy of Chronicles–Volume One, Dylan’s autobiography. The hood stayed on throughout the meeting, turning a gesture of artistic consistency into something that, to outsiders, might look like a defensive maneuver.

Perhaps this is the intended paradox: Dylan has spent his career evading labels, yet precisely when he tries to hide, his goes viral. In many ways, it’s an act of loyalty to himself. At 85, with a career that has left an indelible mark on music and politics, he continues to defy conventions. At least he took off his gloves to shake the Pope’s hand.

#3666. You Can Finally Drive A Dreamcast, Thanks To Sonic

Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds is gearing up for a second year of action, and while you can expect new courses, modes, and characters to join the game, the real headline act here is the new cars coming to it. As part of the Sega Consoles Pack, players will be able to tear around courses while driving a four-wheeled Sega video game console, with each vehicle expertly blending the design of that classic gaming hardware into a lean-and-mean racing machine.

The new cars are based on the Sega Genesis (or Mega Drive for anyone who lived outside the US), the Sega Saturn, and Sega's final home console, the Dreamcast. According to the Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds development team, the idea was to incorporate design elements that would instantly remind players of each console into their respective vehicle frames, like the rounded form of the Dreamcast or the angular silhouettes and subdued tones of the Saturn. The team even went so far as to recreate the Dreamcast’s Visual Memory Unit using original reference data from that era.

"Rather than directly recreating the hardware itself, we translated rounded forms into fenders and nose sections, while angular lines became body panels and hoods, adding the sense of speed expected from a racing machine," the development team explained in a PlayStation Blog post. "While preserving recognizable colors and components from each system, we also designed around the game’s front-and-rear combination mechanic, incorporating the fun of pairing consoles and controllers into the vehicles themselves."

The end result is a design that instantly clues you in on which console informed its design, while still looking like it can burn some rubber on the track. Sega said that the "Genesis Tower" proved to be challenging and required considerable experimentation so that it wouldn't interfere with various visual elements, but it managed to nail the design in the end.

In addition to the Sega Console cars, Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds will also get a new Duel Mode that is designed to offer a different experience from the standard 12-player races. Each race is a one-on-one showdown, and it will require players to think strategically as they jockey for pole position against their rival.

Released in 2025, Sonic Racing: CrossWorlds has steadily grown with more content throughout its first year. Alongside Sonic and the rest of the Mobius crew, the game has also seen some interesting crossovers announced, like a team-up with the nihilistic mecha anime series Neon Genesis Evangelion. If you're interested in checking it out, you can grab the game on PC for $22 at Fanatical currently.

DJI may be best known for its drones and camera equipment, but the company has also been expanding into portable power, with the Power 2000 being its most capable standalone power station yet. Essentially a large rechargeable battery, it's designed to provide electricity wherever you might need it, whether that's on a camping trip, at a job site, during an outdoor movie night, or at home when the power goes out. And if you've been considering one for any of those situations, the Power 2000 is currently down to $749.99 from its original $1,299 price, taking nearly $550 off what would otherwise be a fairly expensive investment.

It's about the size of a carry-on suitcase and weighs close to 50 pounds, so it's not something you'd strap to your back, but it fits easily in a car trunk. The battery itself is built to last, rated for 4,000 charges before it starts losing any noticeable capacity. Performance-wise, DJI says the 2,048Wh capacity can keep a refrigerator running for up to 40 hours during a home power outage, charge a laptop 18 times, or power a projector for 18 hours. Rounding out its features is its companion app, which lets you check its battery level from your phone without having to walk over to it, a small thing that turns out to be pretty convenient. Let me start off by saying that I LOVE Fathom Entertainment. In fact, I probably attend at least three Fathom Events a year. That said, when I saw that Laika's new movie, Wildwood, was being distributed by Fathom, my first thought was, Uh oh.

This is not a dig at Fathom. It's just that when I think of them, I picture watching Jaws on the big screen, or stuff from the Metropolitan Opera. So, I thought Laika must have had a difficult time finding a distributor with Wildwood. Well, it turns out that Laika chose Fathom specifically so that they wouldn't have to follow the regular Hollywood model.

Which is so Laika, i.e., badass. While Hollywood is veering deeper into AI territory, Laika bucks the trend, sticking to painstaking stop-motion animation. So, even if Wildwood isn’t a massive hit, here's why I'm just happy that it even exists.

When it comes to animation, there are three companies that I put above the rest. First is Studio Ghibli (obviously). Second is Pixar (another obvious choice), and third, well…my third choice might not be so obvious. I think it's because this particular company hasn't experienced the same seismic success as the other two, and that company is, of course, Laika.

While their catalogue might be paltry in comparison to the other two, I think all 5 of Laika's films prior to Wildwood are excellent. In fact, I remember when I first saw Coraline - which is still the company's most profitable movie - in theaters. My wife is a big fan of the book, and when the movie ended, she actually said it was one of the few instances where the movie was better than the book. She attributed this to the stop-motion animation, which she said added an extra layer of creepiness with how inherently jerky the movements are.

I agree. In fact, all of Laika's movies feel enhanced by the stop-motion animation. The Boxtrolls in particular feels like it couldn’t come from any other company. So, whenever a Laika movie comes out, there’s a good chance that I’m going to love it.

Book-to-screen adaptations can be conventional, or they can be something completely different. Take the Harry Potter movies, for instance. Yes, there were details left out of the films, but otherwise, they were pretty much by-the-book (pun not intended) adaptations. Same goes for The Hunger Games movies. If you read the novels, then you got pretty much the same thing with the films.

Wildwood, however, is an unconventional book with an unconventional adaptation. Written by The Decemberists frontman, Colin Meloy, and illustrated by his wife, Carson Ellis, Wildwood is a story where Portland, Oregon is just as important a backdrop as the magical fantasy world that’s presented in the story. The catalyst for the adventure is a child abduction by crows, and it’s a winding tale that gets more intriguing the deeper it goes.

Sure, a movie adaptation COULD have just had traditional animation, or could have even been live-action, but there’s just something special with this particularly unique story - which can be quite scary - being told in Laika’s trademark style. It works.

Lastly, even if Wildwood doesn’t do massive numbers at the box office, can’t we all just be happy that it’s not just some AI slop?

Wildwood is the studio’s longest movie at 132 minutes, as well as the longest stop-motion movie ever made. It also took SIXTEEN FREAKING YEARS TO MAKE! Now THAT’S dedication! The fact that Wildwood even exists seems to be a modern-day miracle, as studios have been gravitating towards more and more AI in their films. I applaud Travis Knight and the whole Laika crew for dedicating their lives to being true to their art form.

So, kudos to Laika and their new movie, Wildwood. Thank you for keeping true art (minus AI) alive.

Rich is a Jersey boy, through and through. He graduated from Rutgers University (Go, R.U.!), and thinks the Garden State is the best state in the country. That said, he’ll take Chicago Deep Dish pizza over a New York slice any day of the week. Don’t hate. When he’s not watching his two kids, he’s usually working on a novel, watching vintage movies, or reading some obscure book.
