#3661. Scott Colom’s Mississippi Votes Are Still Rolling In—and So Are the Views on His Viral Campaign Ads

In an era when short-form-video political messaging reigns supreme, it might be a tiebreaker, and even kingmaker, in Mississippi’s Senate midterm race, where Democratic challenger Scott Colom narrowly leads incumbent Republican senator Cindy Hyde-Smith as ballots continue to be counted on Thursday, November 5.

On October 13, Colom’s campaign released an ad that opens with a clip from a televised February interview featuring Hyde-Smith, a cattle farmer and former agriculture commissioner, responding to a question about rising beef prices by offering that Mississippians “have so many proteins to choose from.” The ad then cuts to a man grilling burgers. “Pick another protein?” he asks. “Sheee-it. I’d rather pick another senator instead.” The ad appears to have been made by content creator Ryan Sayles. Vanity Fair has reached out to Sayles as well as Colom’s campaign for comment.

The message, which highlighted the Colom campaign’s commitment to cost cutting, capitalized on Hyde-Smith’s gaffe to the tune of more than 2.8 million views between X (formerly Twitter), Instagram, and Facebook within the first 36 hours, according to the Clarion-Ledger. Former president Barack Obama’s video endorsement emphasizing Colom’s “Christian faith,” released just a day earlier, earned just over 700,000 views on the platforms in nearly double the time.

Colom currently has the edge in the historically deep-red state: If elected, he would become the first Democratic Mississippi Senator in more than 40 years—as part of the blue wave that swept the 2026 midterms, in which Democrats seized back control of both the House and Senate from MAGA-era Republicans. In Mississippi, which President Trump won by roughly 20 points in 2024, Hyde-Smith was favored to win. That is, until mid-October, when one of Colom’s campaign ads went viral, turning the Southern enclave into a surprise battleground state.

The day before Halloween, Colom made waves when he paid tribute to the Oscar-winning Ryan Coogler film Sinners, casting himself and his twin brother, Andrew, as fictional twins Smoke and Stack Moore, both portrayed by Michael B. Jordan in the movie. The film, which was set in the 1932 Mississippi Delta, follows the Black brothers as they try to keep white vampires away from their juke joint. The ad, titled “Sinators,” and released by Colom on October 30 with the disclaimer that “this is a joke!” shows the two men guarding a door as a blonde woman, who seems to be a proxy for Hyde-Smith, tries to enter. Colom says the duo have to “hold her off until the sun rises on Election Day” in the ad, which garnered more than 380,000 views on X alone prior to the November 3 election, as reported by the Sun Herald. If Colom wins, he would be Mississippi’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era (1865–1877). VF has reached out to Coogler for comment on Colom’s campaign ad.

Colom’s attention-grabbing content hasn’t come without controversy. During the campaign, the candidate was compelled to delete another ad that featured an artificial-intelligence-generated depiction of Hyde-Smith running away from reporters after the state attorney general Lynn Fitch threatened legal action against him. (Fitch, a Republican, helped support Texas’s lawsuit challenging the 2020 election results, and was also counsel for the petitioner on Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the case which ultimately overturned Roe v. Wade.)

Shortly before the release of the Sinners ad, but after the AI dustup, the Senate Majority PAC, the flagship super PAC for Democratic Senate candidates aligned with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, announced it would spend $1.2 million on a broadcast TV and digital ad campaign for Colom. “It is clear Colom is running a competitive race that has put Hyde-Smith on her heels,” Senate Majority PAC spokesperson Lauren French said in a statement to The Hill.

Colom, a local prosecutor, and Hyde-Smith, seeking her second full term in the Senate, had a past connection heading into this political stand-off. Hyde-Smith blocked Colom’s nomination for federal judge in 2023, citing his support for transgender rights and his having previously been boosted by a George Soros–linked PAC, according to the Mississippi Free Press. Colom told ABC News this “has nothing to do with the run for me…. As a Christian, I forgive her. It’s about the people in Mississippi.”

Since Mississippi elections do not have an automatic recount process, the opponents face a potential legal challenge over the results of their Senate race, in which Colom holds a razor-thin lead over Hyde-Smith. Colom later echoed a similar sentiment. “It’s not about me. It’s about the people in Mississippi,” the smiling Colom told reporters while speaking to constituents at a local establishment on Thursday morning. “They decided to go in a new direction.”

Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 launches on November 19. If you're planning to buy the $80 edition but want to upgrade later to the $100 version, you might be interested to know if such a thing is possible.

Thankfully, yes, it is-and it's very easy to do.

Rockstar will offer an "Ultimate Edition Upgrade" for $20, so for anyone who buys the $80 version and decides they do want the additional perks, they can upgrade. This applies to both the digital edition of GTA 6 that you can buy from the Xbox and PlayStation stores, as well the code-in-a-box physical edition.

The $100 Ultimate Edition, which is not sold in stores, includes a lot of extras, including vehicles, weapons, clothing for your in-game characters. The items are "threaded across all aspects of Jason and Lucia's story," Rockstar said, with new items becoming available "behind each chapter." Additionally, people who buy the $100 version get access to in-game businesses that won't be available to everyone else, including a hair salon, a tattoo parlor, a mod shop, and more.

Meanwhile, all preorders for GTA 6 come with the The Vintage Vice City Pack
and one month of GTA+.

In other news, preloading for GTA 6 begins November 10, and that's good news considering the game weighs in at a whopping 212GB. The game officially unlocks at midnight local time, so pack your bags for New Zealand if you want to play it sooner.

Those moviegoers are hoping that Brand New Day's credits scene teased his role in either Avengers: Doomsday or Secret Wars. So the actor will hopefully be returning to his superhero role sooner rather than later.

In the above clip, Holland is joined by costars Jacob Batalon and Zendaya. Zendaya is still not done yet, as she's gearing up for the upcoming release of Denis Villeneuve's Dune: Part Three. #3656. This Autonomous Camera Robot Is My New Best Friend

Like any pure-hearted geek, I've wanted to own a droid ever since I saw Star Wars as a kid. Now, I actually have one: It's Beni, a new gadget from Mondo Robotics, and it has me saying, "Artoo who?" It's not just my Upgrade of the Week; it's possibly the upgrade of my life.

Beni is an all-terrain camera robot that was born as a project on Kickstarter, but unlike so many other Kickstarted projects, it's actually really cool. It takes 4K video while autonomously following its subject wherever they go. If you want to get action footage, there's no need to hassle with a tripod or another person: You can control it with a remote, or you can make it follow you. It can also be set to track you from the side or circle you, and you can adjust what it is doing from the app or remote control on the fly, so with minimal effort, there's no limit to the kind of elaborate shots it can pull off. Plus it's adorable. Just look at this little guy:

Being cute wouldn't matter if Beni was just a gimmick, but the footage it takes is actually really impressive. Check out this clip, which I recorded with no planning of any sort; I just locked Beni's camera on this skater and told it to follow him wherever:

See how smoothly it glides over the uneven concrete? How effortlessly it handles inclines? I even launched it off a huge ramp and it landed on the other side, righted itself, and got back to business.

Here's an example of the kind of footageyou'll get when you put it in "circle you" mode (and again, this was recorded with no prior planning):

The way it just slides under that bench? Come ON. That's just slick.

Yes, Beni is a slightly silly product, but as slightly silly products go, it's pretty inarguably awesome. Here is a short list of things I love about Beni:

It's super easy-to-use. I got it up and running moments after taking it out of the box and downloading the app. You can easily figure out how it works on the fly.

It's a multi-terrain robot. You can get an extra set of bigger, beefier wheels, but even with the stock tires, this thing worked great on uneven concrete, grass, and dirt.

It's rugged. While Beni does have obstacle detection ability, it runs into things a lot anyway, but that's not a problem. Beni can take massive, epic spills, slam into walls, and get kicked by children, and it will right itself and proceed on without a hitch. It's amazing to watch.

It actually works the way you expect it to. I know that's a low bar to clear, but it's rare for a flashy piece of tech to actually do what it says it promises, and Beni does.

It's adorable. A lot of work went into making Beni as friendly-looking as possible—it does tricks, blinks its "eyes," responds to gestures, and you can even give him a little baseball cap. Beni's vibe is positive.

It's great for social interaction. If you have a little robot following you around, people will want to talk to you. I'm not a huge fan of people, but if you want to make friends at the park, this robot will at least open the door.

It's not as expensive as you might imagine. Beni will run you $750 for the base model, and $899 for the "Explore Combo" with larger wheels, a charging stand, and a little hat. While $750 isn't cheap, for what you get, it's actually a pretty solid deal. Everything costs a fortune now anyway! You deserve a robot.

Beni isn't quite ready to make its debut yet. Right now, you can pre-order one on Mondo Robotics site, with a release planned for some time in early November. This is the company's first product, so it's not yet clear if Beni will ever be sold via third-party retailers like Amazon.

#3655. PLL's Lucy Hale and Ian Harding Reveal If They Will Work Together Again

12 Dates of Christmas allowed Lucy Hale and Ian Harding to play love interests again after Pretty Little Liars — but do they have plans to reunite again in the future?

“From your lips to God’s ears. How fun would that be?” Hale, 37, said during an exclusive interview with Us, to which Harding, 40, replied, “What if we just went through every genre?”

The pair suggested a horror movie next where they are a “newly married couple” but one of them “is a ghost.” For Hale, the project didn’t matter as long as she got to share the screen again with Harding.

“Ian actually is the best. I love working with you. I love you as a person,” she told him. “And it was just nice to have all that built in history and something new to do.”

Harding felt the same way, adding, “It was so fantastic. We were kind of remarking on this earlier about how we just stepped back into it. There’s the novelty of a new movie, a new set that you’re on and your very first day. Maybe there’s a little bit of jitters but I felt that way for about seven seconds and then it just was good to be back and getting to play with a dear friend.”

Hale and Harding captured our hearts when they played Aria and Ezra, respectively, in Pretty Little Liars. After the show came to an end in 2017, Hale and Harding weren’t in a rush to find their next collaboration.

“This was our first attempt and our last. No, I’m kidding,” she quipped. “This was our first attempt. Of course we’ve kept in touch here and there. But we live across the country from each other.”

Hale continued: “I just thought he was perfect for this and I was hopeful that he would say yes.”

Harding was thrilled at the prospect of sharing the screen with Hale again, telling Us, “I obviously enjoyed working with Lucy many years ago and I also know the love that people have for that show and perhaps even our dynamic. So I didn’t want to waste it on something ridiculous and so I loved this idea because it kind of plays on certain tropes. I just wanted to really play with her so this gave us the vehicle to do it.”

12 Dates of Christmas follows a woman who has prioritized her work life over her personal life and is persuaded to go on 12 dates in 12 weeks just in time for Christmas. One of the disastrous dates was played by Carter Jenkins, which served as a throwback for Hale after she went out with the actor in real life.

“I’ve known since I was 15. He was actually my first boyfriend. That was my first boyfriend and we’ve been friends ever since,” Hale told Us. “He’s the best. I can’t remember where he took me on a date. I think the date was a movie he was in. And I think we got sushi with his mom after.”

While Hale’s character went on 12 disastrous dates, the actress didn’t pull much inspiration from her life, telling Us, “I’ve been fairly lucky. I never did the dating thing in my 20s. I was always in monogamous relationships. But I did do a fair share of dating a couple of years ago. But I must be very lucky because I don’t have any disastrous dates. Compared to [my character] Christina in [the] movie, nothing too crazy.”

12 Dates of Christmas is streaming now on Hulu.

Shortly after Julian Fellowes' The Gilded Age hit the small screen, it joined the ranks of HBO shows that the world talking. Season 4 of the hit series has officially begun on the network (and streaming with a HBO Max subscription), and one very famous fan of the show is none other than global pop star Taylor Swift. She reportedly themed her wedding to Travis Kelce around the show, and she also does a killer impression of Carrie Coon's Bertha Russell. Luckily Jimmy Fallon finally showed the actress that impression during her recent appearance on The Tonight Show (which streams with a Peacock subscription).

The Gilded Age Season 4 started off with a bang, and I'm so psyched to finally see my first season live after binge-watching the first three. Swift is presumably hyped too, especially because she can whip out her impression of Carrie Coon again. A post shared by The Tonight Show (@fallontonight)

#3653. Inside Ye’s Yeezy Runway Show in Los Angeles After His Antisemitism Scandals

Once I clawed my way through the crowd of leather pilot jackets and passed the overzealous security guards who checked my ticket thrice, I walked through a borehole into the new Yeezy flagship store in Los Angeles’s Koreatown, where Ye stood off in the corner talking to some professional cool kids. Hundreds of people gathered on Wednesday night inside the white, brightly lit, cavernous space connected by tube-like passages for his label’s first runway show in four years. Rappers Big Sean, Kid Cudi, Rich the Kid, and A$AP Nast showed up—so did influencers Quenlin Blackwell and Fai Khadra. The streamer N3on, Ye’s daughter North, and his wife Bianca Censori also attended. And there were hundreds of unticketed fans waiting outside, hoping to get in.

“I’ve been waiting for a Yeezy show for a minute,” Kid Cudi told a camera crew on his way inside. “It’s just beautiful to see my big bro back out there doing his thing.” The musician’s team said he was “on hiatus” when Vanity Fair reached out for comment afterward. A woman standing next to me online started loudly complaining as people tried to cut her. “I just wanna see Ye,” she moaned.

And there were some other attendees who seemed more interested in making their own content. “I’m trying to network,” N3on told his Kick audience on a livestream from the show. “Everyone’s here bro…I’m looking for some collabs.”

The show started with the sound of the first note (E6) of the piano part at the beginning of Ye’s song Runaway. Models marched around a giant mound in the middle of the room in leather trench coats, militaristic jackets, shorts cut like briefs, and monochrome combat uniforms in shades of bone, charcoal, black, and red. Some of the models wore chunky combat boots that rose up the calf; others balanced on thin stilettos, including a pair of knee-high cream boots that looked like they belonged to a space-age dominatrix. It was utilitarian and a bit fetishy. The pacing of the runway walks was relentless, as if Ye was hitting you over the head with this concept until you thought it was cool. After the show, Ye walked out to a standing ovation, wearing an all-black leather outfit, black military boots, and a huge gold tiger-shaped belt buckle.

There is something fascinating about the fact that Ye can still draw adoring crowds like this one in Koreatown, and sell out football stadiums while other artists find themselves on black lists for doing way less (Javier Bardem, for example, claims he’s lost roles and brand endorsement deals because of his opposition to the war in Gaza). Ye’s last major runway show was in October 2022, during Paris Fashion Week, when he sent models down the runway wearing shirts emblazoned with the words “White Lives Matter.” The stunt led to a public confrontation with then Vogue fashion editor Gabriella Karefa-Johnson, whom Ye proceeded to attack online after she criticized the collection (Vogue, like Vanity Fair, is owned by Condé Nast). The whole thing, plus his breakup with Adidas (a brand that was started by two former members of the Nazi party) over a series of antisemitic comments, amounted to a huge fall from grace for someone who once enjoyed the patronage of Anna Wintour and helped reshape the next generation of streetwear.

One reason for Ye’s continued commercial viability is, of course, his artistic prowess. There are certain artists who become too big to fail, not because they’re too wealthy or too powerful, but because their old work has become so deeply embedded in popular culture that people can’t let it go, while their new work continues to push boundaries. That might be the case for Ye—even if this latest show wasn’t particularly groundbreaking or original. If I’m being generous, the new line was giving Boots, the Netflix military dramedy set in the ’90s about a gay marine. But, given what we know about Ye, parts of the show could’ve also been interpreted as skinhead-coded. And it certainly didn’t feel like I experienced a display of genius—a term we need to stop using to describe Ye. He probably doesn’t need us to put him on that pedestal (his ego is big enough), and I remain skeptical that a truly great artist can be capable of spewing so much hate. Art is about empathy.

I suppose most of the people cheering at Wednesday’s show had learned to compartmentalize. They had found a way to separate the designer who completely changed the sneaker game and ushered in a new era in streetwear from the guy who declared his love for Hitler, threatened to go “DEFCON 3” on Jewish people, and released a song called “Heil Hitler.” Or perhaps they really believed the apology Ye published as an advertisement in The Wall Street Journal earlier this year, in which he attributed his antisemitic behavior in part to bipolar disorder and a brain injury. Or maybe the antisemitism never bothered them in the first place.

I was asked to cover this show because I’m based in LA—I’m typically not a style correspondent. But still, I was plenty curious to see what Ye was up to. On the drive over, I thought about the ethics of covering his first big commercial venture since 2022. Maybe I would be giving him exposure he didn’t deserve. Or, maybe my presence amounted to some kind of tacit endorsement. But I dismissed that thought because I knew plenty of Jews who went to Ye’s concert at NRG Stadium in Houston last week, and I didn’t equate their attendance with bigotry. But it raises a lot of interesting questions about the politics of art and fandom. Does going to see the Michael Jackson movie mean you don’t believe the sexual abuse allegations against him? Do I have to forgive Ye’s antisemitism if I want to keep The College Dropout and My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy in my listening rotation? Maybe it’s kind of similar to how carnivores need to be okay with the murder of animals if they’re going to eat meat. I guess I’d have to be willing to forgive Ye in some sense if I plan to keep singing “couldn’t afford a car, so she called her daughter Alexis,” out loud on the StairMaster at Equinox.

Whatever one thinks of Ye personally, his influence on fashion and music is undeniable. The muted colors, exaggerated proportions and futuristic sneakers that helped define Yeezy have spread through the industry. His fingerprints are all over contemporary fashion, including the celebrity brands that followed in his wake. (Cough cough: Skims and SKYLRK).

Wednesday’s show, titled Season 01, was billed as a reset for Yeezy. So, it makes sense that the show took place in something of a primordial cave. But it’s going to be hard for him to ditch some of the baggage he’s accumulated over the last few years. Standing outside the show was a man wearing a navy suit, white shirt, red tie, and Trump ’28 hat—a loud reminder that Ye hobnobbed with white supremacists like Nick Fuentes and ran for president with the far-right conspiratorial political commentator Milo Yiannopoulos as his campaign manager.

Ye perfectly summed up my feelings about him in one of his own songs. “I miss the old Kanye, straight from the Go Kanye.”

#3652. This Pricey New Accessory Gives Your Kindle a Feature That Used to Be Standard

It has been 14 years since Amazon made a Kindle e-reader without a touchscreen, and while I certainly don't miss the days of slowly paging through my e-book library with the arrow keys on my Kindle Keyboard, the move to touch navigation did have one unfortunate result, at least for a small subset of readers: the loss of physical page-turn buttons. Once standard on all Kindles, they eventually became a premium feature available only on the pricey Kindle Oasis, before being dropped from the lineup entirely when that device was retired in 2024.

While this fall's overhaul of the Kindle lineup introduced upgrades like a metal enclosure and a flush-front design, Amazon hasn't exactly reintroduced physical buttons, but the company has launched a new accessory to appeal to the roughly 5% of the market that loves buttons (per Kevin Keith, Amazon's vice president in charge of Kindle), which essentially turns your new Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition into a Kindle Oasis: the Kindle Page-Turn Cover.

Releasing alongside the new flush-front Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition, the Page-Turn Cover is made of plant-based leather (in one of three colors to match your Kindle—Graphite, Fig, or Seaglass Green) with a magnetic front flap, a soft interior, and a right-hand bezel made of lightly textured plastic that houses two thin, elongated buttons. When you slot your compatible Kindle into the case, connecting it magnetically and via the built-in pogo pins, it will automatically pair with the device, allowing you to turn pages with a button press instead of a tap.

By default, the top button will advance you forward by one page, and the bottom button will do the reverse, though you can change which does which in your device settings. While the physical buttons on some Boox and Barnes & Noble Nook devices allow you to map different functions—like skipping an entire chapter or scrubbing through a book quickly—to a long-press or double-tap, as of this writing, the Page-Turn Cover will only let you turn one page at a time. The buttons also only work for turning pages; you'll still navigate your library and the device menus using the touchscreen.

If you're a lefty, or prefer to swap which hand you use to hold your e-reader, you can change up the orientation by turning off Lock Rotation on your device; when you flip it over to hold in your other hand, the text will automatically reorient itself, and the buttons will continue to work with your existing settings.

You might think that changing pages with an accessory would slow down your device, but in my testing, the Page-Turn Cover actually seems to turn pages faster than tapping the touchscreen. Though the new Kindles are quite speedy, there's still a perceptible lag between when you tap the screen and when the display changes to a new page. Not so with the Page-Turn Cover attached; although the very first page turn after attaching it is a bit laggy, after that it is basically instantaneous. I can't imagine this will be a game-changer for anyone—the difference is a mere fraction of a second—but it's worth noting all the same.

While this is Amazon's clever solution to satisfy the physical button die-hards without overhauling the design of its entire lineup, it does come at a cost to the reader—a literal cost: The Page-Turn Cover is around $80, and it's only compatible with the $250 Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition or the $320 Kindle Colorsoft Signature Edition, the only models with the metal backing, pogo pins, and accelerometer necessary for the case to function.

In short, that means if you want a Kindle with physical buttons, you'll have to shell out at least $330, or $80 more than the third-generation Kindle Oasis cost when it launched back in 2019. (For what it's worth, you can get the Oasis-like Boox Go 7, one of my picks for the top non-Kindle e-readers, for around $270).

While most people probably don't think twice about tapping the screen to turn the page, some folks just prefer the feel of tactile buttons or would rather not have to worry about holding their device wrong and accidentally jumping forward a chapter or two.

If you've made do without them so far, you probably aren't missing them, but if you're an old-school e-reader (or just a particularly tactile person), they are definitely a nice bonus. Are they worth an $80 upgrade? That's going to depend on the reader.

#3651. Zac Affleck Admits He ‘Messed Up’ Marriage to ‘Dream Girl’ Jen Amid Divorce

The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives star Zac Affleck is reminiscing on his history with his estranged wife, Jen Affleck, days after she filed for divorce.

“Looking back at these clips hurts so much,” Zac, 30, wrote via TikTok on Friday, November 6, alongside a montage of throwback footage of himself and Jen, 27, throughout their relationship. “I married my dream girl, and I messed it up.”

He continued, “Jen, I’m sorry. I was supposed to protect your heart and I failed. I’m sorry for the way I spoke to you. I’m sorry for dimming your light.”

Jen and Zac, who met on Mormon dating app Mutual, got married in 2019 before welcoming three children together. The now-exes announced in June that they are expecting baby No. 4 — just months before Jen filed for divorce at the beginning of November. (Jen and Zac both state they had been discussing a separation for awhile.)

“I’m sorry I was so young and immature,” Zac continued on Friday. “I’m sorry I couldn’t make the changes I needed to, and I’m sorry I let things get to this point.”

Acknowledging his shortcomings as a husband, Zac further stressed that he hopes they can peacefully coparent their soon-to-be-four kids moving forward.

“I can’t change the past, but I can promise to keep working on myself and do everything I can to be the best father, coparent and friend moving forward,” he stated. “I want to approach this next chapter of life with nothing but love and gratitude for everything we shared. And the beautiful family we created and will continue to raise.”

Zac and Jen had long been candid about their marital struggles ever since Mormon Wives premiered in 2024.

“Jen came to me about a year ago after Dancing with the Stars and told me she was unhappy and wanted a divorce, and I basically begged her to stay,” the DadTok social media personality said in a TikTok video posted earlier this week, referring to Jen’s DWTS season 34 stint. “I told her [I would] work on things, become whatever she needed me to be and, ultimately, we just couldn’t make it work.”

He added at the time, “It sucks because I really do love Jen, and I still love Jen. And yeah, when I first met Jen, she had this light about her, unlike anyone I’ve ever met, and she really does have such a good heart. I will continue to support her and be her biggest fan.”

#3650. Godzilla Minus Zero Shows The Horrifying Aftermath Of A Kaiju Attack Like Never Before

This article contains spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

"Godzilla Minus One" was a revelation — a movie that broke records and made history at the Oscars. Director, writer, and VFX supervisor Takashi Yamazaki didn't reinvent the kaiju wheel the way Hideaki Anno's "Shin Godzilla" did, but he did deliver an incredible updated take on the 1954 original movie for modern audiences. After a decade of American movies that became sillier and sillier, Yamazaki's film felt like a shock to the kaiju system: a Godzilla movie that was scary and treated its titular character like a god. Now, "Godzilla Minus Zero" is bigger and badder, even if it does have a lot of issues.

The film aims higher and dreams bigger, with a sense of scope and scale beyond what we've seen in kaiju movies for years. This movie doesn't need more than two giant monsters, but it still feels bigger than "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" or even "Pacific Rim." The VFX work is breathtaking, and the spectacle worthy of the biggest IMAX screens. Though some of the character work leaves a lot to be desired, the main characters are actually interesting and worth following — especially the scientist with a thirst for revenge against the U.S. for the nuclear attack on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

But arguably the most unexpected yet effective aspect of "Godzilla Minus Zero" is how it works as a direct sequel to "Godzilla Minus One," portraying the wounds both visible and invisible left behind by Godzilla's attack on Tokyo, and the collective grief still felt two years later. More than anything, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has the most harrowing imagery you'll ever find in a Godzilla movie.

Throughout "Godzilla Minus Zero" we see clouds of smoke and some sort of devastation as constant reminders of what Godzilla did. But for Takashi Yamazaki it's not enough just to imply that characters are still struggling with the aftermath of Godzilla's attack on Tokyo; the film also shows it.

At one point, we get a flashback showing the direct aftermath of the attack on Ginza from the previous movie. We see a hospital just overfilled with the stench of death, overrun with the injured and dead, screams of agony drowning out any other sound. That this scene comes after a grisly flashback showing the aftermath of the Hiroshima bombing adds to the parallels Yamazaki is drawing between both cataclysmic events, while also adding a historical weight to the devastation and horror of what a Godzilla attack would mean. It's no wonder "Godzilla Minus Zero" has an R-rating; the imagery of Ginza after Godzilla destroyed it in the last movie, as well as the sight of the devastation King Ghidorah left in Matsumoto City, is absolutely harrowing.

What makes this work so well is that we've never really had a proper Godzilla sequel before — one that really focused on the aftermath of the previous movie's attacks. Every movie essentially resets the action as it prepares for the next kaiju fight. The closest we've had to a reckoning is in "Monarch: Legacy of Monsters," with the focus on Cate Randa's PTSD after witnessing Godzilla attacking San Francisco. This, however, is on a whole other level. Nothing is implied, and the horrors are right there on the screen. We've had many Godzilla movies before, but none have made a kaiju fight look this horrifying.

#3648. These Are the Best Arc Browser Alternatives, Now That It's Shutting Down

Khamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.

Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.

Well, it happened: The Browser Company has finally announced that it will be sunsetting the Arc browser before the end of 2026. The writing has been on the wall for well over a year now: Arc had already been put on ice, receiving only maintenance updates after the Browser Company switched its focus to Dia, an AI browser that shares Arc’s framework but lacks the wonderful interface features that made Arc such a joy to use.

This is sad news for the Arc faithful. If you're one of them, or if you’re looking for an alternative to the regular browsers like Safari and Chrome, all hope is not lost. Export your Arc data, and try out one of these Arc-like alternatives.

Zen has become the de facto option for all users looking to find something that looks and works like Arc. In some ways, it’s better than Arc; in some ways it falls short.

I’ve been using Zen for months, and I’m quite happy with it. The only downside I can see is the Firefox web engine; while Gecko has come a long way, it can still sometimes fall short of Chromium, mostly because Google Chrome is such a popular browser, most websites are designed to run best on it. When I run into an issue with a website, I tend to switch to Chrome for a while. Zen can also sometimes be a memory hog, but once I got better at tab hygiene (automatically closing older tabs and being vigilant about workspace management), the experience got quite a bit better.

And yes, there is extension support: Anything that runs on Firefox will run here too. Firefox has most of the important extensions covered, and it’s the only major browser that still supports the full-scale uBlock Origin ad blocker (which works like a treat in Zen, too).

Alternatively, you can go to the opposite end of the spectrum and try out a maximalist browsing approac:. For a while, Microsoft Edge was the cleaner, faster, better version of Chrome, but now, that title goes to Vivaldi. Under the hood, Vivaldi uses the same Chromium engine that powers Google Chrome, so all your websites will work as expected, and all the extensions will be familiar. But Vivaldi is an extremely customizable browser, and for a certain kind of user, it might be the perfect fit.

There are tons of built-in features. It comes with an ad blocker and integrates with ProtonVPN for free, limited VPN access. You can add a free reader, email accounts, note-taking, and a calendar to the sidebar. Using the Web Panels feature, you can dock any website to the sidebar as well (this works well for media and messaging sites).

Vivaldi also has robust tab management features: You can use two websites in split screen (like with Zen and Arc), and you can organize tabs in workspaces. You can also group related tabs in Tab Stacks, Vivaldi’s unique two-level tab management system. One thing Vivaldi lacks by default is a vertical sidebar, which even Firefox and Chrome now support, though it can be added using a mod.

If you want to keep to a Chromium-based browser, but one that offers all the customization features you can think of, go for Vivaldi. At its core is a powerful, fast, and reliable browser that you can slowly remake to be your own.

Helium: Think of it as a minimalist version of Google Chrome. Same Chromium engine, but no Google tracker, no popups, ads, or extra features.

Dia: If you really want to use something that’s built by the same team as Arc, and don’t mind the AI features, you can try the Dia browser as well. It’s not an exact replacement, but Dia now has an option to use a vertical sidebar and pinned apps.

Quiche: If you were using Arc on iPhone or iPad, try using the Quiche browser, which is our favorite browser for the iPhone. It’s a tastefully designed independent browser, with a fully customizable layout.

#3647. Why Prince William Briefly Split From Kate Middleton, Photographer Reveals

Prince William had his reasons for breaking up with now-wife Princess Kate Middleton before he popped the question.

“When they got engaged, there was a couple of us invited in to meet Catherine,” royal photographer Arthur Edwards said on the Friday, November 6, episode of Hello’s “Right Royal” podcast. “I asked him, ‘What did you break up for?’ He said, ‘Because I wanted to be sure. Because I want this marriage to last forever.’ I think it will.”

William and Kate, both 44, met while in college at University of St Andrews in Scotland. After several years of dating, they briefly went their separate ways. The Prince and Princess of Wales ultimately reconciled before William proposed in 2010 with late mother Princess Diana’s sapphire-and-diamond engagement ring. (Diana died in a fatal car crash in 1997, years after her divorce from now-King Charles III.)

“I spotted Diana’s ring and I said, ‘I need to get a picture of that.’ They called me out afterwards, and I went in the room to photograph it,” Edwards, 86, recalled of William and Kate’s engagement photocall. “Her hand was shaking with nerves! I said, ‘Oh, hang on, hold it steady, just till I get the ring sharp.’ Anyway, it was good.”

He continued, “I wished them all the best, and they were incredibly happy. Every time I see them now, they are a good team.”

William and Kate got married the next year in a 2011 royal wedding ceremony held at London’s Westminster Abbey. They have since expanded their family, welcoming sons Prince George, 13, and Prince Louis, 7, as well as daughter Princess Charlotte, 11.

William and Kate’s marriage, however, went through trying times in 2024 when the princess was diagnosed with an undisclosed form of cancer. (Kate revealed in January 2025 that she was now in remission after undergoing chemotherapy.)

“She’s an amazing mum, an amazing wife and, literally, our family couldn’t cope without her,” William said on the U.K.’s Heart Radio in May. “She’s been absolutely stunning, brilliant.”

At the time, William gushed that he was “so proud” of how effortlessly his wife had appeared to return to her regal duties in recovery.

“She’s been amazing. She’s been through so much in the last couple of years, particularly,” he noted. “And yeah, she’d been looking forward to the Italian trip a lot. I’m really glad it went really well. … She spends, God knows how much time now, looking through all the paperwork. She’s a proper pro on [her patronage for] early years. Most evenings I’m fighting to get past in the bedroom, what paperwork that she’s got lined up, ready to read. I’m so pleased it went well for her, and yeah, I think she came back buzzing.”

#3646. Carrie Coon on ‘The Gilded Age’, ‘The Liberation’, and Parenting

Carrie Coon and I are supposed to be talking about her new film, The Liberation—a gripping drama about a suburban mother who leaves her family to join an all-woman cult in the 1980s. But when we meet for tea at the London West Hollywood hotel, it doesn’t take long for our conversation to turn to general doom and gloom. Between the moment I order a custom-made ginger tea—which I’m now calling “the Carrie Coon special”—and when it arrives at our table, we’ve already started talking about fascism in America, how hard it is for an actor to find enough work to earn health insurance, global warming, and the devastating fires in Los Angeles.

“I don’t do small talk anymore. I’m not good at it,” says Coon, taking a sip from her own ginger tea—a blend she started having this restaurant make for her after getting hooked on it while filming The White Lotus in Thailand. “I’m just like, ‘So we’re all going to die. How you feeling about that?’”

But even when she’s talking fire and brimstone, Coon’s charming warmth keeps the conversation from being too dark and stormy. If Coon were leading a cult, I might join. She’s funny and empathetic; she makes this sweet, quick “aww” sound if you compliment her or share something she’s sympathetic with. Maybe Coon, who was raised in Ohio, simply can’t shed her Midwestern sensibility, even though she transforms onscreen into characters with much harder, and sometimes pricklier, outer shells. Coon has earned four Emmy nominations for playing the stubborn small-town cop Gloria Burgle in Fargo, the lonely lawyer Laurie Duffy in The White Lotus, and twice for the ambitious social climber Bertha Russell on The Gilded Age, which just debuted its fourth season on HBO.

Carrie Coon and Morgan Spector in season 2 of The Gilded Age.

She reveals a different side of herself in The Liberation, Guy Nattiv’s drama that opens in limited (and Oscar-qualifying) release November 6 before going wide January 8. Her character, Rita Cooper, is a Holocaust survivor whose trauma and stagnation in her family life cause her to abandon her husband (Tracy Letts, Coon’s real-life husband) and two daughters (Bella Ramsey and Odessa Young) for an all-female spiritual group led by a charismatic leader named Ricki (Lily James).

The film is a strong showcase for Coon as she transforms both physically and emotionally. When Rita joins the commune, she loses weight and her identity as she falls further under Ricki’s spell. “People are struck by me playing someone who feels weaker or more frail, because I’m often put into roles where I’m strong, verbal, intellectual, brassy,” says Coon. “I think it’s unusual for them to see that level of vulnerability in my performances. But of course, I think of myself as capable of all that.”

I nervously admit to Coon that when I watched The Liberation, I was troubled to find that, as a mother of two young kids, I could understand Rita’s choice—to leave behind all the demands and burdens of family and household, to run to a place where you could focus solely on yourself. It’s hard to say this out loud.

Coon makes that sympathetic “aww” sound. “We all have that moment. It’s a fantasy, but haven’t we all thought, ‘I could leave right now; what would happen if I just didn’t come back?’” she says. “That’s why I found her so compelling, because she walked away from her family and chose to invest in her self-actualization and her healing in the ’80s. It’s a really risky choice, but, I suppose, just undeniable for her.”

Coon and Letts, who married in 2013—in a hospital where Letts had just received emergency gallbladder surgery—have two kids together who are now five and eight years old, just a few years ahead of my own. Juggling life as a working mother can be challenging, especially in invisible ways. “I think a lot of the cognitive load is so heavy, and people don’t really understand,” says Coon.

Carrie Coon, Leslie Bibb, and Michelle Monaghan in The White Lotus.

When Coon was cast in the third season of HBO’s hit The White Lotus, playing a woman who goes on a luxury vacation with her two longtime best friends, she was gone for a total of 10 weeks. At the time, her daughter was only three. “That was very hard, and that was a very difficult decision,” she says. “I’m not sure it was a great decision, ultimately. I don’t know if we would do it again the same way.”

She’s had other moments of feeling spread too thin, especially just before she went to film His Three Daughters—the 2023 movie that cast Coon, Natasha Lyonne, and Elizabeth Olsen as three sisters who reunite to care for their ailing father. “I turned to Tracy and said, ‘I can’t do this anymore. I can’t do both things,’” she remembers. Maybe as her kids get older— “little kids, little problems, big kids, big problems,” she says—she will actually have to shift her focus. “In this world where we have no schema to navigate the challenges they’re facing, I would have to take a step back again and be with them,” she says. “I don’t know. It’s hard to say.”

Elizabeth Olsen and Carrie Coon in His Three Daughters.

Coon and Letts’s kids joined them for part of the time while they filmed The Liberation in Vancouver. During the first half of the movie, Coon wore hip pads and other body-shaping additions to make Rita seem more weighed down by her responsibility and the trauma of having been a child in a concentration camp. Coon says she could also lean into the exhaustion she already felt: “We were co-sleeping in a little apartment, and it was not easy,” she says. “And so I was like, ‘Great, I don’t have to look like anything. I could just be tired.’ So I kind of allowed that exhaustion I normally feel, which I try to overcome in my daily life, just to creep in more.”

When Rita leaves her family for the isolated commune, Coon’s environment also shifted: She moved to a new filming location, and her family left town. In the mornings, she’d swim or stretch. She’d also lost 10 pounds and shorn her hair for the role, transforming from Rita into Naya—the new name Ricki gives her character, a common practice in cults. “Carrie’s a very, very strong, physical actress,” says Nattiv. “Rita is the matriarch of her family. She’s a strong woman, intelligent—and then she’s not. She loses everything. It was amazing to see how she shifts between Naya and Rita.”

Nattiv based The Liberation on his grandmother Rita—who really had been in a concentration camp as a child, and joined a commune in her adult life. Rita had given testimony to Yad Vashem, the World Holocaust Remembrance Center; Coon watched it as she prepared to play the role. She also watched and listened to hours of testimonies of women who had been in concentration camps in Poland, learning “the sort of very specific way that particular trauma is held in the body, the challenge of speaking the unspeakable.”

I wondered if watching so many hours of these stories, so much horror and pain, was difficult. “Well, if I’m really honest, I found that I was drawn to listening to them instead of the news,” says Coon. “I started listening to them as a comfort, because they were a story of resilience. Thinking about the unspeakable atrocities that were happening around me in my very own country with my own tax dollars—and yet here are people on the other side of something like that, articulating those stories and what they learned.”

The present political climate is ever-present in Coon’s mind, as well as on her social media accounts. (A few of her more recent X posts: “Failed president,” “Close the camps,” “The president has nothing but ‘tranny’ jokes. How pathetic. How empty.”) For the past few weeks, she’s been encouraging people to vote, especially her fellow Ohioans. As she admitted, she’s not one for small talk.

Carrie Coon (center) with Odessa Young, Bella Ramsey, Sharon Taylor, and Tracy Letts in The Liberation.

“It’s absurd. It’s untenable,” she says. “We’re in a really precarious moment because people’s lives are untenable all across the board.” She recognizes her own privilege—that she and her husband are both able to work, that they can afford childcare—but says she’s worried for actors who can’t find roles in this shrinking economy. “Even just the labor of making tapes, the free labor, there’s no protection,” she says. “We have these rules in our union, but no one’s really following those rules. What young actor is going to make that phone call and complain?”

She’s also noticing how few female-centered films get told on the biggest stages, with the biggest budgets. “What happens when you’re living in an authoritarian regime is everybody gets scared, and everybody gets safe, and everyone’s making really safe choices. It’s not what people want,” she says. “Women are tremendous economic drivers in this economy, and we still aren’t making art for them.”

Coon will do her part, with films like The Liberation. She’s wrapped work on another independent movie, Honeymoon/Funeral, a romantic comedy from Fresh Off the Boat creator Nahnatchka Khan that also stars Rebecca Ferguson and Greta Lee. Next year, Letts heads to London from April through October to do Death of a Salesman at The National, which means more maneuvering for their family unit. “We’re thrilled for him. And yet that’s going to be a really interesting time for our family,” she says. “So I don’t have as much work lined up, and I’m okay to be patient. I feel good about being patient right now.”

But she does have one wish for the future: She’d like to do a comedy. “No one’s letting me do that. My family is surprised by my career because it’s just not the way I occurred to them as a person at all. People are expecting to meet a very serious and lugubrious actress that needs a lot of special drinks or something,” she says. While taking another sip from her custom, off-menu ginger tea.

#3645. The Newest Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition Is Finally Worth the Extra Money

I love e-readers, but I'd be the first to admit that as far as the general public is concerned, they are just about the least exciting tech devices around—and that goes double for the Amazon Kindle. Any attention the space has gotten over the past couple of years has involved obscure players like Boox and weird concepts like the phone-shaped Palma or the tiny Boox Picco. But the clear leader in terms of market share is still Amazon, and despite some minor innovations over the years, the device hasn't received an essential upgrade in around a decade: A Kindle is a Kindle is a Kindle.

I'd still say this holds true in 2026, even after the company unveiled a complete redesign of the Kindle lineup (this, a few months after significantly raising prices across all of the devices). While the new flush-front display is nice-looking (and Amazon is quite proud of the new process it has developed to add colored bezels by painting them directly onto the outer glass screen), competitors have offered similar designs for years, and it's hard to get too excited about "innovations" like an $80 case that adds back the physical buttons that used to be built in or finally opening up the firmware to allow for the use of a Bluetooth page-turn remote.

But one thing has changed about the 2026 Kindle lineup: I think the $50 premium Amazon charges for the top-of-the-line Signature Editions of the Paperwhite and Colorsoft is finally truly justified.

Amazon introduced the first "Signature Edition" of the Kindle Paperwhite back in 2021, and while the 25% price increase didn't get you nothing, the features it did add weren't too exciting: At 32GB, it had three times the storage versus the standard Paperwhite, but how important is a ton of storage when most e-book files are tiny? (That's still enough room for more than 6,000 texts, well more than even true bookworms will read in an entire lifetime.) Other bonuses, like wireless charging and an auto-adjusting front light, won't matter at all to a huge subset of readers, and it's hard to think of "no ads on the lock screen" as an extra perk.

But the latest Signature Editions of the Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft actually give you more for the price premium, and for the first time, I would recommend shelling out the extra cash. While the important specs are still the same as the standard model:

7-inch, 300ppi flush-front display (with color content on the Colorsoft maxing out at 150ppi)

USB-C charging with battery life "up to 12 weeks on a single charge," per Amazon

Bluetooth support for wireless headphones

...the Signature Editions give you quite a bit more this time around, including, most noticeably, a totally new design with an all-metal rear panel that gives the devices a much sleeker look and feel without adding much in the way of weight (the standard plastic models weigh around 7.2 ounces, while the Signature Editions weigh 8.1 ounces). The new design makes the Signature Editions feel truly premium.

But that's not the only meaningful addition. Once again, alongside wireless charging and automatically adjusting lighting, the Signature Editions have a boosted 32GB of storage, which is still probably overkill, but worthwhile if you like to load your device with a bunch of audiobooks or (in the case of the Colorsoft) color comics.

You also get an accelerometer, which means the display will auto-rotate if you flip it upside down, giving you more flexibility in how you hold it (especially if you're springing for the new Page-Turn Cover, which brings back physical buttons à la the beloved, discontinued Kindle Oasis). Moreover, there's a new ability to turn pages by double-tapping on the bottom sides or back of the device rather than touching the screen (though it only works for moving forward in your book).

Speaking of which, you'll need to go for the Signature Editions if you want to use accessories like the Page-Turn Cover or the also-new Charging Stand (not yet available for pre-order), as only the Signature Editions include the built-in magnetic pogo pins you'll need to connect them. (If you're interested in the Kindle Click page-turn remote, it at least works with any Kindle from 2024 or later.)

Finally, if you care about your Kindle looking pretty, it's worth noting that only the Signature Editions are available in Seaglass Green (for the Paperwhite) and the reddish-purple Plum (for the Colorsoft).

Outside of those extras, the 2026 Kindles don't feel much different than the 2024 models. According to Amazon, they are the fastest Kindles ever, but that's mostly hype—any recent Kindle will turn pages quickly enough that you'll barely notice the speed difference, if you notice it at all. They all still run on the same firmware, which is both a good thing (Amazon makes it extremely easy to browse for and buy books and audiobooks directly on the device; there are a ton of options to search through and sort your library; and quality-of-life features like being able to sideload books via email using the "Send to Kindle" feature are a godsend) and a bad thing (I hope you like being locked into the Amazon ecosystem).

One change to the entire 2026 Kindle lineup is already proving divisive: Judging by reactions on the Kindle Reddit, not everyone is in love with the new flush-front design, which eliminates the raised bezels around the screen that were present on the 2024 model, but at the cost of adding a thin layer of glass over the e-ink display.Depending on how picky you are, you may find fault with this setup, as the additional layer of glass slightly reduces text clarity by putting more distance and another barrier between your eyes and the text or images in your book. Is this something I noticed myself? No—I don't have an older Kindle to make a direct comparison, and the text is still much, much sharper (and the front lighting more even) than what I see on competing e-readers like the Boox Go 6 or the Xteink X4 Pro. But there is a contingent of readers already lamenting the change, so take that for what you will.

The question to consider whenever a new device model rolls around is simple: Is this worth the upgrade? If you have a working Kindle from any time after the introduction of temperature-adjustable lighting, I would say no—the 2026 models are nicer, but they still don't do anything to make them worth it, especially at the new higher price points. That said, if you are in the market for a new Kindle, I'd suggest opting for the Paperwhite over the entry-level model, which has a smaller screen and lacks the warm light option—and if you're getting a Paperwhite or Colorsoft, you might as well pay the premium for the Signature Edition, because it's finally worth the extra money.

Just when you thought you'd escaped the troubled town of Hawkins, the Upside Down is reaching out its tendrils to pull you back in. Netflix has announced a spin-off prequel series called "Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure" that will be set in the 1950s, before the events of both the main show and the stage play "Stranger Things: The First Shadow." It will premiere in 2028.

Per Netflix, the series hails from the Duffer Brothers and "Stranger Things" writer Kate Trefry. "We've been dreaming of 'Other Worlds: A Stranger Things Adventure' for many years now, and to see it become a reality is surreal and exhilarating," Matt and Ross Duffer said in a statement. "It's 'Stranger Things,' but also thrillingly fresh, with a new setting, new heroes and villains, and new ... actually, we're not allowed to say any more. Now, on to casting. In the meantime — watch the skies, nerds!"

Kate Trefry will serve as showrunner, co-creator, and writer, while "Pride & Prejudice" filmmaker Joe Wright will direct the first three episodes. "[W]e have had the time of our lives returning to all the horror, wonder and mystery of the flagship, while also telling a wholly new story, one we hope will blow your minds and break your hearts all over again. There are so many more mysteries to explore. Welcome to Other Worlds," Trefry said.

This was inevitable. "Stranger Things" is one of the biggest hits in Netflix history, and it's spawned a merchandising bonanza for the streamer. While the main series has ended (and it ended on a bit of a frustrating note), an animated show, "Stranger Things: Tales From '85," already exists, not to mention the aforementioned stage show "Stranger Things: The First Shadow."

In theory, Netflix could keep things going forever with this approach. Since it's established that creepy stuff has happened in Hawkins for seemingly decades, the franchise could jump around in time. Hell, we could even get a modern-day "Stranger Things" series where those darn kids watch that darn TikTok all day. Talk about scary!

As someone who lives in Los Angeles, I get that Universal Studios Hollywood is a very different theme park than Universal Orlando Resort. I mean, we’ve only officially had our very first outdoor roller coaster with Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift for about two months now. Regardless, as a local who lives within 15 minutes of the theme park on the hill, I actually think the perks you get with the upper tier annual passes are stellar, and I think a lot of theme park fans are sleeping on this.

Like any theme park, there are options when it comes to choosing an annual pass for USH. At the time that I bought one for myself, I decided to splurge on the highest tier available in December 2025. While that other theme park in Orange County that’s also known as the Happiest Place on Earth kept raising prices and cutting back on perks and left me in a position where it made more financial sense for me to just pay for a ticket when I could make a day of it, Universal Studios Hollywood gave me more than enough incentives to welcome me in as an annual passholder.

First of all, I spent time doing all the calculations to see what the best value would be for what you get and whether I thought I would go enough times to make it worth the money. Ultimately, I decided to go all in on the Platinum Annual Pass for $599.95.

Sure, that’s a chunk of funds, but when you consider there are no blackout dates over the 15-month period (the 12-month pass was offering a bonus three months at the time of purchase), free general parking (with minor restrictions), Universal Express after 3 p.m., a complimentary general admission Halloween Horror Nights ticket (so you don't have to miss the great haunted houses), invitations to special events, and 15% off food and merchandise, it’s an amazing deal that I’ve made extensive use of.

Every time I’ve gone to USH this year, it’s been great not to have to worry about checking blackout days. I can go on a whim if I so chose; I don't have to make a full day of it. The best part and biggest value really has been the Universal Express perk. For me, I’m good with going a bit later in the day so that I don’t have to hassle with waiting in line for more than a few minutes, and it’s nice not to have to pay for parking. It all feels very easy, whether I go for a couple hours or spend a good portion of my day there.

As it gets closer to the March 2027 expiration date for my Platinum Annual Pass, I was definitely leaning towards renewing. It’s actually the most positive I’ve felt about any theme park annual pass I’ve ever had. Then this week, Universal actually decided to sweeten the deal. They upped their Annual Pass game even further by adding a brand-new Diamond Annual Pass. Now, not only do you get all the benefits that come with Platinum, but Universal Express works from park opening, you get a complimentary general admission ticket for Universal Fan Fest Nights, the discount is raised to 20%, and best of all, you get a complimentary VIP Experience ticket.

Yes, $999.95 is a large chunk of money and is an upgrade, and I totally get it will take a bit of thought. While it takes six visits to the theme park to justify the cost of a Platinum Annual Pass, it takes about 10 visits with a Diamond. But if you’ve never gotten to be a VIP at USH (which I’ve only done in Orlando as part of a media trip), it comes with Unlimited Express, a guided tour, a special meal, and valet parking, which would normally run you anywhere from $359.95 to $519.95 just on its own.

I understand that a lot of the theme park annual pass conversation in Southern California tends to revolve around the Disneyland Resort, but whether you’re feeling priced out there, you want to add something additional, or you are just looking for something different, you shouldn’t sleep on what Universal Studios Hollywood has to offer.

From the iconic Backlot Tour to the amazing Universal Studios rides that everybody should experience at least once, USH does have a lot to offer. Whether I stick with my Platinum status or move up to Diamond is still undecided, but if you’re a theme park fan, you definitely shouldn’t sleep on this, or at least checking it out.

#3641. Inside PS, The Private Members-Only Terminals at LAX, Miami, and Paris Airports

There are 10 terminals at the Los Angeles International Airport. One through nine are for the general public: terminal one for Southwest, terminal two for Virgin Atlantic, the international hub in the numberless terminal B. Each one is packed with weary, edgy travelers lined up for security, coffee, or a meal. You arrive at your terminal via rideshare and depart via rideshare—so long as your ride is a premium black car. If it isn’t, you must take a 20-minute bus ride to a parking lot called “LAX-it,” where you wait amongst the hordes for your UberX to arrive as it slowly inches through crippling traffic.

The 10th terminal promises to deliver you from this misery. It’s around the back of the airport complex, off the 105 in El Segundo, next to several cargo holds and a Gate Gourmet facility where airplane meals are carted off to various jets on the tarmac. When you arrive, no one asks for a boarding pass. A security guard checks your name off a list, and a valet whisks away your bags with care before you’re ushered into your own private suite with amenities galore: squishy velvet couches and boucle chairs, Assouline coffee table books, free iPhone chargers, and chocolate-covered almonds and gummy bears. A fridge comes with sparkling waters and canned matcha drinks—a far cry from the plastic Dasani bottles found at Hudson News. A private bathroom boasts Le Labo soaps.

While you’re waiting for your flight, you can get a manicure, a table massage, or even a haircut. You can request a pair of Normatec Elite compression boots (retail price: $1,099) to help with your circulation before takeoff. Or if you are feeling more social, you can head to “the Salon,” where abstract art hangs on the wall and chandeliers dangle from the ceiling. Order the coconut chia pudding or bagel-and-lox platter if you’re there for breakfast, duck confit agnolotti or a Mediterranean chicken panini on house-made ciabatta for lunch. For dinner, there’s a New York strip, and caviar service is always available.

When it’s time to go, you’ll pass through a private security check with a dedicated TSA agent. Then you’ll climb in a BMW (suitcases already loaded) which drives you across the tarmac directly to your plane. Forget boarding with Zone 8 or gatechecking your carry-on.

The Salon at PS at LAX, designed by Elle Decor A-List interior designer Cliff Fong.

This is PS at LAX—a private, members only terminal at Los Angeles International. It’ll cost you to get in: One-time access to the Salon (and nothing else) without a membership is priced at $1,295. For frequent fliers, an annual baseline membership starts at $1,250 and goes up to $4,850. Private suites cost an additional $3,650 or $4,950 for four people, depending on the type of membership.

Unsurprisingly, it’s become a see-and-don’t-be-seen hub for LA celebrities wary of attracting the camera-wielding masses at commercial airports (and the paparazzi that stake out the terminal). Gigi Hadid, Gabrielle Union, Hailey Bieber, Jamie Foxx, and Kourtney Kardashian are just some of the famous faces that are known to frequent PS at LAX.

But this year, PS is pushing beyond the Hollywood stars eager to escape the clutches of Deuxmoi. In the past six months, the firm has opened private terminals in Miami (taking over the historic Pan-Am space) and Dallas. Paris is coming in early 2027. The seclusion, the gourmet food, and the luxurious interiors (curated by Elle Decor A-List designers Jean Liu for Dallas and Cliff Fong for Miami and LA) are all nice draws, but there's another reason PS CEO Amina Belouizdad Porter cites for why customers are willing to shell out thousands of dollars on top of a first-class ticket.

The Atlanta airport on March 23, 2026. Government shutdowns have caused disastrous scenes at American commercial terminals.

Because, well, it has been. The last fiscal year has seen three government shutdowns, the longest of which lasted for 76 days. TSA Deputy Administrator Ha Nguyen McNeill told Congress that the agency experienced the longest security wait times in its 24-year history during the shutdown that stretched from February 14 to April 30, 2026. Some airports, including Atlanta, had lines up to five hours long. The logistical meltdowns hit at a time when air travel has never been more popular: In 2025, nearly 907 million people flew commercially in the United States. Belouizdad Porter says that those disruptions led to a direct increase in PS customers.

The growing crowds at airport lounges also nudged some travelers over the edge. Credit card companies long ago realized that offering lounge access enticed new customers, with Chase, American Express, Citi, Capital One, and more getting in the game. But demand exceeded square footage, and many of those lounges suffered from overcrowding and subpar service, selling the dream of an aero oasis that never was.

“There have never been more airport lounges,” David Mack writes in the New York Times, “Yet there also have never seemed to be more lounges that are not worth the hassle…Sometimes the lines for the lounges are the longest in the airport.”

(Though the only thing worse than an overcrowded airport lounge might be getting stranded outside. Reddit is currently up in arms about the obscene food prices at the newly renovated Burbank Airport in California—price tag: $1.3 billion—where a cheese and bean burrito costs $25.)

Another contributing factor? The rising costs of private jets. While the terms “one percent” or “.1 percent” are often thrown around when it comes to PJ owners, the reality is only 0.003 percent of America’s population can afford even fractional ownership. Demand for private aircraft surged after the pandemic, raising prices, and now the average net worth of those who own a jet is $190 million. For those with fractional ownership, it’s $140 million. Yet there are still plenty of mere decamillionaires looking to dodge the misery of the airport. As Sartre put it: Hell is other people.

Previously, “You could either fly round-trip first class for $6,000 but deal with the airport, the friction, and the crowd,” Belouizdad Porter says. “Or you could fly private round-trip and it's $200,000.” PS operates somewhere in between. “I think there’s a real appetite for that middle ground: the convenience of private aviation without the commitment or expense of chartering an entire plane,” says Lucie Kittel, founder of luxury travel advisory firm Domino Travel.

And besides, even if you do reach the level of private jet ownership, you still can’t always avoid the flying masses. A midsize jet that fits six to nine people costs between $10 and $20 million dollars and can fly 2,000 to 3,000 nautical miles. If it’s on the shorter end of that range, it can just make a trip from New York to California—but not to Europe. There’s also the issue of safety: The country is currently facing a pilot shortage, and more experienced candidates often work with mainstream airlines who can provide higher salaries. Larger planes can also better navigate rough weather.

Carriers like United and Delta know all of this, which is why they’re beefing up their luxury experiences. Delta recently announced it was investing over $1 billion in retrofitting its premium cabins, and new Delta One Terminals at JFK and LAX allow first-class ticket holders to avoid overcrowded TSA lines and the standard lounge. “Most of my clients flying out of JFK are choosing Delta One,” Kittel adds, “and they love the experience.”

Thanks to the artificial intelligence boom—the latest phase of a 15-year bull market for stocks—there’s been an explosion of multi-multi-millionaires in America. While not all of them can fly private, they certainly can devote large sums of money to separating themselves from the hoi polloi. Both startups like PS and established players are now competing for that sub-ultra-wealthy dollar.

#3640. Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir Knows How To Get Star Trek Back On Track [Exclusive]

Andy Weir, the author of the hit novels "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary," has seen the state of modern "Star Trek" and feels he knows how to fix it. In brief, he wants to get back to basics. In a new interview with /Film's Jeremy Mathai, Weir said he feels that the franchise should focus on making a TV series — not a movie — about a Starfleet vessel on a simple mission of exploration into deep space. No bells and whistles, no gimmicks. Just plain, baseline "Trek."

What does Weir mean by getting "Star Trek" back on track? Well, the franchise has experienced a lot of ups and downs throughout its 60-year history, and we're at a point where, many might agree, "Star Trek" became a little too ambitious for its own good. Starting in 2017, "Star Trek" churned out eight (!) original shows (nine, if you count "Very Short Treks"), and one TV movie. The two current Trek shows — "Strange New Worlds" and "Starfleet Academy" — will run their course next year. There are currently no new "Star Trek" shows in active production.

The franchise had an excellent run from 1987 through 2005 (the beginning of "Star Trek: The Next Generation" through the end of "Star Trek: Enterprise"), but by the end of that era, the saga had kind of petered out, and audiences had lost interest. "Star Trek" experienced a resurgence in 2009 with J.J. Abrams' reboot movie, and that carried through two hit sequels. That era, however, could never get its feet underneath it for a fourth movie, and that, too, petered out. Now the Paramount+ era is petering out as well.

Andy Weir thinks a single show about exploration might be the way forward.

In his interview with /Film, Andy Weir rightfully pointed out that "Star Trek" has always functioned best when it is a weekly, episodic TV series about varied adventures throughout the galaxy. Weir feels that making a new movie at this point would be unwise. He also notes that this proposed new series wouldn't have to rely on nostalgia, existing characters, or the USS Enterprise. To quote:

"[I]f I was the boss of 'Trek' [...], I would try to establish ... You've got to make a show, a series. I personally wouldn't try to go straight to films. I would go back to a series, a streaming show maybe that's just called 'Star Trek,' and then work from there. It doesn't have to be about the Enterprise. 'Star Trek' is a rich genre that has lots and lots of cool stuff in it. It could have that same feel. It could be about a different ship exploring strange new worlds and new civilizations."

Weir pointed out that "Star Trek" follows a specific DNA, which is, in his words, "this is a spaceship that goes out, finds new things, and has adventures." For him, "Star Trek" shouldn't aim higher than that, especially not after a decade of streaming shows that reached in all directions at once. The Paramount+ era has seen many shows taking place across the timeline of "Star Trek," with some being episodic and some being serialized. Some contain R-rated levels of violence, while others are aimed at toddlers. It's all too much.

Of course, the idea of a "Star Trek" series about a single starship, not the Enterprise, going on weekly adventures in deep space was the premise of 1995's "Star Trek: Voyager." Weir feels, though, that "Voyager" was not exactly what he means. He also thought that its immediate predecessor, "Star Trek: Deep Space Nine," while amazing, wasn't quite the "Star Trek" of a generation previous. Weir said that the original 1966 "Star Trek" made use of the franchise's DNA, as did "Next Generation," but after that, each show became a departure from the desired norm. He said:

"'Voyager' departed from it a little too much. People didn't like it. 'Deep Space Nine' had its own completely cool story. It was more of a political thriller, and they got away with it, but they didn't try to be 'Star Trek' with a slight twist. They're like, 'We're "Babylon 5." We're doing our own thing. We're doing it in the Star Trek universe, but we're doing our own thing.' So that's what I would do with Star Trek, is go back to the basics, go back to a ship exploring the cosmos."

"Babylon 5" is another sci-fi series, contemporaneous with "Deep Space Nine," that was also set on board a space station and that involved a lot of political intrigue. /Film loves "Deep Space Nine," but some people, like Weir, argue that it wasn't quite true to the Trek spirit. There wasn't enough trekking for his taste, one might suppose. But if the franchise did some simple star trekking, Weir would be happy.

With a new film in development, the folks in charge seem to be taking a different approach.

#3639. Five Hacks Every Wordle Player Should Know

Wordle’s biggest draw is its simplicity: Anybody can look at five blank spaces and think of a five-letter word. But when it comes to playing Wordle well, and enjoying the game over time, you might do better with a few tips. I have a nearly 100% win rate in Wordle—more about win rates below—so here are some of mine.

If I could only give one strategy tip, it would be this: Your first guess, and even your second and third, shouldn’t be attempts to solve the puzzle. Instead, you should be gathering information about possible solutions.

This means that if you guessed a word ending in “ER” and those letters turned green, you should not try another word ending in ER as your next guess. If you guess a completely different five-letter word, say BENCH, you can find out whether B, N, C, and H are in the solution, while also getting information about whether there’s an E in the second position (which helps you know whether words like LEVER and METER might be in play).

There is a toggle in the game interface that requires every word to use green squares from your previous guesses. It’s called “hard mode.” If you ask me, this should be called “luck mode,” because it takes away one of the game’s best strategies for smart solvers, as guessing letters you already know is just wasting guesses.

I wrote more about this strategy here, and included more examples. Use this tip, and you’ll avoid the trap of losing after guessing FOUND, ROUND, POUND, MOUND, SOUND, and WOUND when you could have used MARSH as your second guess and instantly figured out the answer (HOUND).

There are competing schools of thought on choosing the best starting word for Wordle, an issue I have considered in depth. But to summarize the best advice: Choose a word with five different letters (no repeats) that includes at least two or three of the English language’s most common consonants.

Those most common consonants include T, N, S, H, R, D, L, and C. That means TRASH is a great starter, and so are CRANE and STEAL and STARE. For best results, use E and/or A as your vowels, since these are some of the most common vowels in English.

A starting word needs to give you information about what might be in the solution, but you don’t gain a ton of information with just five letters. So I recommend having another starting word that doesn’t overlap with the first, but expands the amount of information you can collect to 10 total data points.

After all these years, my trusty pair is still ARISE and TOUCH. That gives me all five vowels and a good sampling of the most common consonants, as discussed above. (Only N is notably missing, but I can always play that in a later guess.)

Feel free to come up with your own pair, where the second guess fills in gaps left by the first. If you like to start with a vowel-heavy word like ADIEU, use more consonants in your second move: perhaps THORN. Or if you start with TRASH, perhaps follow it with OUNCE.

I pride myself on my 100% Wordle win rate, but the truth is, I’m actually at 99% right now. The NYT’s “About Wordle” page says that “Win % counts the percentage of total puzzles played that you have won,”  but that doesn’t seem to be entirely correct. It also does not say how the app handles rounding. I believe I’ve lost three times over the 1,368 games I’ve played, which is actually a 99.8% win rate. But after every loss, the count has eventually gotten back up to 100%.

What I’ve figured out is this: As soon as you lose a game, your 100% win rate drops to 99%.But if you win (I am pretty sure!) another 200 in a row, you can earn that last percentage point back. I haven’t kept a perfect count since my last loss, but I’m pretty sure I’ve played more than 100. And despite losing a few games over the years, I’ve usually managed to keep a 100% win score.

For its first few years, Wordle never repeated a solution. If you could remember ever seeing a certain word as a solution, it was guaranteed not to be that day's answer. But that changed in February of 2026, when the New York Times officially announced that previous solutions may be reused.

Not the day you're after? Here's the solution to today's Wordle.

Of course, it’s going to be at 9 p.m. ET, so it won’t be competing against Shifting Gears, but it’s still going up against the rest of ABC’s Wednesday night lineup. The Rookie will debut its ninth season on January 6, at the same time as Baywatch, while The Rookie: North will premiere right after. Of course, as for whether Baywatch will live up to the hype is unknown, but it should be an interesting night of shows nonetheless.
