#3607. 5 Best Sci-Fi Movies Of 1995, Ranked

1995 was a big year for movies. "Toy Story" launched one of cinema's most reliable hit-makers in Pixar and helped redefine what animation could be. One of the greatest crime thrillers of all time came our way with "Seven." Michael Mann's crowning achievement "Heat" was gifted to action lovers around the world. Nicolas Cage delivered his Oscar-winning performance in "Leaving Las Vegas." But it was also one heck of a year for science fiction.

In terms of historical context, Steven Spielberg's "Jurassic Park" revolutionized Hollywood just two years earlier with its blend of CGI and practical effects, with the industry rapidly adopting computer generated visuals (not always with great results). Meanwhile, other movies were still relying heavily on practical effects, which gives movies from this era a specific feeling. It was a unique time for science fiction, a genre that's often been at the forefront of adoption for new technology in cinema while serving as a breeding ground for underrated gems.

We're going to take a look at the best of the best that sci-fi had to offer viewers in 1995. From groundbreaking anime to rubber suit monster movie goodness and everything in between, there's a little something for everyone here. Let's dig in.

I can't sit here and rightfully say that "Species" is A-class cinema. I can't say that it's the best that the science fiction genre had to offer in the year of our lord 1995. What I can say is that, more than 30 years removed, it's a delightful relic of its time, one that is sexy, ridiculous, and a great deal of fun. Sci-fi doesn't always have to be serious to be seriously enjoyable.

Directed by Roger Donaldson, the film centers on Xavier Fitch (Ben Kingsley) who intercepts a space transmission containing the genetic sequence for an alien life form. He uses it to produce "Sil" (Natasha Henstridge), a gorgeous alien-human hybrid. Fitch's team is concerned by her rapid rate of growth before Sil destroys the laboratory and begins a violent quest for a male human to impregnate her. The U.S. government dispatches top assassin Preston Lennox (Michael Madsen) and a team of experts to stop her.

"Species" is a wacky movie that features some incredible makeup effects and not-so-great CGI. It has Oscar-caliber actors like Sir. Ben Kingsley giving his best to a bonkers script, while guys like Michael Madsen gladly ham it up. It was also a breakout role for the movie's lead, Natasha Henstridge, who has a true scene-stealing presence about her. She is undoubtedly the main reason why this movie sticks out in so many people's minds all these years later.

This also spawned a franchise, with the "Species" sequels bringing DND and T&A to the DTV market. I can't in good conscience recommend those midnight movie sequels to the masses, but I can easily defend the original as a worthwhile bit of '90s sci-fi goodness. (Ryan Scott)

The "Gamera" movies are many things. The original entries are campier kaiju classics oft-remembered as corny fuel for some of the best episodes of "Mystery Science Theater 3000." But the franchise has also produced some genuinely excellent entries in the genre. Case in point: "Gamera: Guardian of the Universe." Directed by Shūsuke Kaneko, this launched a whole new era for the classic Japanese monster, with this particular entry serving as an excellent launching pad for Gamera's grand return.

In this "Gamera" cinematic adventure, a ship runs aground on a mysterious atoll leading to an investigation by insurance representative Kusanagi (Akira Onodera). He discovers an ancient bead that he gives to his daughter Asagi (Ayako Fujitani). Meanwhile, ornithologist Nagamine (Shinobu Nakayama) investigates reports of a new species of large bird named Gyaos. As the Gyaos begin to attack, an ancient guardian with a bond to Asagi emerges.

By the mid-'90s, so much of Hollywood was already relying heavily on CGI to create special effects. Part of what's great about "Guardian of the Universe" is that it still has that tangible, rubber suit monster magic. Yet, technology had gotten better since the '60s and '70s, allowing for those practical effects to shine even brighter. The result? Some of the best practical kaiju action one could ever hope to find.

This film redefined what a "Gamera" movie could be. No longer was this just the lesser-than, turtle-like cousin to "Godzilla." Gamera was undeniably cool now. As was Gyaos, an impeccably designed addition to the franchise. It also served as a springboard for several sequels, including "Gamera 3: Revenge of Iris," one of the best sci-fi movies of 1999. It was a damn fine time for monster movies. (Ryan Scott)

There are dozens of "Godzilla" movies of varying quality dating back to 1954 when the King of the Monsters first debuted on the big screen. But for those who have a fondness for a time when the one they call Gojira was still a rubber suited monster duking it out with other monsters made of rubber, it's hard to do better than "Godzilla vs. Destroyah." Directed by Takao Okawara, it's one of the best "Godzilla" movies of all time.

The film wastes no time as it opens with a burning Godzilla, on the verge of meltdown that could threaten all of humanity, emerging to lay siege to Hong Kong. Meanwhile, horrifying new organisms are discovered in Japan and these crustacean-like creatures are seemingly born of the Oxygen Destroyer, the weapon that killed the original Godzilla. These separate monster problems ultimately lead us to a kaiju clash for the ages.

This is the final entry in the so-called Heisi era of the "Godzilla" franchise, which has by far the best practical monsters in the 70-plus year history of the series. One would be hard-pressed to find more impressive monster designs than that of Destroyah, a hulking, terrifying, hellish vision that is worth the price of admission alone. Plus, the design of the burning Godzilla is unique and metal AF.

With lots of sci-fi craziness, just enough cheese, and some of the best practical kaiju action ever put on the silver screen, this is a must-see for monster movie lovers. Not for nothing, it's the only "Godzilla" movie that currently boasts a perfect critic score on Rotten Tomatoes. It deserves it, in my humble opinion. (Ryan Scott)

A time-travel movie, a post-apocalyptic movie, and all-around a mind-melting piece of sci-fi, "12 Monkeys" is a wild ride. Arguably Terry Gilliam's best film, it loosely adapts Chris Marker's 1962 experimental short film "La Jetée," and follows Bruce Willis as James Cole, a convict sent back in time to find out information about a man-made virus that wiped out most of humanity back in his time. What starts as a relatively simple mission devolves into an exploration of madness, time, and dreams, set in a world that is slowly coming apart. Though made in 1995, the film's focus on how we perceive information and decipher the truth among all the noise is as relevant today as it's ever been. This is not a feel-good movie, but rather a story of rebellion and resilience in a world that tries to tear you apart for perceiving things differently, and Gilliam adequately captures that thought with a cold and dark film that reflects the slow descent into madness of its protagonist.

Even if there's little hope to be found by the end of the movie, "12 Monkeys" is still thrilling and hugely entertaining. It walks the line between commerciality and art, with Gilliam employing two of the biggest stars in Hollywood at the time (Willis and Brad Pitt), while also presenting them without an ounce of vanity. It's a big production, but it sneaks in a provocative and idiosyncratic story with a bleak vision of the future. It also has a layered story that never compromises its singular vision. (Rafael Motamayor)

There are few sci-fi films as generation-defining as Mamoru Oshii's adaptation of Masamune Shirow's "Ghost in the Shell." This is a film that's inspired countless filmmakers around the globe, in both animation and live-action. We wouldn't have "The Matrix" if it wasn't for "Ghost in the Shell," and titans like James Cameron and Steven Spielberg count themselves among its many fans. Plus, it's just genuinely a thrilling and monumental piece of science-fiction cinema. The film is set in the then-distant future, at a time when most people have some sort of cybernetic implant and some even have cyber brains that allow access to the internet. The story follows a cyborg public security agent hunting down an enigmatic hacker.

Mamoru Oshii does a great job of condensing the complex and dense plotting of the original manga, while adding his own take on the material. This is a dark film with austere seriousness that meditates on the nature of self, identity, and our relationship with technology. It can take several viewings to fully grasp the many thematic layers present in this film and the way each scene builds on some thematic idea, adding to the main character's crisis of identity as she contemplates how much of her humanity is left under all her cybernetic implants. "Ghost in the Shell" is also a straight-up beautiful movie to look at, with Production I.G delivering a stunning combination of traditional cel animation with CGI animation. In many ways, this is the '90s answer to "Akira" in how the film pushes forward what animation can do, with lens effects and attention to light and shadow serving to make a film that looks like nothing before or since. (Rafael Motamayor)

#3606. I Love Christopher Nolan’s Robert Pattinson-Oriented Oppenheimer Story. Robert Downey Jr. Telling It Is Even Better

The inception, no pun intended, of Christopher Nolan's Oppenheimer is quite the legendary tale at this point. This is probably because it involves the very buzzy and prolific actor Robert Pattinson planting the idea in Nolan’s head, despite having nothing to do with the movie. The director, characteristically, had a very matter-of-fact version of the story that people love. However, the way Robert Downey Jr. tells it makes it even better.

In an interview with Tara Hitchcock, Christopher Nolan talked about how he initially had an interest in J. Robert Oppenheimer and his role in American history. He specifically noted that a speech by Oppenheimer was actually used as a catalyst for Tenet and the way they wanted to tell that story. He said:

I wrote a thing about this incredible moment that Oppenheimer and the scientists of the Manhattan Project had, where they could not completely eliminate the possibility that when they triggered that first gadget – that first atomic device – they might start a chain reaction that would destroy the world. And we use that as a metaphor for Tenet, which Rob was in.

The Batman star recognized this interest, and by the end of the production, Pattinson decided to give Nolan a book of Oppenheimer’s speeches as a wrap gift on Tenet. Clearly, this interest in the speeches and the story had legs, as it helped inspire one of the best movies in the last decade and even led to a Best Picture win. I guess you can say that Robert Pattinson is really great at gifts.

In true Robert Downey Jr. fashion, the way he tells this story has its own special kind of energy. During his Actors on Actors interview with Mark Ruffalo, Downey told the tale like a fable, showing this gesture as a kindred energy between two creative men. He told Ruffalo (via Variety):

Pattinson gives him unwrapped Oppenheimer's letters—these moments in life where you realize the inception of something occurred in the most organic way. And also, Pattinson in Tenet was an incredible departure for him. So this incredible departure from one of our younger peers turns into him making a personal gift to arguably one of the greatest directors of—of his generation, turns into him deciding that it's sticking with him.

The way Downey tells it, it was a kinship moment. Robert Pattinson was seeing his career turn with Tenet, making him a more serious, sought-out character actor. And this made way for Nolan’s own transition, as he pivoted from tales based in sci-fi and action to one entrenched in the inner world of one of our most fabled historic figures. It was a world-stopping moment for two of our great creatives that went on to start a new and important chapter in both of their careers. It’s a beautiful way to put it, and it speaks to the storyteller that Downey is.

Pattinson may not have been in Oppenheimer and opted to do both Mickey 17 and The Batman instead; however, his impact on the Oscar-winning film is obvious. Clearly there was a connection with these two creatives, as Downey puts it, that made their separate careers flourish and then come together again for The Odyssey this year. It’s a great pairing, and I hope this partnership continues for years to come.

You can revisit Oppenheimer now, as it is currently streaming with a Peacock subscription. Christopher Nolan fans can also see him reunite with Robert Pattinson in The Odyssey, which is currently playing in select theaters around the country. It is one of the best films on the 2026 movie schedule, so make sure to check it out while you still can.

#3604. Wardogs Season 3 Will Add A Mode That Limits What Weapons Players Can Use

Wardogs' lengthier Season 3 will introduce Limited Mode, which should be friendlier to new players

Bulkhead and Team17 shared the first details on what players can expect from Wardogs Season 3 in a new video. One of the most notable additions is Limited Mode, a new way to play Wardogs that restricts what weapons and other upgrades players have access to.

In its Road to Season 3 video, Bulkhead explains that it learned from the backlash towards Season 2 and will now mostly stick to its own vision for the game rather than overreacting to the loudest demands from the community. As part of the adjustments, progression is being brought back more in line with Season 1, and Wardogs' seasons will now last three months.

While a major meta-game progression overhaul is happening in 2027, Wardogs is introducing multi-track unlocks in the meantime, meaning that some items are no longer locked to a specific progression track. It's also part of why Bulkhead is introducing Limited Mode servers, so players don't feel outclassed simply because they haven't gotten as far through the in-game progression as other players.

On Limited Mode servers, players will be restricted to certain weaponry and ammo types, only be able to use up to tier-2 armor, and not have access to certain vehicles. Cash and XP earned in Limited Mode can be spent in the standard game mode, so it's probably what players new to the game will want to check out first in Season 3.

Improvements to Wardogs' anti-cheat systems are also coming as part of Season 3, with almost half of the Season 3 video being dedicated to highlighting that. Bulkhead has not released patch notes for the new season just yet. Those can be expected closer to launch.

Wardogs Season 3 will begin on Nov. 12. The game is still only available in early access on Windows PC. A 1.0 Windows PC launch is planned for 2027 before the game eventually comes to consoles in 2028.

#3603. Kate Middleton Dresses Down for Appearance at Mental Health-Focused Charity

During a surprise engagement in West London, Kate Middleton reminded fans that she is the queen of country-set dressing. Prince William's wife joined the team at Dose of Nature, a charity that “prescribes” time spent outdoors to help improve mental health, telling staff members and volunteers that connecting with nature is a “healing” experience for her.

The future queen dressed down for the occasion, wrapping up warm in what looked to be a Barbour jacket and a pair of jeans. She left her hair to flow in waves and accessorized with her trademark “big blue” sapphire engagement ring.

At Pensford Field, where Dose of Nature has a site near Kew, the Princess of Wales met the charity's founder, Dr. Alison Greenwood, and clinical lead, Dr. Georgina Gould, as well as volunteer nature guide Tom, who told Catherine that support from Dose of Nature had made him more confident and resilient.

“Our journey has been very very different, but it’s so wonderful to hear how your nature connection and how it’s been so healing for you, and I felt the same,” Catherine said to him.

“The fact that you’re able to provide that to so many other people in this community; that sense of purpose and meaning, and belonging, through that experience, I think is something that has got the longevity and the sustainability of feeling like, almost without knowing what’s to come, without having the control in your life of knowing what the future might hold, the fact that you feel that you can cope with things, because you feel that interconnection, I think that makes it holistic in a very true essence,” she added.

The Princess of Wales visits Dose of Nature.

Kate Middleton has long been a champion of the importance of nature for mental and physical well-being. In a recent essay, she wrote: “By spending time in nature or being creative, we can nurture the very skills and emotions that cannot be digitised: awareness, empathy, humility, and above all, love.”

The future queen has been working with the Royal Foundation Centre for Early Childhood on a project to “support the healthy development of babies and young children,” as she explained in a recent video, delivered from Cornwall while dressed in ME+EM.

“In this tech-driven, digital age, spending time outdoors has never been more important,” the Princess said.

“This project is about how nature, creativity, and relationships can best support the healthy development of babies and young children,” she continued. “My hope is that through this practical, nature-based research, we can build supportive environments that help make nature more accessible, benefiting babies, young children, and their families across the UK.”

The Princess of Wales has spent many years dedicated to early childhood research, working hard advising the Foundation, even during her cancer treatment. This May, she visited the University of East London’s Institute for the Science of Early Years and Youth to see how the University’s researchers use state-of-the-art wearables and brain recording techniques to study how the diverse early living environments and relationships experienced by babies influence early stress—both in the child themselves and their parents and caregivers.

#3602. The Best King Ghidorah Movie To Watch After Godzilla Minus Zero Is Streaming On HBO Max

"Godzilla Minus Zero" may not be as good as its immediate predecessor, but Takashi Yamazaki brings some truly spectacular kaiju action to the big screen in his "Godzilla Minus One" sequel. The film has a sense of scope and scale that we haven't really seen in the 70-year-old franchise, with impeccable VFX that capture the sheer destruction of the giant monsters that battle it out in the movie. Yamazaki also captures the true horrors of what a kaiju attack would look like, putting the film's R-rating to good use with some gruesome imagery.

The highlight of the movie is, surprisingly enough, not Godzilla. Instead, it's the golden, armless dragon with three heads and two tails known as Ghidorah. "Godzilla Minus Zero" retains Ghidorah's alien origin while reimagining him as a translucent blob that absorbs creatures and adopts their traits, allowing him to evolve into a three-headed dragon that shoots lightning and can make things float.

Though Ghidorah's design unfortunately leaked before the film's release, he still looks absolutely perfect. More so, the character brings some silliness to Yamazaki's take on the Godzilla universe, as the inclusion of aliens means future sequels can now bring in anything from Mechagodzilla to even Gigan. And yet, Ghidorah remains scary and awe-inspiring. It's easy to see why he's been Godzilla's main archenemy for decades and is the one kaiju that, at least in the eyes of the public, presents a real threat to the king of the monsters.

Unfortunately, despite him showing up in over a dozen movies, most of Ghidorah's film appearances aren't that great. Luckily, the best Ghidorah movie, by far, is currently streaming on HBO Max — namely, the king of terror's debut in the appropriately titled 1964 film "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster."

"Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" was released back in 1964 as the fifth film in the Godzilla franchise, bringing together Godzilla, Mothra, and Rodan, who must all team up to take down the titular Ghidorah (lest the kaiju cause humanity to perish).

This is not only one of the best Godzilla movies of all time, it's also a hugely important film in the long-running franchise. That's because the movie marked a change in the king of monsters, introducing the idea of Godzilla as humankind's savior rather than just a destructive force. Up until that point, Godzilla would either attack human cities or battle other kaiju, but the latter scenario tended to center around some kind of territorial dispute or petty grievance. In other words, Godzilla would act more like a grumpy old man trying to keep kids off his lawn than a hero.

"Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster," however, fully transformed Godzilla into a force for good that would team up with other monsters in an effort to defend the people of Earth. Indeed, for decades after that, the king of the monsters would mostly help defend humans against other threats, taking on the likes of MechaGodzilla, Biollante, and plenty of other kaijus.

On top of that, "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" is just plain fun as a movie. Director Ishirō Honda finds a great balance between the serious tone of his original 1954 "Godzilla" (which focuses on the horror that surrounds the kaiju) and the campiness that would become a staple of the "Godzilla" franchise in the coming years. It's a rather ambitious film, too, with four monsters sharing the screen, yet it never feels too busy or disjointed.

Though Godzilla has fought plenty of villains over the last 70 years, none have managed to leave a lasting impact the way King Ghidorah has. When he was first introduced, kaiju were either all bad or portrayed as animals we should root against. But Ghidorah was the first proper villain of the "Godzilla" franchise, and he is treated as such. "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster" takes its time teasing the arrival of the titular dragon, building dread and making sure you understand Ghidorah is a big enough threat that Godzilla would actually join forces with other kaiju to take him down.

It's why 2019's rather underrated "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" borrows so much from "Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster," pairing Godzilla with the same allies he has in the 1964 film in order to square off with the more powerful Ghidorah. That movie understands that a three-headed dragon that shoots lightning is already a pretty imposing image and the perfect way to make Godzilla appear heroic.

Now, "Godzilla Minus Zero" has continued that tradition, turning King Ghidorah into a terrifying monster. This new movie isn't in a hurry to bring Godzilla back, and in the meantime, we watch as Ghidorah lays waste to Japan, causing harrowing devastation with his terrific powers (including the ability to make buildings levitate, which he uses to kill a whole bunch of people by dropping them to their painful deaths). The film also introduces the idea of Ghidorah constantly evolving, with his design changing throughout the movie as he grows heads, turns golden, and ultimately gains Godzilla-like dorsal plates, along with the king of the monsters' ability to wield atomic breath.

Ghidorah will always be Godzilla's greatest foe, and you can watch his first and best appearance on HBO Max.

#3601. 10 Shows Like 'The Diplomat' You Should Watch Next

You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Following its recently concluded fourth season, Netflix's political thriller The Diplomat has been renewed for a fifth season, and even better, it's the rare streaming show that seems to keep to a fairly regular schedule, meaning there's likely to be more of the Keri Russell-led espionage drama coming by late next year. If you're looking for something with the same political thriller vibes to watch in the meantime, here are 10 other series to stream now.

Diplomat creator Debora Cahn got her start on The West Wing, but honed her political-espionage craft on this show, for which she served as writer and, later, executive producer. The series begins with CIA case officer Carrie Mathison (Claire Danes) coming to suspect that decorated Marine Corps scout sniper Nicholas Brody (Damian Lewis), recently rescued from an al-Qaeda compound, has been turned and is planning a terrorist attack on the United States. As she has been diagnosed with bipolar disorder, her superiors don't give Mathison's suspicions much credence, kicking off a cat-and-mouse/is-he-or-isn't he? game between the two. As the show progresses, Carrie moves up the ranks until she's working directly for the president. Both leads won Emmys for their performances, and the series took the Outstanding Drama prize in its first year. Stream Homeland on Hulu and Netflix.

Focusing largely on the seedier side of international espionage, Slow Horses, based on the novels by Mick Herron, shares with The Diplomat a dry sense of humor about the consequences of institutional and human failures. With nods to the great spy dramas of John le Carré, Slow Horses updates the setting without losing either the thrills or the style of a time-honored genre. The “Slow Horses” of the title are a group of has-been MI5 agents—they’ve all made messes of significant jobs, but are still seen as having some use, if only in dull administrative tasks. Naturally, the members of the group (led by Gary Oldman's endlessly flatulent Jackson Lamb) find themselves in deeper waters than anyone thought them capable of navigating. Kristin Scott Thomas is the spymaster, navigating political pressures, misogyny, and her own unrepentant ambition in trying to do her job. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV.

An action drama that plays a bit like a spy thriller, The Night Agent stars Gabriel Basso as Peter Sutherland, an FBI agent who works overnights in the basement of the White House watching a phone that never, ever rings (dream job, honestly), until the night it does. Peter gets a call from Rose Larkin, a cybersecurity expert whose aunt and uncle were just killed; unbeknownst to her, they were also government operatives, and rescuing Rose sees Peter delving deep inside a web of conspiracy and corruption that plays out over three seasons, with a fourth and final on the way. While a bit more action-heavy than The Diplomat, it still plays in that realm of government secrets and conspiracies. Stream The Night Agent on Netflix.

There was a moment, around the turn of the millennium, when The West Wing seemed like a heightened but not entirely implausible picture of politics in action; its ripped-from-the-headlines style gave it an edge that allowed us to imagine smart, thoughtful people getting jobs in government, trying to do the more-or-less right thing despite systemic and personal flaws (it's also where The Diplomat's creator Debora Cahn started her TV writing career). The show's world can be a little frustrating when contrasted against our more explicitly appalling actual one, but it's a thoroughly pleasing fantasy nonetheless, with President Matin Sheen leading a White House staff through various diplomatic, military, and political crises. Stream The West Wing on Netflix and HBO Max.

Sidse Babett Knudsen stars as Birgitte Nyborg in this popular import. She's a minor Danish politician who watches other politicians fall to scandal and incompetence as she rapidly and unexpectedly ascends to the job of prime minister. The espionage and action are entirely incidental (but not nonexistent) here, as the show deals instead with the moral and political compromises that are seemingly intrinsic to statecraft. There's been talk of an American remake for years now, but you should just watch the original. Stream Borgen on Netflix.

Shonda Rhimes was already a powerhouse producer and screenwriter with several successful seasons of Grey's Anatomy under her belt when Scandal debuted, but its blend of political thrills and sexy, soapy drama truly solidified her brand—and her spot atop the modern TV landscape. Kerry Washington stars as Olivia Pope, head of the D.C.-based crisis management firm Olivia Pope & Associates (OPA), who is the person to call when you've got a PR disaster to fix. If you want to get a sense of the stakes involved, consider that Tony Goldwyn costars as Fitzgerald Grant III, who is both the president of the United States. and also Olivia's lover. Stream Scandal on Hulu and Netflix.

Téa Leoni plays Elizabeth McCord, a former CIA analyst who gave up that hectic life to become a political science professor. That's all going great until the Secretary of State dies under mysterious circumstances and she's called up by her old CIA boss, who's now the president, to take over the job. With her outsider's perspective and resistance to political considerations, she's surprisingly good at the gig, navigating foreign and domestic crises while also trying to figure out who the hell killed her predecessor, and whether they're coming for her, too. Stream Madam Secretary on The Roku Channel.

You could absolutely watch the original American take on this show, which stars Kiefer Sutherland—they have essentially the same premise—but this South Korean remake earns a few extra points by only running for a compact 16 episodes, making it far leaner and meaner. Education Minister Park Mu-jin (Ji Jin-hee) is fired from his job one day before an attack occurs amid an announcement of peace talks with the North, wiping out the entire presidential line of succession. His dismissal having not yet been finalized, the largely unambitious Minister Park is forced into the job, even as questions linger over the attack that put him in the role. Stream Designated Survivor: 60 Days on Netflix.

It's a different time and setting, but all the Keri Russell spy action you could want as a Diplomat fan. Set during the Cold War 1980s and created by former CIA officer Joe Weisberg, The Americans follows Soviet KGB intelligence agents Elizabeth (Russell) and Philip Jennings (the ever-reliable Matthew Rhys), living undercover lives posing as an American couple in the DC metro area—and raising their American-born children. The critically acclaimed show makes much of its period setting and a central conflict that places two spies in the heart of suburban America, even as they're tasked with undermining the Reagan-era government under which their children are growing up. Stream The Americans on Hulu.

A power struggle for leadership of an entire country is at the heart of this juicy political thriller. Prime Minister Park Dong-ho comes to believe that the president has been corrupted by powerful, wealthy individuals and companies (something that could only happen in South Korea, obviously). Deputy Prime Minister Jeong Su-jin sees the problem, too, but she's not so sure about his solution: He wants to have the president assassinated. But how much better is he than the man he would be replacing? And how pure are her motives in potentially putting herself in line for the top job? Stream The Whirlwind on Netflix.

60 Minutes underwent a major creative overhaul this past summer, which saw executive producer Nick Bilton and CBS News Editor-in-Chief Bari Weiss make considerable staff changes. Several notable series alums were fired and, since then, several new employees have been added. However, when the show returned for Season 59 as part of the 2026 TV schedule, some familiar faces were still on the air, including host Lesley Stahl. Now, Stahl is getting candid about remaining with the show under Weiss’ leadership after the firings.

Stahl – who’s been with 60 Minutes since 1991 – opted to remain with the news magazine program alongside fellow series veterans Bill Whitaker and Jon Wertheim. Ahead of the trio jointly confirming their decision to stay, there had been considerable speculation about their plans. Stahl spoke about her choice while being honored at the Power 100 luncheon this past week and claimed that she’d been on the receiving end of backlash for staying with the show. Via The New York Post, Stahl explained why she and her colleagues chose to stay:

I myself have been under attack on social media because of my decision to stay at ’60 Minutes’ under the new regime. It was not an easy decision. It was one I made with my colleagues Bill Whitaker and John Wertheim. There was an urge to walk out and protest in solidarity with our colleagues who had been abruptly and cruelly fired. But we decided to stay out of a fear, a fear that if we didn’t, ’60 Minutes’ would vanish.

60 Minutes Alum On The Show’s Bari Weiss Era And One Thing She Still Finds ‘Disturbing’

On May 28, which has reportedly since been deemed “Black Thursday" within CBS News, 60 Minutes correspondents Cecilia Vega and Sharyn Alfonsi were fired alongside others like series EP Tanya Simon and executive editor Draggan Mihailovich. Days later, longtime correspondent Scott Pelley was fired as well after reportedly accusing Bari Weiss of “murdering” the show. In the months since then, Pelley, Vega and others have made claims of editorial interference against Weiss and claimed they were asked to exude bias in their reporting.

Bari Weiss herself has been at the center of backlash as well due to the claims of journalistic partiality. At this point, the Free Press founder has denied the assertions and emphasized her intention to improve 60. Since the show returned in September, ratings have reportedly been under the average of the previous season. Weiss addressed those concerns during a recent conference and stated that the series was doing “tremendously well.” Stahl also addressed that decrease in viewership while speaking at the luncheon:

Many loyal viewers over the last 58 years have tuned us out, we presume, in protest. To those who stopped watching, I’m asking you please to come back.

Back in June, Stahl discussed the state of 60 Minutes back in June. She addressed the wave of firings and referred to the fallout as the “hardest chapter” of her career. Stahl – who’s been in journalism for over 50 years – also said the series of firings “was by far the worst experience I’ve been involved in, or even witnessed.” At the time, Stahl also said she’d met with Bilton to stress that while she and her colleagues understood that more needed to be done to the show, she hoped that the broadcast wouldn’t be “tampered with.”

Since then, Bari Weiss and Nick Bilton have added Ross Douthat, Gianna Toboni, Trevor Phillips and Sebastian Junger in host and correspondent roles for 60 Minutes. Lesley Stahl’s future on the news program beyond this current season remains uncertain. In any case, it’s evident that a new era is currently taking shape not just at 60 but at CBS News as a whole.

#3599. Marvel's 2027 Release Schedule: All 8 Movies And TV Shows Explained

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

While there is only one Marvel Cinematic Universe movie premiering in 2027, if the production goes as planned, there are plenty of Marvel projects debuting throughout the year. Whether they're a part of the MCU or other titles based on Marvel's countless comic book properties, there is enough to keep fans excited. These range from returning animated shows and miniseries to eagerly anticipated live-action projects on television and the big screen. We're gathering them all here together so you can keep track of each of them in one convenient place.

From announced release dates and cast members to the details that we know so far, each of these projects offer tantalizing directions for Marvel's superheroes and supervillains. We're also including projects that aren't produced directly by Marvel Studios, some of which are no less exciting. As with all release dates in television and film, the premiere dates mentioned here are subject to change.

With that in mind, here is Marvel's 2027 release schedule with all eight movies and TV shows explained.

When it debuted in 2025, the Disney+ animated series "Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man" breathed new life into fan-favorite webslinger. Set in its own universe, the show has Peter Parker (Hudson Thames) receive a well-connected mentor in Norman Osborn (Colman Domingo) as he starts his superhero career. The show takes its cues from the MCU, with guest heroes and villains appearing semi-regularly, but visually, it's inspired by the artwork of Steve Ditko and John Romita, Jr. Through it all, the series maintains sight on how Peter's double life takes a toll on his high school life and the importance of having a good mentor figure.

"Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man" set up Season 2 with Norman obtaining a piece of the symbiote that gave Peter his powers in this universe. This hints at the inclusion of Venom, with Josh Keaton cast as Eddie Brock, a fun nod after Keaton played Peter in "The Spectacular Spider-Man." Peter's long-lost father Richard Parker, revealed to be incarcerated, was also silently introduced at the end of the season, setting up an uncomfortable family reunion. With Gwen Stacy also joining the show, "Your Friendly Neighborhood Spider-Man" is set to go deeper into the superhero mythos when it returns on January 13, 2027.

It feels like just yesterday that Charlie Cox made his big return to reclaim the mantle of Daredevil, after Netflix canceled the original version of the superhero series in 2018. Fast-forward nearly a decade later and we're preparing for the third and final season of the Disney+ revival series "Daredevil: Born Again." The second season finale set up Season 3 with Matt Murdock (Cox) revealing his superhero secret to the world, resulting in his incarceration for his violent vigilantism. Just as Season 2 saw Jessica Jones (Krysten Ritter) and Luke Cage (Mike Colter) return, Season 3 will bring back Danny Rand (Finn Jones) and Elektra Natchios (Élodie Yung).

Though "Daredevil: Born Again" was canceled by Marvel months before its Season 3 premiere, we're still looking forward to it. The series remains as intense and brutal as it ever was on Netflix while incorporating more nods to the wider MCU around it. Plus, this could be the last time that we see Daredevil and the Defenders back in action again, at least with the familiar Netflix era actors in their roles. Sure to put Matt Murdock and his friends through the wringer, "Daredevil: Born Again" Season 3 will hopefully continue to not pull its punches. It's expected to premiere in March 2027.

The acclaimed animated movie "Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse" ended on a cliffhanger that left audiences hanging back in 2023. After delays surrounding "Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse" pushed back the sequel's intended release date by several years, it looks on track for a June 18, 2027 premiere. The movie will answer what happens to teenager superhero Miles Morales (Shameik Moore) after he was stranded in an alternate universe with a more brutal doppelganger to contend with. The preceding movie's co-director Justin K. Thompson reunites with "Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse" co-director Bob Persichetti for the sequel.

At the time of this writing, Sony hasn't so much as released an official teaser trailer for "Spider-Man: Beyond the Spider-Verse." This restrained promotional approach has served the studio well before, specifically with the gangbusters reception to this year's "Spider-Man: Brand New Day." We're certainly at the edge of our seats to see if the creative team can stick the landing and, two movies in, they haven't let us down so far. The "Spider-Verse" movies are ranked highly among the best Spider-Man movies ever so, going "Beyond the Spider-Verse" should be worth the wait.

Fans had to wait just over two years for "X-Men '97" Season 2, but that gap reportedly won't happen with Season 3. A continuation of the beloved "X-Men: Animated Series," what some would consider the definitive versions of the characters, the mutant superheroes were left reeling coming out of Season 2. The villainous Apocalypse (Ross Marquand) was defeated, but the X-Men had lost several of their own, most notably Nightcrawler (Adrian Hough). Meanwhile, mutantkind's relationship with humanity is more fraught than ever while Mystique (Randall Carpenter) has her own fiendish plans.

"X-Men '97" Season 2 was a dazzling return for the hit revival series, and Season 3 looks to tighten its narrative focus by comparison. One of the weak points of the second season was dividing its narrative across three separate timelines for the first half of the season. Based on how Season 2 ended, Season 3 will likely unfold entirely from a single timeline, as its characters face new threats. A more sophisticated storytelling approach to its classic preceding series, "X-Men '97" has fans of the show revisit these enduring characters without treading too heavily on pure nostalgia.

We were pleasantly surprised how dark and intense "Marvel Zombies" got compared to the rest of Marvel's recent animated output, bringing a horrific edge to an alternate MCU. The series is set to get a line of two-part specials set in its world, each focused on a different character in its world overrun by ravenous undead. After "Marvel Zombies" cut the Winter Soldier from its first season's story, the character will headline the first of these specials. The show is set to be directed by Bryan Andrews, who directed the main series, with its episodes expected to debut on Disney+ in October.

Given the ending of "Marvel Zombies," it's unclear if Bucky Barnes' story will take place before, during, or after the main series. "Marvel Zombies: The Winter Soldier" will be followed by a 2028 special "The Fist of Khonshu" and 2029 special "The Last Guardian." These specials are poised to expand the terror-fueled scope of the main series while depicting how different characters react to the zombie apocalypse. With his particular set of skills, Bucky is about to be put to the test in "Marvel Zombies: The Winter Soldier" and we'll be there to watch in October 2027.

With "Avengers: Secret Wars" reportedly moving its production into 2027, a delayed release date may be in the cards for the MCU movie. But, at least at the time of this writing, the upcoming film is still officially scheduled for a wide theatrical release on December 17, 2027. As the sequel to "Avengers: Doomsday," details about "Secret Wars" are currently being kept tightly under wraps until "Doomsday" debuts. This extends to the movie's cast list, though Samuel L. Jackson has claimed that his next Marvel movie as Nick Fury will be the 2027 release.

While plot details remain unconfirmed, the movie is expected to adapt the 2015 comic book series "Secret Wars" by Jonathan Hickman and Esad Ribic. This storyline saw Doctor Doom rule over a composite reality formed by the remnants of the multiverse with the heroes banding together to overthrow him. Hickman himself is a consultant on "Secret Wars," so the movie may follow its comic book source material more faithfully than anticipated. Regardless, we're excited to see where the MCU goes next after the cataclysmic turn of events that's sure to unfold in "Doomsday."

After a 35-episode single season, "Iron Man and His Awesome Friends" came to an end in April 2026. This paves the wave for another early-age animated series, "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends," which is set to premiere sometime in 2027. Like "Iron Man and His Awesome Friends," this series features versions of its popular superheroes as children working together and enjoying their friendship. Though the voice cast hasn't been announced, it's set to include Spider-Man, Captain America, Iron Man, Black Panther, Black Widow, Thor, Ms. Marvel, and Hulk.

No official release window for "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends" has been announced so far, bu, if it matches "Iron Man and His Awesome Friends," it should be in the summer. It's also unknown how many episodes the show's first season will receive. But the series will air on Disney Jr. and likely be available to stream on Disney+ afterwards. A good primer for younger audiences into the Marvel Universe, "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends" is an inviting tour of its superhero-filled world.

For viewers who may be too young for the "Spider-Verse" movies, the animated series "Spidey and His Amazing Friends" has got them covered. The early age-friendly show premiered in 2021 and is set to release its sixth season on Disney Jr. in 2027 before coming to Disney+. Like the "Spider-Verse" movies, the show revolves around Peter Parker (Nick A. Fisher), Miles Morales (Carter Young), and Gwen Stacy (Audrey Bennett). Like "Marvel's Avengers: Mightiest Friends," the show features grade school iterations of the superhero characters as they get into super-powered hijinks and celebrate their friendship.

No official release window has currently been announced for "Spidey and His Amazing Friends" Season 6, but historically, the show has released new episodes during the summer. The series features the trio facing all the usual supervillains in Spider-Man's rogues' gallery but with the action and stakes far less intense. It's unknown which new characters are joining the show in Season 6, but Season 5 added Silk (Aveline Choi) to the heroic ensemble. Bringing freewheeling and fun set of adventures starring younger webslingers, "Spidey and His Amazing Friends" is a great gateway into the world of Spider-Man.

#3598. Will Josh O’Connor Be The Next James Bond?

Let’s clear up any potential misunderstandings: there are no official announcements on who will play James Bond at this time. But a British tabloid says that a conversation at a pub has revealed the top-secret casting—if an anonymously sourced rumor is to be believed.

A long list of stars are reportedly auditioning for the 007 role, but even former James Bond Pierce Brosnan says the casting process is a mystery. “I’m just the man in the street who is eager to see who is going to play this epic role of cinematic history,” Brosnan tells Vanity Fair. “All the men who are on the list now are actors I admire.”

According to UK publication The Sun, the decision is rumored to have been made: a recent colleague of Josh O’Connor, a 36-year-old actor from Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, says Disclosure Day star has been cast in the role. If true, Turner beat out likely contenders including Callum Turner and Aaron Taylor-Johnson.

Josh O'Connor at UK premiere for Disclosure Day on June 04, 2026.

The news comes as a bit of a game of telephone. Until last week, O'Connor was in the case of Golden Boy, Clifford Odets' 1937 drama about a violin player turned boxer in Depression-era New York City. Citing the claims of one of O'Connor's cast mates, an unnamed source tells The Sun “I bumped into one of Josh’s Golden Boy cast mates at The French House."

“Out of nowhere, and oiled by a few glasses of lager, they blurted out that Josh was the next James Bond."

When the source pushed back, the thespian grew more insistent. “They said that he had confided in them about getting the role when the cast of Golden Boy had celebratory drinks after the play finished its run on Halloween," a claim that implies the decision has been made for over a week.

Josh O'Connor, winner of the Outstanding Lead Actor In A Drama Series award for The Crown, at the 73rd Primetime Emmy Awards on September 19, 2021.

If this rumor comes to fruition, it would not be the first time O'Connor took on an iconic UK role. In 2021, he took home the outstanding lead actor Emmy for his role as then-Prince, now-King Charles III, in Netflix series The Crown. While in his role as the future king, he was encouraged to tap into a side that one might not expect.

“It’s Prince Charles as Walter White," he told The Guardian in 2020, making a reference to crime series Breaking Bad. "Our job was to make people feel sorry for [Charles], so that in season four, when he turns into this at times monstrous character, we understand how he got there.” A heel turn that isn't unBond, especially the darker Bond we grew used to with Daniel Craig. (Craig, in fact, has a direct connection to O’Connor, as the pair co-starred in Knives Out: Wake Up Dead Man.)

Speaking with the BBC, O'Connor did not confirm the casting rumor—but he didn't deny it either. (Vanity Fair has reached out to O'Connor's representatives for comment, but has not yet received a response.)

"To be considered in that same sort of bracket is extraordinary," O'Connor said this week.

"It's an incredibly bizarre pinch me moment...even being uttered in that same sentence and being considered for something like that. But I am afraid, there is nothing to say beyond that."

#3597. The JBL Vibe Beam Earbuds Are on Sale for $30 Right Now

If you want reliable earbuds that cost less than tonight's dinner, JBL is a reliable brand to fall back on, with plenty of budget-friendly models that lack the bells and whistles of pricier options while still delivering on sound and battery life. One of the most popular picks is the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds, which are down 40% at $29.99 (originally $49.95).

These earbuds aren’t reinventing the wheel, but they do check important boxes. They last up to eight hours without the charging case, and up to 32 hours with the case. Ten minutes of charging will get you a couple of hours of playback, and they have an IP54 rating, making them dust- and splash-resistant. The built-in mics work well in reasonably quiet rooms, but may struggle to separate your voice from loud background noise. Another perk is Find My Buds, which helps locate misplaced earbuds via a sound that’s played.

With 8 mm dynamic drivers, they deliver punchy bass that translates well to adrenaline-pumping workout music, and adequate vocal clarity for music and podcasts. Though the default tuning is relatively balanced, you can tweak it on the app’s equalizer to adjust it to your liking. They lack ANC and Bluetooth multipoint pairing, which isn’t surprising given the price point, but still pack in a solid amount of features and quality into $30, making the wireless JBL Vibe Beam earbuds a good value for everyday bargain earbuds that get the job done.

There’s no question that when Sydney Sweeney releases an ad campaign, it gets people talking. Whether it's selling soap infused with her bathwater, starring in an ad for American Eagle that led to serious backlash, or becoming an equity partner in Novig and doing an ad where she wore nothing but footballs, she knows how to make a viral moment. However, while these instances burn big and bright for a moment, do they actually turn into long-term sales? Let's talk about it.

When Sweeney’s first campaign with American Eagle launched, it was met with an intense amount of discourse. While it faced serious backlash, as some thought the campaign was promoting eugenics based on how it used the word “jeans” like “genes,” it did bring in 790,000 new customers in six weeks, and in Q3 of 2025, sales grew 1% according to Adweek. It also reportedly added about $400 million in market value and upped web traffic by 100%.

Then, after both Sweeney and Travis Kelce’s AE campaigns launched, there was a growth in sales around the holiday, as American Eagle Outfitters reported “record holiday-quarter sales of $1.8 billion.”

While Sweeney’s first campaign with American Eagle was a very big deal and did make an impact, the second did not lead to the same kind of gains. In this new report, it’s stated that in Q1 of 2026, AE’s sales fell 2% (even though total comps rose to 8% due to a 25% jump from the brand Aeire). In reference to that, Jay Schottenstein, the CEO of AEO, said that the overall results were mixed.

Michael Gunther, Consumer Edge’s SVP of Research and Market Intelligence, explained that when it comes to American Eagle’s second campaign with Sweeney, there’s “little evidence of a sustained improvement comparable to the original campaign’s holiday performance.”

Overall, it would seem that Sweeney’s campaigns do generate sales. However, once the shock of her ads wears off, sales dwindle. For example, when her Dr. Squatch ad about her bathwater came out, it “drove a 20% week-over-week jump in revenue,” according to the brand’s then-VP of Global Marketing, John Ludeke. However, in the months after that, Consumer Edge’s card data showed that Dr. Squatch’s slice of this market went down by 25 basis points.

It was also reported that while the brand sees double-digit growth in its future, it has seen a slowdown in bar soap sales. Dr. Squatch’s CEO, Josh Friedman, did make it clear, however, that Sweeney’s ad campaign was also successful because it ultimately helped the brand launch a body wash line.

As for the actress’ latest ad campaign with Novig, which did cause backlash, it’s had some notable early wins. Novig has raised funding at a $2 billion valuation, which is up from the $500 million it was at earlier this year. Along with that, first-time despitores went up over 281% in the weeks after Sweeney’s ad premiered. So, things are looking up for this partnership; the question is, can it be sustained?

The data seems to say her work provides sales in the short term. The long term is a bit of a different situation. However, if there’s one thing that’s certain, it’s that getting Sydney Sweeney in an ad is sure to generate a big conversation.

#3595. Commander Shepard’s Actors Are ‘Wildly Hopeful’ for Mass Effect, Despite Everything

‘Nobody has shut off the electricity because the community is the electricity’

EA shut down BioWare, laid off its staff, and canceled the in-development Mass Effect: Universe in October. That news sent shockwaves throughout the industry and through the communities that have sprung up around BioWare’s games. Mass Effect fans were hit particularly hard, and have started a petition to save Mass Effect. Some even purchased a time on a billboard in Times Square to advertise it.

Fans have tangled with a mix of emotions knowing that it’s unlikely they’ll ever get to play a new BioWare-developed Mass Effect again. But, if you ask the voices of Commander Shepard, they’re oddly optimistic about the future despite the circumstances. Polygon recently spoke to Mark Meer and Jennifer Hale, the voice actors for Shepard, about the strength of Mass Effect’s community, the closure of BioWare, and the studio’s legacy.

“My first response was sadness and concern for everybody who worked at Bioware,” Meer said.

After gutting the studio a year ago, EA laid off BioWare’s remaining around 50 employees on Oct. 21, bringing an end to its 30-year legacy. Meer noted that BioWare was a source of pride in Canada, and especially in Edmonton, where the studio was based. Canadian fans are even petitioning their government to save BioWare, and that petition will be presented in the House of Commons, meaning the Canadian government will formally address it in some way. “They were such a force in gaming and they were such a legend,” Meer said.

“BioWare was, in some beautiful, quiet ways, a very Canadian company,” Hale said. “Their games were inclusive. Their games bucked against tradition and [BioWare] did it their own way, quietly, but excellently. And they moved us forward, not by shouting and preaching, but simply by doing it in a very cool way.”

Hale was once overtaken by a wave of sadness about BioWare, but hers occurred some 20 years prior, when the studio was acquired by EA, which meant it became beholden to the whims and projections of shareholders and was no longer able to operate independently. EA’s 2025 sale to private investors, including Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, only further clashed with “the original spirit of BioWare,” as Hale put it. (BioWare reportedly was asked to remove LGBTQ-adjacent imagery from a video presentation, for example.)

“So, when I heard about the closure, I got wildly hopeful,” Hale said, acknowledging that optimism “sounds weird” at this moment. Like in her initial reaction to the closure, Hale described her optimistic vision for the future, one where EA is willing to part with the Mass Effect IP and that the fans “come together to own this IP as kind of a Mass Effect collective for the fans by the community, because there's some incredible devs in this community, incredible creators.”

Much has been made of if EA will sell off BioWare as a way of paying off the debt it’s taken on as a result of its sale. Though BioWare is closed, all its assets and franchises — from Mass Effect to Dragon Age to Jade Empire — still belong to EA. Former BioWare executive Mark Darrah thinks it’s possible EA could sell off BioWare IP, while former technical director Romain Toutain thinks it’s unlikely EA would sell anything. Regardless, that won’t stop people like Hale and Meer from hoping. “That was my dream that happened right away,” Hale said. “I like to hold onto the fiction that makes me feel good, because you never know.”

That’s a sentiment the community will surely share, especially as the shock of BioWare’s closure hasn’t completely gone away yet. Fans are still sharing their grief and love online, and the Shepards have noticed.

“The outpouring of love for those games, it was something to behold,” Meer said. He and Hale both support the #SaveMassEffect petition (which has more than 300,000 signatures), but noted they do not have any sort of organizational role in the campaign. “Ultimately, I think it's people showing that they're not really ready to let this universe go, and they would like to see more of it,” Meer said. “If it is just them showing how much it's meant to them, I think that's valid as well.”

All of this has happened on the eve of N7 Day, an annual celebration of all things Mass Effect that falls on Nov. 7. (Chosen because of Shepard’s in-universe N7 designation — it essentially means they’re the cream of the crop among humanity’s soldiers.) Cast members from Mass Effect have gathered on N7 Day the past few years, and this year will be no different.

“I don't think [N7 Day is] going to go away,” Meer said. “The fans have been doing it themselves for the last few years. So I think that you're going to see that continue.” He’s excited to see the fans post about Mass Effect, especially the cosplayers, and will gladly share them.

“Mass Effect hasn't needed a company behind it for a few years in order to have the kind of community power that it has,” Hale said. “Nobody has switched off the light or cut off the electricity, because the community is the electricity. Maybe there's not another game itself in development at the moment, but Mass Effect has a life of its own.”

Hale has been in the video games industry for decades, and acted in BioWare games even before Mass Effect, as did Meer. She’s seen how much things can change, and how the industry is currently in a cycle of corporations trying to get bigger and bigger. Companies are absorbing and purchasing each other at rates that are unprecedented compared to even a few years ago. “It's very hard to make creative turns” at the sizes they’re at, Hale said. She compared the current state of corporate culture to the mobile game Slither.io, where you play as a snake gobbling up other snakes until it becomes too large and easily dies. “And then all the little worms take over. It's kind of like that,” Hale said.

She’s hopeful indie studios will be those “little worms” rising up, and you can see some of that already. Mass Effect director Casey Hudson left BioWare years ago, and eventually co-founded Arcanaut Studios (also based in Edmonton). He’s directing Arcanaut’s upcoming Star Wars: Fate of the Old Republic. Next year’s I-can’t-believe-it’s-not-Mass-Effect Exodus is the first game from Archetype Entertainment, a studio that’s home to several BioWare veterans.

Those games and more will carry the BioWare torch forward. “There is this real thirst for games that really have storytelling and a narrative,” Meer said. He named that rich storytelling and “characters that people really took into their hearts” as BioWare’s legacy. Because even if the studio is gone, the memories players made with characters like Garrus, Tali, Joker, Liara, and more aren’t.

“Things have their seasons,” Meer said. “Hopefully we shall see the season for Mass Effect again.”

#3594. Thunderbolts Storyboards Reveal A Major Marvel Character Was Cut From The Team

Marvel Studios' "Thunderbolts*" assembled the most motley crew of heroes in the Marvel Universe yet, and turned that collection of ex-assassins and criminals into the New Avengers. The Thunderbolts/New Avengers stand out mostly due to their lack of flashy superpowers, aside from Ghost's (Hannah John-Kamen) intangibility and Bob/Sentry's (Lewis Pullman) shadow-controlling alter ego, the Void. The rest are merely highly trained humans, some with a boost from knockoff super-soldier serums.

But a leaked storyboard frame, credited to artist Anthony Winn, show a much stranger character was considered to appear in "Thunderbolts*" — The Man-Thing, aka Dr. Ted Sallis. (See the storyboards of Man-Thing in "Thunderbolts*" below.)

A mix of science and magic turned Ted into a giant being made of plant and swamp matter, the Man-Thing. Created in 1971 by Stan Lee, Roy Thomas, and Gerry Conway, Man-Thing has been a member of the Thunderbolts in the comics. Including him in the movie would be drawing on that history.

"Thunderbolts*" director Jake Schreier previously said, in an interview with SFX Magazine, that he had wanted Man-Thing to appear in the movie. But Marvel had other plans for the character, and "it all worked out for the best." Those plans were the 2022 Disney+ special "Werewolf by Night," where titular werewolf Jack Russell (Gael García Bernal) saves Man-Thing from being hunted by the monster hunters of Bloodstone Manor. Personally, I'd think "Werewolf By Night" setting up Man-Thing's existence in the MCU would've made it easier for "Thunderbolts*" to include him, but apparently that was not the case.

It was rumored that Marvel Studios was considering a "Thunderbolts" movie for several years before "Thunderbolts*" actually arrived in theaters come 2025. Rumors from 2019 suggested a completely different team line-up was in consideration: Ghost, Zemo (Daniel Brühl) from "Captain America: Civil War," Justin Hammer (Sam Rockwell) from "Iron Man 2," and General Thaddeus Ross (the late William Hurt), Emil Blonsky/Abomination (Tim Roth), and Samuel Sterns/The Leader (Tim Blake Nelson) from "The Incredible Hulk."

Ghost is the only overlap between this lineup and the final movie's. Instead, a mostly-reformed Abomination guest-starred in Disney+ "She-Hulk" while Ross (recast with Harrison Ford in the role) and the Leader were key villains in "Captain America: Brave New World." Zemo returned in Disney+ series "The Falcon and the Winter Soldier," which introduced eventual Thunderbolts member John Walker (Wyatt Russell). Zemo (who, in the comics, founded the Thunderbolts) was planned to appear in a "Thunderbolts*" post-credits scene, but the idea was scrapped.

The final cast of "Thunderbolts*" pulled mostly from 2021's "Black Widow," and could've gone even further. "Black Widow" villain Taskmaster (Olga Kurylenko) shows up at the Thunderbolts' first meeting but is killed by Ghost. She was meant to have a larger role originally, but that wound up on the cutting room floor.

While he didn't make it into "Thunderbolts*" and hasn't been seen since "Werewolf By Night," will Man-Thing return to the MCU? In a recent episode of "VisionQuest," the assassin Paladin (Todd Stashwick) mentions tangling with a werewolf who is a nice guy during the daytime. That's almost certainly Jack Russell, so the MCU hasn't completely forgotten about "Werewolf By Night."

#3593. If You Loved 'Below,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Foggy, cold, and hardscrabble, the community of Snook’s Arm, Newfoundland, is the perfect spot for ocean-borne horror in Netflix's Below. This sense of place sets the series apart, though the characters who inhabit it are equally fascinating. Led by Josh Hartnett’s grounded performance as Calvin, the show has atmosphere for days, and a creepy and compelling story that effortlessly balances chills and deep emotional beats.

If you ate this show up like a voracious sea creature and you’re craving more slow-burn, deeply human horror (and you’ve already explored all the similar streaming series out there), it’s time to move on to feature-length terror, and there's one classic movie that fits the bill.

When it comes to kindred sea monster stories, Jaws is the obvious choice. Seaside setting? Check—a pre-glam Martha’s Vineyard stands in for Amity Island, with beautiful beaches and crashing waves to spare. A tight community under threat? Check—Amity Island feels like a very real place, and its citizens have concerns and grudges as legitimate as Calvin’s in Below. Shocks and frights? This is Jaws, a film that transformed the entire business of blockbuster movies, renowned to this day for its masterful depiction of a relentless natural force threatening an entire town.

The basic story also echoes Below's: When a young woman is killed by a shark during a night swim, Amity Island Police Chief Martin Brody (Roy Scheider) tries to close the beaches to protect the public, but Mayor Vaughn (Murray Hamilton) refuses, as Amity Island depends on the tourist trade for its survival. After a young boy is killed, Brody teams up with shark hunter Quint (Robert Shaw) and oceanographer Hooper (Richard Dreyfuss) to hunt the beast, and the three soon find themselves in over their heads as they discover how big and relentless the shark really is. Both stories share themes of economic necessity trumping safety in a changing world and concepts of a small group of people fighting a terrifying natural threat.

Like almost every horror film or series since 1975, Below owes a debt to Jaws in terms of storytelling and technique. From the isolated, ocean-centric setting (and monster) to the way Below shows you only flashes of its central terror, if you enjoyed the series, you will absolutely love the classic that influenced it. Stream Jaws on Netflix, or rent it on Prime Video.

Already seen Jaws, or rewatched it, and still in need of more terrifying movies in the same vein as Below? Here are a few more movies that you’ll love.

The Bay takes a different approach to its scares than Below—it’s a found-footage horror film. But it shares the remote, water-centric setting, the focus on a small community, and a story that pulls from the terror of a fundamental element—water—being polluted and corrupted. In the coastal community of Claridge, Maryland, citizens fall severely ill and begin dying in large numbers, sparking chaos. As investigators race to discover the source of the affliction, the carnage gets seriously gnarly. Just like in Below, the ultimate threat stems from the way people recklessly abuse the world we depend on for survival, and the local residents are center stage in the fight. Stream The Bay on Tubi or rent it on Prime Video.

One aspect of Below that resonates strongly with viewers is the human element; the Penney family’s internal tensions feel earned and real, and the way the larger community struggles with several existential crises is messy in a gloriously human way. The Host is also about a family struggling against a horrific, waterborne monster—when a mutant creature attacks a crowd near the Han River, Park Gang-du loses his grip on his young daughter, and she’s snatched up by the monster. But when Gang-du receives a phone call from his daughter telling him she’s still alive but trapped with the creature in the sewers, his family escapes quarantine, gears up, and goes after her, no matter the odds (or the corrupt government agencies standing in the way). Stream The Host on Kanopy or rent it on Prime Video.

Based on H.P. Lovecraft’s The Shadow Over Innsmouth, Dagon begins with four friends on a boat off the coast of Spain. When a storm wrecks the boat and injures one of them, a couple—Paul and Barbara—travel on foot to a nearby village to seek help. What they find instead is a terrifying place paying the price for worshiping a demon named Dagon in exchange for wealth and safety—but at a price that slowly rose, eventually transforming the villagers into something inhuman. Just like Below, the movie explores the choices communities make to survive, and the personal costs that aren’t always clearly understood. Stream Dagon on The Roku Channel or Tubi, or rent it on Prime Video.

If you loved Below’s foggy, liminal feel and the constant dread of what might be lurking in the mist or under the waves, unseen until it’s too late, John Carpenter’s classic is a must-watch. As the small coastal town of Antonio Bay approaches the centennial of its founding, a strange fog rolls in from the sea and envelopes the town. As the body count rises, the true story of the town’s founding and subsequent prosperity is revealed—and the long-deferred price for the crimes of the town’s ancestors is in the fog, determined to find some element of justice. Stream The Fog on Kanopy or Plex, or rent it on Prime Video.

If remote communities like Snook’s Arm are inherently creepy to you, check out Offseason. When Marie (Jocelin Donahue) learns that her mother has passed away and has been buried in Lone Palm, the isolated beach town where she grew up, she’s outraged—her mother was very clear that she didn’t want to be buried there. Marie travels to Lone Palm as tourist season ends, just a day before the bridge to the mainland closes for the year, which gives the town a liminal, nightmarish aspect familiar to anyone who’s lived in a tourist town during the offseason. As a storm moves in, Marie and her boyfriend find the townsfolk behaving quite strangely—and soon, it all whips up into a maelstrom of terror that fans of Below will appreciate. Stream Offseason on Hoopla or rent it on Prime Video.

Bobby Flay definitely hasn't left The Food Network, as he’s got plenty of competition shows to host amid the 2026 TV schedule. But, outside of cooking up a storm, he has also cooked up some sweet love with American chef and restaurateur Brooke Williamson. However, he didn’t do it alone. Flay recently credited actress Scarlett Johansson with his meet-cute romance, and I definitely wasn't expecting to get these details.

While Flay and Williamson interviewed with People, he spoke about hanging out with a friend who helped set him up with his romantic partner. Without name-dropping, he gave some hints like this friend being a huge movie star and being married to SNL’s Colin Jost. Of course, that latter detail was a dead giveaway regarding Johansson!

Flay apparently first met Williamson when they were both judges of Supermarket Stakeout back in 2020. However, he didn’t get together with the Top Chef winner until season 6 of BBQ Brawl five years later. Here’s his true tale of why it took him so long to ask Williamson out and how Johansson helped pick up the pace:

And I was just telling [Johansson] this quandary I was having that I was, like, totally falling for somebody that I work with. And I’m just frustrated because I’m not gonna go there. And I just don’t know what to do. And she told me I was out of my mind. That’s how I sort of came to terms with it. And literally on the very last day of that season of BBQ Brawl, I went up to [Williamson] and I was like, ‘I need to talk to you about something.’ And she’s like, ‘What?’ And I was like, ‘If you’re still interested…’ It had gone on for a while. ‘If you’re still interested, I’m ready to make a commitment to you.’ And that was sort of the beginning of the beginning. There was nothing but support and thrilled that we had decided to make it an actual thing.

Aww, that is too cute for words! It’s adorable that, for a man who knows how to put two and two together when cooking up a delicious dish, he had trouble putting himself together with his beautiful co-worker. I also can't help but love Johansson’s honesty in telling her friend to make a move. The actress may have only played Black Widow in the Marvel movies, but she was a real hero for Flay. And now, Flay and Williamson have been together for over a year.

Before Brooke Williamson, Flay was married three times, so he's certainly had his share of experience with relationships. With that in mind, Flay went on to explain to People what he wanted in a new romance and how that all aligned with Williamson:

I mean, to me, the most important thing is I want a life partner that I’m committed to. I don’t need all of the documentation. But at the same time, I need to make sure that Brooke feels like she’s committed to. We were in London and we were sitting on a bench in The Regent’s Park, and I was like, ‘I got you a gift.’ And I said, ‘But before I give you the gift, like, you’re cool with not getting married, right? Like, we’re on the same page?’ Because we had obviously talked about that. And she’s like, ‘Yeah, yeah, absolutely.’ I was like, ‘Okay.’

So Flay surprised his partner with a huge diamond ring that cemented his commitment to her without a wedding of sorts. To some, it may seem confusing to give the woman you love a ring without the promise of marriage. However, I find it pretty cute, as it’s like a promise ring that still pledges loyalty. And, of course, at the end of the day, it's Flay and Williamson's business as to what they want their relationship to be.

On that note, Bobby Flay and Brooke Williamson seem to be quite happy, and I love to see it. Also, kudos to Scarlett Johansson for intervening a playing a bit of cupid. Fans can watch Flay and Williamson’s Food Network shows using a Hulu subscription or an HBO Max subscription.

Just your average South Floridian cinephile who believes the pen is mightier than the sword.

#3591. Netflix's Answer To Hazbin Hotel Has Much Higher Rotten Tomatoes Scores

It's hard to overstate the pop culture impact of Hazbin Hotel, but Netflix's answer to the beloved adult animated series is even more critically acclaimed. Hazbin Hotel had a storied journey to the small screen, beginning as a YouTube pilot by Vivienne Medrano that debuted in 2019. The pilot racked up tens of millions of views before production companies A24 and Bento Box picked it up, and it premiered on Prime Video in 2024.

The series, an explicit musical black comedy, centers on the plucky princess of Hell, Charlie Morningstar (Erika Henningsen), who uses her titular hotel as a rehabilitation center to redeem sinners so they can be accepted into heaven. This inventive premise has united typically disparate subcultures, from musical theater lovers to die-hard animation fans, earning GLAAD nominations and over a billion Spotify streams for its soundtrack. With season 2 airing in 2025, Hazbin Hotel has seen such a streaming success that Prime Video renewed it for three additional seasons, with season 5 being its last.

Though not an exact Hazbin Hotel replica, Netflix has a similar comedy series: Haunted Hotel. Created by Rick and Morty and Community writer Matt Roller and executive produced by Dan Harmon, Haunted Hotel premiered on Netflix in 2025. After two seasons and with Haunted Hotel season 3 officially confirmed, the Netflix show may not have reached the pop culture heights of its Prime Video competitor, but it beats Hazbin Hotel in one major way.

Beyond titles that could easily be mistaken for one another, Hazbin Hotel and Haunted Hotel have rather similar premises. In Haunted Hotel, single mom Katherine Freeling (Eliza Coupe) moves to upstate New York with her two children, where she becomes the reluctant owner of the Undervale Hotel. Things hit a snag when Katherine discovers that the hotel is full of zany undead spirits, including her deceased older brother Nathan (Will Forte), all of whom refuse to check out.

While both shows follow lovable women in over their heads trying to corral a bunch of ghosts into doing what's right (or at least paying their hotel bill), Haunted Hotel and Hazbin Hotel differ fundamentallyin tone. Haunted Hotel is a dysfunctional family sitcom with a supernatural twist, while Hazbin Hotel is a full-on musical extravaganza.

Hazbin Hotel season 3 is in the works, but series creator Vivienne Medrano has now revealed the fate of season 5 of the hit animated series.

Hazbin Hotel's massive fandom is entirely thanks to its inventiveness, but this may be why it has a slightly lower Rotten Tomatoes score than Haunted Hotel: 85% compared to Haunted Hotel's 89%. Take this with a grain of salt, since Hazbin Hotel has twice as many reviews on the aggregator site as Haunted Hotel, but it still reinforces that a fresh take on the familiar will almost always get more praise than a wild swing—even if it's a hit.

If Haunted Hotel and Hazbin Hotel don't give you enough of a supernatural adult animated series fix, there's also Helluva Boss. A Hazbin Hotel spinoff, Helluva Boss focuses on another business: Immediate Murder Professionals, aka I.M.P. Run by literal imps, I.M.P. is an assassination company that carries out hits on the living on behalf of vengeance-seeking sinners.

Choose the movie with the higher Rotten Tomatoes score.

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

Sign in to claim your place on the leaderboard!

As it's also created by Medrano and takes place in the same universe as Hazbin Hotel, expect the same rousing musical numbers and even darker humor. However, Helluva Boss is actually more similar to Haunted Hotel in that, rather than having a sweeping serialized narrative like Hazbin Hotel, it's much more episodic, focusing on the day-to-day pains of running a business, albeit a very unconventional one. No matter which series is your favorite, it's a helluva ​​​​​​good time to be an animation fan.
