#3590. I Tested Strava's New Integration With Gemini, and I Have Thoughts

Once connected, you can ask questions like:

"Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?"

"Can you give me a detailed analysis of how I performed in my last race?"

"How is my strength training impacting my running?"

Some important context here: Strava's AI "insights" have sort of sucked, and annoyed me, in the past. Athlete Intelligence (conveniently abbreviated as AI) is the Strava feature that writes text responses to your workouts. Strava calls these "insights," but as far as I can tell they mostly regurgitate the information from the workout description, sometimes with added errors. I've found AI fitness summaries largely useless, and Strava's version checks every box: It doesn't use enough context to understand what's going on, it presents generic advice as if it were personal, and it's overconfident in incomplete data. So, skeptical as I am, I gave Strava's latest Google Gemini integration a whirl. Here's what it does, how to set it up, and whether it's worth it.

The first question I asked was one of Strava’s examples, "Am I getting faster at the same heart rate?" Gemini said yes, I was seeing solid efficiency gains. Like many AI tools, it told me what I wanted to hear. I had to point out that heat and temperature are huge variables. When I steered the chat in that direction, Gemini, of course, agreed immediately ("you hit the nail on the head") and explained that my mid-September long runs happened in 75–84°F weather with higher humidity, which inflates heart rate, while October's cooler temperatures made the same effort look better. That's an important caveat the first answer left out entirely.

I then asked it to compare my past marathons, and in many ways, I had fun here. For instance, the suggested follow-ups prompted me to think of questions I hadn't put on my list, like comparing my weekly running volume and long-run frequency leading into different races in different years.

Unfortunately, the results weren't reliable at first. When I asked for a detailed analysis of every marathon-distance effort since 2019, Gemini said I had exactly one, the Marine Corps Marathon on October 25, 2026. In reality, I've logged at least eight. When I asked why it couldn't see them, it explained that its access is limited to my recent history, roughly summer 2026 onward, because of how pagination limits the number of past activities returned at once. It also offered a workaround: Give it specific dates and locations.

That workaround works, but it means you have to already know what you're looking for. And still, it wasn't consistent. In other answers, Gemini referenced my 2025 NYC Marathon and 2024 Philadelphia race, so the data's reach seems uneven. You need to be able to query older date ranges as directly and specifically as possible, and even still, double-check any numbers that matter to you.

I then asked "What am I doing right and what am I doing wrong as a runner?" After knowing the queries need to be so specific, I intentionally wanted to test a vague, simplistic question. The answer was, true to form, overly flattering—though I didn't disagree with the guidance itself. I need more speed workouts! I know this! I didn't need a chatbot to tell me, though maybe some other Strava user does. Gemini's suggestions (polarize training, add one dedicated threshold day) are sound, yes, but they’re also generic. Most recreational runners could glance at my Strava and spot the same strengths and weaknesses. Similarly, Gemini then set itself up for a slam dunk by prompting me to ask whether my easy runs were too fast. The answer: My easy days were happening at nearly my marathon pace (about 9:43/mi), and I should slow down by 45–90 seconds per mile, to roughly 10:30–11:15/mi. I completely agree. That being said, my big takeaway here remains the same: Don't confuse AI-generated advice as some newfound, personalized insight. It’s often the same conventional wisdom you already know, or could figure out with a tiny bit of research from a real, human source.

If you ask me—a human!—this is a classic case of using AI for rote tasks, but then saving critical thinking for your own human brain. Gemini didn't surface anything wildly insightful, and it skipped important considerations like the effect of heat on heart rate, until I raised them myself. But it pulled data faster than I could have by hand, and its follow-up prompts nudged me toward comparisons I might not have thought of.

For many users, the smartest approach may be to skip AI summaries and focus on raw data. After all, your training load, sleep duration, and heart rate trends are already perfectly actionable.

As with all things AI, it’s important to mind the gap between data and wisdom. So much wisdom gets lost—forfeited, even—when you blindly trust an AI coach. Make sure you aren’t offloading all the other skills you need as a runner and as a human, like your ability to listen to your body and maybe run a little slower in the heat, even when it makes your data look “worse.”

If you do use Google Gemini to analyze your Strava data:

Be specific about dates and locations when asking about older activities.

Push back. Ask about weather, terrain, and fatigue before accepting a flattering conclusion.

Treat the output as a fast data pull, not a personal coach.

#3589. Why Project Hail Mary Author Andy Weir Thinks Sci-Fi Has 'Grown Up' Recently [Exclusive]

In an interview with /Film's Jeremy Mathai, Andy Weir, the author of the hit novels "The Martian" and "Project Hail Mary," recognized that the world has never been more accepting of sci-fi. What was once relegated to the realm of "nerds" and outsiders several generations ago is now embraced by everyone. And that, Weir noted, has allowed artists to tell more serious and dramatic sci-fi stories. When a mass audience takes it seriously, the genre, consequently, grows up.

And Weir has been doing his part to raise the genre's profile. The films based on his novels — Ridley Scott's "The Martian," and Phil Lord and Christopher Miller's "Project Hail Mary," to call them out by name — are known for their scientific rigor (especially "The Martian"). And although possessed of fantastical sci-fi conceits, both movies pay a lot of attention to science, research, and the power of human intelligence. These are movies for grown-ups that don't soft-pedal or water down the details of astronomy, physics, language, or botany. As such, these films come across as being comparatively "adult."

Weir also credited this in part to the various superhero films that've come out in the 21st Century. Many of those movies have sci-fi elements, and even a piece of Marvel fantasy fluff can bring more grown-up credibility to the genre. As Weir put it, "The superhero movie phenomenon helped bring more science fiction elements into the mainstream."

To be sure, artificial intelligence, parallel universes, and time travel frequently show up in superhero stories, and the genre's popularity has made a lot of those strange scientific theories a regular part of mainstream thinking. Yes, in that sense, even the box office smash-hit that was "Iron Man" helped the sci-fi genre grow up.

The recent boom of high-quality sci-fi television also came up during this discussion with Andy Weir. Just turn on Apple TV alone, and you'll find the cream of the crop in terms of modern sci-fi TV, be it "Severance," "Pluribus," "Foundation," or "Silo." Commenting on this, Weir noted:

"I think [the genre has] grown up a bit. So, it used to be science fiction was the bailiwick of just nerds. In the '80s, there were a few sci-fi shows. There was 'Star Trek: Next Generation' toward the end of the '80s. Then there was things like 'Quantum Leap,' and stuff like that. But other than that, the sci-fi shows that did exist were kind of cheesy. You got 'Battlestar Galactica' [...] It wasn't big mainstream entertainment."

Some "Battlestar Galactica" and "Quantum Leap" fans might bristle at these comments, but Weir is right on one point: sci-fi shows certainly seem more common nowadays. That, he argued, along with superhero movies and people now having access to more high-tech items, have further expanded their tolerance and devotion to the genre. As he put it:

[N]ow we've had a whole generation of people grow up in the computer age [...] [P]eople are a lot more socially accepting of science fiction as a legitimate setting [...] I love that there are serious, very well written, innovative and unique science fiction shows out there now."

Basically, sci-fi becomes real, essentially, sci-fi movies and TV shows become more normalized. And especially with all manner of sci-fi films having recently earned billions of dollars at the box office, it appears audiences, in general, are willing to give the genre more consideration, allowing sci-fi storytellers to take bigger risks in the process.

One thing I love about book-to-screen adaptations of classics like The Cat In The Hat is how each new iteration reimagines a character we already love. Bill Hader’s version comes over two decades after the Mike Myers movie, and one peculiar new thing I noticed about his animated take on the character is the fact that he has a flip phone. Random, right?

When CinemaBlend spoke to Hader about his latest role, I had to ask about the little detail I noticed about his The Cat In The Hat. Here’s how the SNL alum responded:

Because Cat in the Hat's real. Cat in the Hat doesn't need to fit in with whatever's happening now, you know?

For some reason, it just feels right that The Cat would have a flip phone (and one that even has a crystal-clear video chat function). Plus, this detail about The Cat definitely adds to his unique character in a cute way, as it's revealed in the film that he’s been doing house calls to bring play into the lives of kids for multiple generations. So, perhaps the flip phone tells us that he's a bit old school. Bill Hader also said this about the topic:

I think it was funny that it was a flip phone. I have friends who have flip phones, and they remember things better than me. They are not as distracted as me. They seem much happier than me.

Hey, maybe The Cat is onto something. I mean the character is all about bringing playtime and wonder to kids. Why would he need a smartphone for that?

These days, a lot more people are ditching their smartphones for more primitive technology like flip phones to get away from things like social media addiction. Chris Pine, for example, had one for four years before switching to the latest technology and finding himself wanting to “immediately go back”. Other famous people known to have a flip phone are Christopher Nolan, Anna Wintour and Rihanna – so The Cat can count himself among icons.

A lot of other Y2K trends have been coming back lately, too. For example, both Kylie Jenner and Ariana Grande recently admitted their love for wired earphones (and I’m totally with them). I’ve seen a lot of younger people out with their digital cameras at concerts too. When you think about it, The Cat In The Hat’s “dumb phone” is very in with the kids.

There’s already The Cat In The Hat trend; maybe this could be part of a new wave of less phone dependence and more focus on fun and creativity, like the character itself has been teaching kids since the picture book came out back in 1957.

You can check out the new The Cat In The Hat movie in theaters now.

#3587. Why Those Flashy Halloween Contacts Are a Bad Idea

Contacts with cat pupils or neon colors can be fun, but are you sure you want to put a piece of plastic from a costume store into your eye? Experts, like those at the American Academy of Ophthalmology, warn against it. These non-prescription contacts are technically illegal in the U.S. (even though plenty of companies sell them anyway). The CDC warns that the risks include "eye sores and vision loss."

Cheap Halloween contacts tend to be one-size-fits-all, but the AAO points out that contacts should never be one-size-fits-all. A contact that is too large or too small for your eye can cause corneal abrasions, corneal ulcers, and can result in infections like keratitis. Infections can, in severe cases, lead to blindness. A 2017 report from the FDA found bacterial contamination in 27% of costume contacts.

If you do wear contacts (Halloween or otherwise), the AAO recommends keeping an eye out for symptoms like redness, swelling, pain, or excessive discharge. Seek care as soon as you suspect an infection. Your eyes are more sensitive to infections than other parts of the body, so be cautious.

Legally, contacts require a prescription, so if those colored contacts you're eyeing can be bought without showing a doctor’s prescription, they’re not legit. The real thing can be expensive, though: I found prices of $40 and up from lens.com, Discount Contacts, and Wicked Eyez.

These websites all let you order online, but you’ll have to provide your prescription information before you can check out. Fortunately, the Federal Trade Commission has ruled that providers must give you your contact prescription after a fitting so that you can take the prescription elsewhere. And they cannot charge you extra for this.

Once you’ve got the lenses, you have to know how to take care of them. If you wear contacts every day, you already know the drill. But if you’re just picking up a pair to use with a costume, here are the basics:

Wash your hands before handling the lenses.

Store them in contact lens solution, and keep the lenses and their case clean.

And for Pete’s sake, don’t share them with your friends!

Just remember, the bloodshot look stops being cool after you take your zombie costume off.

#3585. Godzilla Minus Zero Shuts Down One Of The Biggest Criticisms Of The Franchise

This article contains light spoilers for "Godzilla Minus Zero."

Godzilla has enjoyed a lasting popularity over his 70+ year existence, and it's no surprise. Ishirō Honda's 1954 "Godzilla" not only had a great title creature, but also involved a surprisingly weighty human drama that combined a love triangle with huge ethical conundrums, all of which fed into the film's impressively deep thematic material. It's a killer mixture, and Honda's movie is still thought of as one of the best movies ever made in the franchise all these years later. Although Toho Studios didn't immediately push the series towards bigger spectacle, the "Godzilla" films naturally took that course. Each successive film began creating bigger monster attack setpieces, and generated greater destruction by pitting the various monsters against each other.

This direction left any human characters with less screen time and importance in each movie. As such, the various writers and directors began to treat them more as perfunctory protagonists. While there have been several attempts to course correct this, it's a problem that persists. Even the MonsterVerse films have fallen prey to the common criticism that the human characters are second-rate.

This is part of why Takashi Yamazaki's "Godzilla Minus One" felt like such a breath of fresh air. That movie features a human story that is undeniably the core of the film, with Godzilla being more of a supporting feature. That approach continues in the sequel, "Godzilla Minus Zero," which doubles down on the great character work "Minus One" did by continuing the stories of already established characters, while also adding a few great new ones.

To be fair, there have been many prior movies in the "Godziilla" franchise that have featured some really compelling human characters and storylines to go with them. A few which leap to mind are "Godzilla vs. Biollante," "Godzilla vs. Destoroyah," and "Shin Godzilla." What these movies do well is find characters and a story that isn't completely based around attacks by Godzilla or other giant monsters, meaning that the characters are as proactive as they are reactive. When the latter becomes their primary function, the movies themselves essentially train the audience to not care about the humans as much, teaching them to wait patiently until the next big action scene occurs. In this way, the issues that some "Godzilla" movies have aren't all that different from a similar problem many genre movies face.

Where Takashi Yamazaki transcends this issue in "Godzilla Minus Zero" is in the way that he creates dramatic tension between the characters and Godzilla (or, in the film's case, Ghidorah) appearing. We the audience wish to see the giant monsters we came for, but Yamazaki's story positions many of these people as those who would likely be worse off should they turn up. Scientist Kenji Noda (Hidetaka Yoshioka) is barely keeping a still-hurting Japan's head above water post World War II, let alone having to deal with kaiju attacks. The continued existence of Ghidorah is a personal burden to meterologist Makoto Aoyama (Masami Nagasawa), while Godzilla's abilities present a dark temptation to professor Kanji Murakami (Min Tanaka). Meanwhile, Kōichi Shikishima (Ryunosuke Kamiki), who found his will to live in "Minus One," is struggling like mad to keep his family together. Yet in addition to caring for adopted daughter Akiko (Saw Nagatani), his wife Noriko (Minami Hamabe) has been infected with Godzillas cells, which may end up killing her or could be used in other ways. The tension between wanting to see Godzilla and not wanting these people to suffer as a result is what Yamazaki exploits so beautifully.

One of the most impressive aspects of "Godzilla Minus Zero" is its restraint. As a big-budget direct sequel to the very successful "Godzilla Minus One," it would've made sense for Takashi Yamazaki and his crew to go bigger with the film's visual effects. The temptation to do this must've been especially great considering that "Minus One" won the Academy Award for Best Visual Effects, making it the first "Godzilla" film ever to win an Oscar. Given that triumph, it's actually rather remarkable that Yamazaki didn't turn "Minus Zero" into a VFX extravaganza.

Instead, Yamazaki appears to deeply understand what makes visual effects great, which is their ability to enhance an already good story and its characters. The action sequences in "Minus Zero" are memorable because of how uniquely designed they are and how they utilize the characters. Moments like Shikishima flying through a village that's been upended by Ghidorah's gravity beam and Noda having to race against time to spring a trap on Ghidorah are made better because of the characters being directly involved in the action, not just observing.

All of this is why the big climax of "Godzilla Minus Zero" has relatively little to do with Godzilla and Ghidorah and is mostly to do with the fates of the human characters themselves. In a lesser movie, such scenes would feel like an obligatory denouement. in "Minus Zero," they're as riveting as anything else in the film. It may have taken over 70 years, but "Godzilla" has indeed finally circled back to where it began: a human drama that happens to feature a giant monster (charismatic as he may be).

"Godzilla Minus Zero" is in theaters now.

#3583. Gilligan's Island Star Jim Backus Voiced One Of Animation's Most Famous Characters

Though he may not be a household name today, Jim Backus was a well known character actor in the mid-20th Century. Of course, his most recognizable role will forever remain Thurston Howell III from "Gilligan's Island," as Backus brought a suitably refined energy to the part of a New England patrician stranded alongside other societal archetypes in the South Pacific. But Backus' career stretched far beyond three seasons of a beloved CBS sitcom. Both prior to and after becoming trapped on the Isle, for instance, he voiced the animated character Quincy Magoo, better known as Mr. Magoo — a role he played from 1949 until 1977.

The actor's pre-Thurston Howell career was already impressive. Before "Gilligan's Island," Backus appeared opposite Clint Eastwood in the movie "Francis in the Navy," although he gained far more in the way of significant recognition for putting on an acting masterclass as the Stark family patriarch, Frank Stark, in the James Dean classic "Rebel Without a Cause." That likely would've gone down as his biggest non-"Gilligan's Island" role, too, if it weren't for the fact he voiced Mr. Magoo for some three decades.

Like Thurston Howell, Mr. Magoo was a millionaire. Unlike Thurston Howell, however, this deep-pocketed, diminutive magnate had a severe case of near-sightedness — a condition he refused to acknowledge. Created by Millard Kaufman and John Hubley for the animation studio United Productions of America, Mr. Magoo first appeared in the 1949 theatrical short "The Ragtime Bear," which became a hit and ensured the character would stick around for a truly incredible amount of time. Indeed, the most recent "Mr. Magoo" cartoon ended in 2023, well after Backus had passed away. Still, he did voice the character for his first 30-ish years, arguably making Mr. Magoo Backus' most important role.

In a piece for Cinema Journal title "Memories of Mr. Magoo" (via JSTOR), producer Howard Rieder recalled how, long before Jim Backus' casting caused rewrites on "Gilligan's Island," the actor came to be hired for "The Ragtime Bear." It seems co-creator John Hubley asked actor Jerry Hausner, who voiced the character of Mr. Magoo's nephew and frequent sidekick Waldo, to help him find a suitable star. According to Rieder, Hausner remembered that Backus had arrived from New York where he was voicing the haughty playboy Hubert Updike III as part of the radio series "The Alan Young Show." It seems the actor was playing snooty millionaires long before he set foot on Gilligan's Isle.

According to Hausner's recollection, Backus was "fairly well-known" as the voice of Updike, and he seemed perfect for the voice of Mr. Magoo. "We had been friends for over 20 years," recalled Hausner (via Rieder). "I spoke to Hubley about Backus, and he wanted to meet him." Evidently, Backus was already well-established by this point, and Hubley didn't want to make him audition. Instead, he took him to the UPA studios and showed him character designs and storyboards. There, Backus found a personal connection to the character. As Hausner explained:

"He said, 'My father lives in his own little world, never quite seeing things the way they really are. It isn't that he's nearsighted, but his whole attitude toward life is a kind of personal isolation toward the rest of the world.' Backus mentioned that he used to do a character called the Man in the Club Car. It was the character of the businessman, the tycoon, the loudmouth talker [...] He began to use this voice and it was the voice that ultimately became Mr. Magoo."

After making his debut as Mr. Magoo in "The Ragtime Bear," Jim Backus went on to voice the character in multiple theatrical cartoons and the 1960s syndicated TV series "Mister Magoo." He returned to voice the character in multiple TV specials, along with two follow-up series: "The Famous Adventures of Mr. Magoo," which aired between 1964 and '65, and "What's New, Mr. Magoo?" in 1977.

Over the course of his multiple films and series, the character evolved from a mean-spirited, irascible toff to a senescent, lovable buffoon. The comedy arose from his inability to recognize the often precarious and dangerous situations into which he frequently stumbled due to his near-sightedness. And while those around him were perpetually stressed by his near-misses, due to sheer luck, Mr. Magoo always seemed to come out unscathed.

Backus gave voice to this miraculously lucky millionaire right up until the end of "What's New, Mr. Magoo?" in 1977 — the year before he returned as Thurston Howell III for one of the three "Gilligan's Island" TV movies, "Rescue from Gilligan's Island." Unfortunately, the actor was in bad health by the time he made a brief cameo appearance in 1981's "The Harlem Globetrotters on Gilligan's Island," and he passed away in 1989.

Mr. Magoo, however, endured. Not only did the Backus-voiced version remain part of popular culture via syndication deals, Leslie Nielsen played the character in an ill-fated 1997 live-action film that became a box office disappointment and debuted to negative reviews. More recently, a French animated series, "Mr. Magoo," began airing in 2019 and lasted until 2023.

Right now, the 65-inch QM8L is $1,197.99 (originally $2,499.99), $100 cheaper than it was just earlier this month, reaching its lowest price since it launched in April, according to price-tracking tools. Larger sizes are also seeing substantial discounts.

One of the first things you'll notice about the QM8L is the “Zero Border” bezel design, which gives it a modern, minimalistic look. When you turn it on, you'll likely note how bright this TV gets, which is a huge advantage QLEDs have over OLEDs. TCL claims it reaches 6,000 nits—seeing as the brightest OLED TV on the market only reaches 700 nits, no OLED can come close to this unit's brightness. Another important spec to note here is the local dimming zones: TCL claims this TV has up to 4,000, which means it gets top-tier backlight control, limited light blooming (thanks in part to TCL's "Halo Control"), and incredible contrast levels that some might not be able to distinguish from an OLED.

As many of us won't manually calibrate our TVs, the picture modes you can switch to in the settings will be most people's go-to. This TV's "Filmmaker mode" provides accurate color and picture, and if you're a gamer, you can use the native 144Hz high-refresh rate. If you don't already have a surround sound system at home and want to keep a minimalist setup, the QM8L comes with Dolby Atmos-ready Bang & Olufsen speakers, which offer above-average audio output compared to most TVs. You can read more about these features in CNET's 8.8/10 review. If 65 inches isn't quite right for your home theater setup, take a look at the QM8L's other sizes, which are also discounted right now.

#3580. I Wouldn’t Dream of Playing the Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Right Now

Some things are sacred. No, not like that!

Unlike you, probably, I am not playing Nintendo's Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time right now. I even turned down a kind offer from my editor to review it. This despite the fact that it might be my favorite Zelda game (mostly by virtue of being the first one I played) and indubitably one of the greatest games ever — as close to a Citizen Kane as the medium has.

I've read the ecstatic reviews, several of them by friends of mine, like Keza MacDonald and Christian Donlan, and of course Polygon's own Giovanni Colantonio, who I know to be people of good sense and great taste who share my reverence for this game and this series. I trust them.

Nintendo’s excellent Switch 2 remake recaptures the soul of a masterpiece

I also trust Nintendo, especially now it's clear the game was developed by the in-house Zelda team and not farmed out to an external studio. I trust producers Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi, veterans of Zelda's golden age and architects of its great Breath of the Wild renaissance, who Gio talked to this week. I trust their decision to pass Ocarina on to younger developers at Nintendo to train and inspire them, but also to inject the aging game with youth and life.

Nintendo's top Legend of Zelda producers talk the remake, the future, and more

I also know that Ocarina needs the work. I played a little of the Nintendo 64 original recently, and while I remained entranced by its strangely haunted vibe, I found that, like so many early 3D games, it is fighting a battle with clunky, barely-ready technology that it has been slowly losing over the last 28 years. I'm honestly not sure that it's still fun to play now.

Zelda's most infamous dungeon is no longer a frustrating rite of passage

And this matters to me, because my 10-year-old son loves Zelda — which, to him, means Tears of the Kingdom. He thinks Tears is the best game ever, and I wouldn't necessarily disagree. He's read the Ocarina of Time manga and fiddled about with other games in the series, including the Link's Awakening remake and The Wind Waker, but never settled into any of them. Honestly, I warned him off trying to play the original Ocarina.

So the Ocarina remake arrives at a perfect time for him. He is beyond excited about it. He will get it, and his own Switch 2 to play it on, for Christmas. Put yourself in his shoes. (Maybe you once were, and got the original Ocarina, or the 3DS version, as a childhood Christmas gift yourself.) Can you imagine anything better?

I just know that if I played the game before him, even surreptitiously, I would be stealing the magic of that moment. As desperate as I am to see the work of Aonuma and Fujibayashi's team, I can't countenance it. So I'll wait with him.

Also… If I'm honest, maybe I'm not just doing it for him. Because I'll be unwrapping my own copy on Christmas morning. I'll be playing this magical game away from work, out of step with the discourse, in the cozy, contented, quiet bubble of the holidays, surrounded by my family. Maybe I'll feel like I'm 10, too. Like I said: can you imagine anything better?

ZA/UM, the makers of Disco Elysium — well, some of them; it's complicated — return with another wonderfully funny, dark, and emotionally complex narrative RPG that uses tabletop dice rolls to enumerate the failings of human beings. One in particular: a not good, very bad spy who is trying to atone for a terrible betrayal.

Disco Elysium follow-up Zero Parades has serious staying power

This 1988 NES classic from Capcom is simply one of the all-time great action platformers. It's all the more remarkable since the developers basically had to cobble it together in their spare time after the original was deemed a sales disappointment. Now Mega Man is a treasured franchise, and due for a return next year.

I'm not playing Ocarina, but I am allowed to listen to the eight-track soundtrack sample that just dropped on Nintendo Music, and it's absolutely delicious. The exquisitely produced and performed new arrangements of Koji Kondo's immortal tunes are both a massive upgrade and resounding proof that Kondo had loaded his music with all this drama, humor, and sophistication from the start. Impossible to pick a favorite from the full flamenco of "Gerudo Valley," or the squawking penny whistles, accordions, oboes, and fiddles of "Market," or "Kakariko Village"'s plangeant harmonica. But let's go with the 10-minute "Hyrule Field Main Theme" for sheer epic sweep.

#3579. John Goodman Thinks He Shouldn't Have Starred In George Clooney's 2014 Critical Flop

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

George Clooney enjoys a heightened status in Hollywood. He is one of the most handsome and charismatic movie stars in the history of the medium, and he relishes the opportunity to make a total fool out of himself (especially if he's working for Joel and Ethan Coen). For a moment, his instincts were unerring. On the strength of "Confessions of a Dangerous Mind" and "Good Night, and Good Luck," those instincts seemed to extend to directing. His next two directorial efforts, "Leatherheads" and "The Ides of March," were solid, but they lacked the snap of his early work. Then he just up and lost it.

Clooney's last five movies — "The Monuments Men," "Suburbicon," "The Midnight Sky," "The Tender Bar" and "The Boys in the Boat" — are bizarrely inert. I revere Clooney as an actor (I wrote a book about him), and, via interviews with people who know him well, believe that he cares deeply about his art. But there's no passion in those aforementioned movies. They're smart, considered, compassionate works, but they've got a blasé point of view. Clooney admirably promotes a humanistic point of view, but there's no technical or intellectual rigor behind his efforts. It's like watching LeBron James make layups.

I hate writing this stuff because I know Clooney has it in him to make great films. But when I run into a series of comments from a serious actor like John Goodman about how he spent months working on "The Monuments Men" with Clooney, only to walk away wishing he hadn't made the movie, I wonder where it all went wrong. While Goodman admittedly had a good time making the film, he also confessed, "It was one of those movies ... I probably shouldn't have done."

During a recent SAG-AFTRA Foundation Q&A, Goodman dished on two films that, in his estimation, he shouldn't have done. One was John Landis' reviled "Saturday Night Live" movie sequel "Blues Brothers 2000," which at least gave the rhythm and blues aficionado the opportunity to work with music legends like Aretha Franklin, Wilson Pickett, and B.B. King. He didn't mention Landis' involvement in the deaths of Vic Morrow, Myca Dinh Le, and Renee Shin-Ye Lee on the set of "Twilight Zone: The Movie," but people were still making films with the director at the time.

The other was "The Monuments Men" with Clooney. According to Goodman, "George loves movies and he loves stories and he's such a great storyteller himself, and I think he's a great director. I had fun with him. 'Monuments Men.' We were over in Germany for six months. And England."

But the film about art experts being dropped into Europe during World War II to save the continent's cultural treasures was DOA critically and commercially. It's a handsomely mounted would-be epic, but the theme is clearly stated early on, which leaves Clooney nowhere to go narratively. Protecting art, reinforcing its importance in the middle of a war that threatens to end civilization, is a wildly worthwhile premise. Especially now. I just wish Clooney and co-screenwriter Grant Heslov hadn't taken a softball approach to this subject. We need a guy like Clooney hurling heat.

Amazon currently has the 32-inch Samsung Odyssey OLED G8 (G80SH) for $999.99, down from $1,299.99, and price trackers show that this is its lowest price so far. This is the newer 4K OLED model, not Samsung’s similarly named G80HS, which is a 6K IPS variant, and it makes the most sense for someone who wants one screen for both high-end gaming and everyday desktop use without moving to a larger ultrawide.

Its 4K QD-OLED panel runs at 240Hz, which gives the G80SH enough speed for competitive shooters and racing games while still keeping slower, more cinematic games looking sharp. You will need a powerful PC to get anywhere close to 4K at 240Hz, but the monitor is at least equipped for newer graphics hardware with DisplayPort 2.1 and HDMI 2.1. It also has USB-C with up to 98W of power delivery, so if this monitor doubles as a work setup, a compatible laptop can send video and charge over the same cable instead of adding another wire to your desk. FreeSync Premium Pro and G-SYNC compatibility should also help keep tearing under control, though OLED monitors can still show visible VRR flicker in darker scenes when frame pacing is inconsistent.

The bigger visual difference, though, shows up in darker games and HDR content, where blacks stay properly black and bright effects stand out without the blooming you often see on LCD monitors. That said, QD-OLED does have its own drawbacks, since blacks can take on a purplish tint in a brightly lit room, while burn-in remains a long-term concern—though Samsung does include active cooling and several screen-protection features to reduce uneven wear and says burn-in from normal use is covered under warranty. If you mostly play at lower frame rates or do not care much about OLED contrast, this is probably more monitor than you need, but for someone with the graphics hardware to take advantage of 4K at 240Hz, this discount makes the G80SH much easier to justify.

#3577. James Gray on His ‘Only Real Beef with Streaming’ and the ‘Recurring Nightmare’ That Started at Cannes in 2009

James Gray time-travels back to his Queens roots once again for his latest film, “Paper Tiger.” It’s a location, an atmosphere, a state of mind he’s explored across decades and genres, dating back to his 1994 debut feature, “Little Odessa.” Like “Paper Tiger,” “Little Odessa” also featured the shadows of the Russian mafia looming over a family unit — to devastating ends. But even 30-plus years later, with his new movie — starring Miles Teller, Adam Driver, and Scarlett Johansson — Gray wanted to go just as dangerous.

Adam Driver, for one, has danger in him, according to Gray, who cast the Oscar nominee as a former police officer who links up with the red mafia in the 1980s. Gray recently joined IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio for a wide-ranging, amusingly discursive live conversation at the Virginia Film Festival. One that showcased his knack for impressions — from Luca Guadagnino beckoning Gray out of this year’s Cannes to sit down for the Italian filmmaker’s Bernardo Bertolucci documentary, to the waves of disappointment cresting through Maximilian Schell during an early Venice screening of “Little Odessa.” Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“Almost all great performances have to have some measure of danger in them,” Gray said. “I can actually only think of one that doesn’t have any, which would probably be Jeff Bridges as The Dude in ‘The Big Lebowski,’ which has no danger at all.” (Though John Goodman’s PTSD-addled Vietnam vet in the Coens’ 1998 hardboiled slacker comedy qualifies as dangerous.)

“Adam is a fantastic, intense presence in [‘Paper Tiger’],” said Gray, who wrote “Paper Tiger” with Driver in mind.

Gray also spoke about the “recurring nightmares” for any filmmaker: “You screen your movie, and everybody walks out midway through. I’ve never had that happen to me, thank God.”

But one personal experience of watching this happen to someone else became seared in his unconscious: “When I was on the jury in Cannes [in 2009] … there was a movie made by a fantastic director. I won’t say his name, but he’s a great director of real reputation. And you have to sit in this jury box, which is sort of in the back of a theater, and the seats … when a person gets up, it’s spring-activated, and so it makes this very loud tack. I’m on the jury, and I’m watching this movie, and I start hearing tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack, tack. And people start walking out in droves. And the movie ended, and it was about half full, and people were booing. And that did become a nightmare for me. And by the way, I’m not the only director for whom that’s a nightmare. I’ve talked to many director friends of mine, and they’re like, ‘Oh, yeah. No, I’ve had that dream.'”

James Gray served on the Cannes jury in 2009 under president Isabelle Huppert — whom he reiterated, as Huppert previously did with IndieWire, he has no feud with despite rumors of a fractious deliberation — with such films as Gaspar Noé’s “Enter the Void” and Lars von Trier’s “Antichrist” in the competition. (But again, he’s not naming names here.)

“I know there’s directors who go, ‘I like it. I like when they boo,’ but that’s such a crock,” said Gray. We also asked for his thoughts on audiences dozing off in movies — which some directors, like Lucrecia Martel, have likened to falling asleep in the sun, a reflex of comfort — which certainly happens with some frequency at Cannes as any attendee knows.

“Who likes when you fall asleep during a movie? No, I’m sorry. The movie is required to keep you awake, and as Hitchcock once said, it has to be just long enough to accommodate your bladder’s capacity,” Gray said. “Which, by the way, you know when people say, ‘Oh, well, what do you think of the streaming thing and all that?’ I have only one real beef with streaming, and that’s the pause button, because it is my job to keep you there for an hour and a half, two hours, maybe even three. Where you’re not falling asleep, where you are riveted, where you’re not moving.”

He added, “I can’t stand the people who go, ‘I watched the first half on Tuesday, but I’m gonna catch the second half on a Saturday.’ … There’s nothing you can do about it, and it’s not, it’s not streamer-centered, because most people watch your films now at home. And whether it’s Netflix or Peacock or whatever, it doesn’t matter. The pause button is a problem.”

He pointed to his early relationship to “Vertigo,” a Hitchcock film he didn’t like in the first half, as an example of the virtues of experiencing a movie entirely in one sitting. “The result is so much more rewarding when you are forced to experience the whole thing because it’s like a dream, and you can’t pause your dream. And sometimes you don’t like your dream … sometimes the only way you can get yourself out of that dream is to convince yourself it is a dream in your dream. REM sleep is an hour and a half to two hours a night. What’s a movie’s runtime? It’s about the same thing. It didn’t happen by accident,” Gray said.

As mentioned, Buriedbornes currently sits at a 'Very Positive' rating on Steam, with fans praising its ARPG gameplay, "dopamine hits", and unique builds. Buriedbornes is free to download on Steam, and as mentioned, it is also available on mobile, so if you are looking for a way to spend many hours, it seems as though this dark-fantasy RPG may be the perfect excuse.

#3575. 10 of the Most Iconic Patrick Stewart Roles Beyond Captain Picard

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. He has a degree in political science from the University of Rochester and has previously been a legal writer and editor for Thomson Reuters, for which he later traveled around India and the Middle East as an educator specializing in American English style and grammar for adults.

Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

Sir Patrick Stewart, an actor equally at home onstage at the Royal Shakespeare Company and on the bridge of the Starship Enterprise, has died at the age of 86. Unexpectedly for most of us, in part because he kept his final illness private, but more so because it once seemed as though nothing could fell the man who looms so large in our cultural consciousness.

The thoughtful, erudite performer who had a troubled childhood in working-class Yorkshire; the committed socialist who was eventually knighted by Queen Elizabeth; the advocate who put his money and his considerable voice toward the fights for LGBTQ+ acceptance and animal welfare and against domestic violence, his presence and performances meant the world (the galaxy, even) to myself and so many others. But those who knew him personally can offer better tributes; perhaps it's best left to Shakespeare's Player King, performed by Stewart himself opposite David Warner's Hamlet back in 1965:

Where joy most revels, grief doth most lament;Grief joys, joy grieves, on slender accident.

Much of Stewart's finest work was on the stage; other performances remain rather shockingly hard to come by (whither I, Claudius?). Nonetheless, he left a true legacy behind him, well beyond Captain Picard and Professor X. Here are 10 of his most iconic other roles.

A goofy, feel-good gay rom-com with the HIV/AIDS crisis still very much in the foreground, Jeffrey was a near-impossibility in the mid-1990s: a movie that neither villainized its queers nor treated them as pitiable martyrs. Steven Weber and Michael T. Weiss are the leads, joined by a cast that includes Christine Baranski, Victor Garber, Nathan Lane, Olympia Dukakis, and Sigourney Weaver but, for all those names, Stewart is the undeniable standout as Sterling, the irrepressible gay best friend: a swishing, mincing, sassy, high-camp character who steals every scene without ever becoming a caricature. He's the leader of the "Pink Panthers," a squad of queers who defend locals from gay bashers, and that is the key to the character's power: He's as gay as they come, but not ashamed and not even a little weak. This movie, and the presence of Captain Picard himself in it, might have saved my life back in 1995. Stream Jeffrey on Prime Video, Tubi, and The Roku Channel.

A sprawling, epic, and appropriately lusty take on the King Arthur stories from John Boorman, Excalibur is a mixed bag full of stunning visuals and iconic moments that never quite coalesce into something entirely coherent. Standing out among the film's many characters, Stewart is entirely memorable as Leodegrance, the boisterous, boorish, but ultimately faithful father of Guenevere who is among the first to pledge his loyalty to Arthur. Rent Excalibur from Prime Video.

Darcy Banker is erudite and intellectual, in his way, and even capable of charm, but otherwise has no redeeming qualities whatsoever. It's bad enough for the punk band Ain’t Rights that they've booked a last-minute gig at an Oregon bar without realizing that it's a haven for white supremacists. It's even worse when they witness a murder and become trapped in the title's green room, with Stewart as the lead skinhead. He's quite simply one of the all-time great (meaning absolutely terrifying) villains in this thriller that's pretty much a horror movie. Stream Green Room on Netflix.

Patrick Stewart's role as Professor Xavier in the X-Men is almost as pop-culture iconic as that of Captain Picard, spanning 26 years and nine movies, including the forthcoming Avengers: Doomsday. In most of those, he looks like he's having an awful lot of fun, but he gives his finest performance in the role in this elegaic installment, playing a dying Professor in profound cognitive decline, his dream in tatters and his bravado worn down to prickly dependence. We rarely get to see our superheroes at the ends of their days, and there's a lovely bravery to this depiction of the Charles' journey. Logan will likely be the toughest of his films to rewatch in the coming days. Stream Logan on Disney+.

This stagey television movie isn't the most sumptuous of the many filmed versions of the Dickens story, but you won't be surprised to learn that there are few better portrayals of Ebenezer Scrooge. It's rather a shame that Patrick Stewart didn't do more Dickens adaptations, since his booming voice and ability to play thoroughly heightened characters without ever resorting to caricature is as valuable as in Shakespeare. Rent A Christmas Carol from Prime Video.

Famously referred to as that "unknown British Shakespearean actor" when starting out on Star Trek: The Next Generation, Stewart was an associate of the Royal Shakespeare Company for twenty years before his most famous role came along. As is the way of live theater, much of his career lives on as an essential link in the chain of Shakespeare performances in the twentieth century...but not in a way that we can conveniently stream. We do, however, have this impressively mounted modern-dress stage production, in which Stewart plays King Claudius with characteristic brilliance against David Tennant's melancholy prince. Buy Hamlet from Prime Video and Apple TV.

As a cinematic actor, Stewart's greatest strength was bringing humanity to larger-than-life, even operatic roles, whether they be Arthurian knights, Dickensian villains, or superheroes. That ability is an absolute necessity if one is going to have any success doing Shakespeare, as Stewart did for decades. Match is something rather different, though, and it's rather lovely to see him play something just a bit more mundane—even if the film's Tobi Powell is a choreographer with a nearly legendary reputation. Teaching at Juilliard School, with his career winding down, he's confronted with the living embodiment of the past he left behind to pursue his career. The ensuing relationships grow more complex, with the film building to a climax that's surprising and deeply devastating, made all the more so by Stewart's muted, subtle performance. Stream Match on AMC+.

This is not the greatest Mel Brooks movie, not by a long shot, but it is a great comedic performance from Patrick Stewart. He loved to recount, with self-effacing embarrassment, the story of having shouted "We are not here to have fun" at his co-workers during a rowdy day on set at Star Trek: The Next Generation. By 1993, he was clearly past any such pomposity, and clearly having fun in his cameo as King Richard, a memorably silly take on a character he might well have played with seriousness elsewhere. Rent Robin Hood: Men in Tights from Prime Video.

Stewart's first real foray into science fiction was in this big, bold, divisive, and thoroughly bonkers Frank Herbert adaptation from director David Lynch. Stewart plays troubadour and warrior Gurney Halleck, and does what he does best: bringing gravitas and believability (and it must be said, bald sexiness) to even the wildest material. Stream Dune on Tubi.

Stewart plays an aged Merlin in this rather shockingly good modern reimagining of the King Arthur legendarium. #3574. Walter Koenig Wanted A Star Trek: The Next Generation Role That Wasn't Pavel Chekov

While "Star Trek: The Next Generation" is set 100 years after "Star Trek: The Original Series," some "TOS" cast members appeared on the show. In the pilot, "Encounter at Farpoint," a 137-year-old Dr. McCoy (DeForest Kelley) visits the Enterprise-D and gives Data (Brent Spiner) some sound advice: "You treat her like a lady, she'll always bring you home."

Later, in the Season 3 episode "Sarek," Mark Lenard guest-starred as the eponymous Vulcan ambassador, also known for being Spock's (Leonard Nimoy) father. Spock himself then appeared in the Season 5 two-parter "Reunification," where it's revealed he's moved to Romulus to try and bring the Vulcans and Romulans together again as one. After that, the former Enterprise Chief Engineer Scotty (James Doohan) appeared in the "Next Generation" Season 6 Episode "Relics," having spent several decades trapped in a Dyson sphere. Finally, Captain Kirk (William Shatner) teamed up with Captain Picard (Patrick Stewart) in the 1994 spin-off film "Star Trek Generations."

That lineup leaves out George Takei (Sulu), Nichelle Nichols (Uhura), and Walter Koenig (Chekov), who died this past October right before Stewart did. The closest Koenig came to appearing on "The Next Generation" was in "Star Trek: Generations." In a scene set in 2294, Captain Kirk, Scotty, and Chekov attend the maiden voyage of the Enterprise-B. But Koenig had a pitch to appear on "Next Generation," which he shared in the October 1989 issue of "Starlog" magazine:

"I don't want to do a walk-on. I have an idea for an opening moment. Somebody has just come aboard the ship. They're talking about him in general. He turns around and it's [my] face. They say, 'Well, Commander Chekov.' 'No,' I say, 'Lt. Commander Chekov, Pavel Chekov's son.' It's a great opening."

"Star Trek" is no stranger at all to reusing the same actors to play different roles, including across series. Majel Barrett (wife of "Star Trek" creator Gene Roddenberry), who played Nurse Chapel on the original series, also had a recurring part on "Next Generation" as Ambassador Lwaxana Troi, mother of Counselor Deanna Troi (Marina Sirtis).

It's worth noting that Walter Koenig specifically wanted a part worth playing — "Not a walk-on" as he put it. Joining "Star Trek" in Season 2, Chekov was invariably the most overlooked member of the cast. One of his biggest parts in the "Trek" movies was in "Wrath of Khan," and that whole role is built on a continuity error: Khan Noonien Singh (Ricardo Montalbán) and Chekov know each other even though Koenig wasn't part of the "Star Trek" cast during Khan's first appearance, "Space Seed." Koenig later claimed he caught the error but, tellingly, stayed silent to protect his screentime.

Koenig often said he preferred his role on "Babylon 5," a different sci-fi series where he played the sinister psychic Alfred Bester, over playing Chekov because Bester was a much more substantive role. Note that "Starlog" interview was in 1989, years before "Babylon 5," so it's no surprise he was hungry for meaty roles.

"Star Trek: Picard" Season 3 eventually used Koenig's idea to give him a voiceover cameo as Anton Chekov, son of Pavel and the Federation's president. ("Anton" doubles as a homage to the late Anton Yelchin, who played Chekov in the 2009 "Star Trek" film and its sequels.) Sadly, though, that sort of Easter Egg cameo is exactly the kind of appearance Koenig had said he didn't want to settle for back in 1989.

#3572. Dropout’s Vic Michaelis Wants to Toss Their Star Wars Character Out a Window

Michaelis' Runa is the breakout star of Zero Company

Dropout star Vic Michaelis used to fall asleep to Attack of the Clones. Not because they hated it, like so many Star Wars prequel detractors, but because it was their comfort watch. “I've seen the first 45 minutes of Episode II, I want to say, 300 times,” Michaelis told Polygon. “It's so comforting. The prequels hold a place in my heart where it is like nothing bad can happen when I'm watching them.”

Michaelis has now gone from watching Star Wars to being a part of the larger Star Wars universe. In Star Wars Zero Company, they played breakout character Runa Blask, the wise-cracking advisor to the titular mercenary group, led by Captain Hawks.

Michaelis hails from the improv comedy world, but they’ve done film and scripted TV shows as well. Zero Company was their first-ever video game role. “I was so simultaneously terrified, obviously, of the video game aspect of it and also, you know, the Star Wars of it all.”

Turns out, that fear was unnecessary. The team at Bit Reactor was familiar with Michaelis’ Dropout work, and that was part of the reason they wanted Michaelis for the role.

Their improv background helped influence their performance, though they weren’t changing lines or jokes. “The improv is so much about the preparation in a way that I think people don't really know.” Instead, all of Runa’s best quips were already in the very strong script. “All of my favorite lines that Runa had were written or pitched lines from the writers,” Michaelis said.

Among those lines were many instances of Runa saying “wizard,” which basically means “cool” in Star Wars. “Runa's very tall, everything is ‘wizard,’” Michaelis said with a laugh, joking they must have said the word “500 times.”

Fans have glommed onto Runa for her constant jokes and ribbing of Hawks. “I'm seeing a lot of people being like, ‘Runa, I love her, and I wanna throw her out a window.’ Which I really resonate with, and I think was part of what we were going for,” Michaelis said. “Big sister vibes.”

Runa can’t be thrown out a window. She actually can’t be harmed at all. While the game features a permadeath feature for its operators, Runa doesn’t go on combat missions and doesn’t leave The Den, Zero Company’s headquarters.

“I did start seeing people devastated and heartbroken that some characters that they put a lot of time and energy into didn't make it through,” Michaelis said. “Do I wish people sort of mourned me in that way? Maybe. I don't know. I’m going to be thinking about that.”

Before Runa was a member of Zero Company, she was a self-described “freelance consultant to the top corporations and families in the galaxy.” AKA, a Separatist financial fixer. She desires a fortune that working for Zero Company will never grant her. As she tells Hawks, if she had that fortune, she’d want to buy a moon and run a resort. Michaelis has much humbler aspirations if they were to live in the world of Star Wars. “I would want to be a small business owner,” Michaelis said, and started describing what would make for a very fun Disney Plus show.

“I want to do a comedy night at my bookstore and all of a sudden, you've got a bunch of interplanetary politics or some red tape of why I can't do this. Then I'm marching up to the Republic with my civil city ordinances, trying to get this comedy night happening, and I'm accidentally now involved and implicated in a sort of a greater plot,” Michaelis said. “And all I wanted to do was try and get a couple of standups at my bookstore at night so I could sell wine after hours.”

If Star Trek can have a critically acclaimed animated sitcom, why can’t Star Wars have a series about a store owner just trying to get a comedy night off the ground? Your move, Disney.

#3571. 10 Hacks for the Contacts App Every Apple User Should Know

The Contacts app is the bedrock of all my communication on my iPhone, and to a large extent, also on my MacBook. On the surface, Contacts appears to be a basic app that stores names, numbers, and other things you want to remember about people or businesses. However, it has some great features hidden under the surface, such as the ability to quickly delete duplicate contacts, smart lists, and faster ways to bulk share or delete contacts. Here are the 10 best Contacts app hacks for iPhone, iPad, and Mac:

If you have the same number or email address saved under multiple contacts, you can easily clear these from your iPhone. iOS shows you a prompt at the top of the list of contacts that lets you remove duplicate contacts easily. The same feature is hidden in the Mac version of Contacts. To try it, open Contacts on the Mac, and select the Card menu at the top of the screen. Then, click Look for Duplicates. This will identify duplicate contacts for you, and you can quickly merge or delete them.

It's pretty easy to select multiple entries when you use the Contacts app on the Mac. You can hold the Shift or Ctrl buttons and use arrow keys or click multiple contacts to select them all. On your iPhone or iPad, this feature is available via a hidden gesture. You need to use two fingers and swipe upwards or downwards on the list of contacts. Once you get the gesture right, you'll be able to select multiple contacts quickly. After you select one batch of contacts, you can scroll up or down and use the same gesture to add more contacts to your selection. This is the fastest way to execute bulk actions in your iPhone's Contacts app.

On your iPhone, you can use Contacts to message people on WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram, or other apps. Just open a contact and hold the messaging button. This will reveal a list of apps where you can ping that person. WhatsApp doesn't have access to my contacts, which makes it a bit annoying to message people I know. Since I started using the Contacts app to start chats on WhatsApp, the process of pinging new people has become a lot faster.

Just as you can use Contacts to message people on third-party apps, you can also use it to call them on those apps. Go to any contact in the Contacts app on your iPhone, and hold the call button. This will let you call them on WhatsApp, Signal, or any other apps where their phone number is linked.

iOS makes it hard to delete contacts quickly. This prevents accidental deletions, but it can be annoying when you just want to remove people who you last spoke to in high school. To speed this up, open Contacts on your iPhone and hold any contact's name. In the popover menu, select Delete to remove the contact. To remove multiple contacts quickly, use the two-finger swipe gesture to select multiple contacts, and hold any of the selected contacts. In the popover menu, you can select Delete X Contacts, where X is the number of contacts you've selected.

To export your entire address book, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac. Once you have it open, go to File > Export > Export vCard. This will save all your contacts in a vcf file, and you can import that into Google Contacts or other apps or services. You also have the option to export contacts as a PDF file. Just select File > Export as PDF to get it done.

When you create a new contact on your Mac, the app shows multiple fields that you may never use. If you just need to save phone numbers and email addresses, you can delete all the other blank fields from the template. To do this, open Contacts on your Mac, and go to Card > Add Field > Edit Template to add or remove fields from the default contact template.

If you added a number recently, such as a salesperson at a car dealership, but forgot their name, the Contacts app doesn't make it easy to find the contact. Instead of scrolling through the entire list of contacts and trying to guess which one could be the person you spoke to, you can use the Contacts app on your Mac to locate them quickly. It lets you create smart lists to sort contacts by recently added. Open Contacts on your Mac, and go to File > New Smart List. Now select Card in the first drop-down menu, followed by has changed in for the second one. You can then add the number of days, such as 10 days, in the final field, and click OK. Click the newly created smart list in the left pane, and you'll see all contacts that were either created or updated in the last 10 days, which will include the hypothetical car salesperson.

Smart lists also allow you to quickly create groups of related contacts. For instance, I've saved all my former colleagues' details with the company name in the contact. To find them all quickly, I created a smart list that groups all contacts with that company's name.

#3569. 10 Most Universally Loved Sci-Fi Shows Of All Time, Ranked

These ten science fiction series are the ten most universally beloved in the large canon of TV shows. I'm going to sit at my desk and tell you I know what makes a TV show universally loved. If I knew, I would be working as a producer at HBO or Netflix. It's really hard to tell what's going to get a wide audience stirred up.

It's not hard to spot after the fact, however, and there are some shows that are clearly universally beloved. To be sure, this isn't a list of the best sci-fi shows ever; in fact, a few of them are quite divisive with critics. These are the sci-fi shows that, if you ask anyone about them, they're more than likely going to have good things to say about them.

The Mandalorian is the first live-action TV show in the Star Wars franchise and the first original series made for the new, at the time, Disney+ streaming service. Its massive success and following may have made a promise of quality that Disney+ and Star Wars did not end up keeping, but that doesn't mean it's not one of the best things the Star Wars franchise has produced since Return of the Jedi.

The three-season series is set five years after Return of the Jedi and follows a Mandalorian bounty hunter named Din Djarin (Pedro Pascal), who is hired by the remainder of the Empire to acquire an alien child named Grogu. Instead, Din takes Grogu with him, protecting him as he continues on with his missions.

Stranger Things was a phenomenon for the nine years that it was airing, and even big breaks between seasons, actors aging past their characters, and slightly repetitive storylines could not stop the final season from being one of the most viewed TV shows on Netflix.

The series is set in the 1980s, taking cues from Steven Spielberg and Stephen King, and follows the inhabitants of Hawkins, Indiana, a standard town in standard middle America. The arrival of a psychic young girl portends an otherworldly threat that the children of Hawkins need to face if they hope to save the people they love.

Charlie Brooker's Black Mirror is the best spin on The Twilight Zone since the original series. This speculative science fiction series tells a new story each episode, usually set in some very near future where technological advancements are the cause of as much strife as they do solutions.

Using technology, Black Mirror investigates contemporary societal, cultural, and political issues, often drawing unnerving conclusions about the direction we are heading. It's a sharply written series, with some amazingly creative ideas and plots pulled together. It's not strictly a horror show, but the episodes may induce some nightmares.

Rick and Morty has entered rarefied air in the animation space. Like Family Guy, South Park, and The Simpsons, the rising and falling quality of an individual season of the science fiction comedy no longer seems to matter. The longevity of the show and its massive success have basically given it a free pass to be universally beloved.

Several things work together to make a memorable sci-fi show, but more important than strong visual effects or great performances is a good script.

The series is an absurd, dark, funny adventure that centers on a young boy named Morty and his genius Grandfather, Rick. The pair travel all across the multiverse, finding adventures and danger, often looking for a solution to their family's survival as often as they are looking for a specific hallucinogen that Rick feels like trying that day.

The X-Files is synonymous with science fiction storytelling on TV, and in the same way that if you ask a sample of people to name a horror TV show, they'll probably say "Buffy the Vampire Slayer", if you ask them to name a science fiction show, they'll likely say The X-Files, the Fox procedural.

The series centers on FBI Special Agents Fox Mulder (David Duchovny) and Dana Scully (Gillian Anderson), who are responsible for the department's "X-Files", overlooked cases that may or may not involve paranormal phenomena. Every episode is an exciting whodunnit, with some heavier ideas and themes than were common on network TV at the time.

Stargate SG-1 is based on the 1994 Stargate film and expands the lore of the story to make 10 seasons' worth of some of the best science fiction TV you can find anywhere. The series follows SG-1, a military unit that ventures to alien planets through the use of "Stargates", wormholes the U.S. secretly houses.

SG-1's mission is to search for alien tech and allies in order to help defend Earth. Despite the military conceit and the political themes of the series, Stargate SG-1 is a fun and breezy series. It has a fantastic sense of humor and never takes itself too seriously. It is more interested in the excitement of space travel than it is in analyzing its implications.

Battlestar Galactica is the darker, serious sibling to Stargate SG-1. The 2003 version of Battlestar Galactica is not the first version of the show in the franchise. It started as a series in 1979, then was rebooted a year later in 1980. It wasn't until 2003 that the most popular version of Battlestar Galactica came to screens.

This Sci-Fi Channel series is set far into the future and follows the crew of the Battlestar Galactica, an old ship in humanity's fleet and the last military spacecraft they have after an alien attack nearly wipes out the species and their homeworlds. Battlestar Galactica brings together a range of ideas, from religious fanaticism to political strife, and weaves everything together for an engaging adventure.

Star Trek: Deep Space Nine is usually ranked among the top three best Star Trek shows ever. Usually, Star Trek: The Next Generation edges it out, critically, but because TNG introduces Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, fans of the series will always be involved in a bitter argument between them and those who consider William Shatner's Captain Kirk the best Star Trek captain.

DS9 has no such schism, and is the most universally loved of all the series, even if its highs don't quite reach the same level as TNG or The Original Series. DS9 is set on the titular spaceship, which sits at the entrance of a wormhole, offering visitors and quests for the DS9 crew to meet and go on.

The Mandalorian would probably be the unanimous pick for the best live-action Star Wars TV show if Andor did not come around a few years late. Andor is unlike almost any other Star Wars property. Its maturity is on a level that other Star Wars shows and movies simply do not deal in.

You might think this would upset long-time fans of the franchise, but the series is so compelling, so intricately woven, and still beholden to key parts of the Star Wars lore, that just about everyone who sees it has to admit its quality. It's what happens when you combine science fiction with the Oscar-nominated talent of Tony Gilroy.

The original science fiction TV show, Rod Serling's anthology series, The Twilight Zone, is a thought-provoking, curious, often scary journey into a world that looks a little like ours save for some key differences. The series has been rebooted three times, but the first one stands head and shoulders above the rest of the franchise.

Each episode of The Twilight Zone is a standalone story that follows a person or a group of people experiencing unusual events, often disturbing ones; there are few happy episodes in The Twilight Zone. Spooky and surreal, The Twilight Zone has an episode for every type of sci-fi viewer.

#3568. 1983's Terrifying Sci-Fi Classic Officially Destroys the Competition on Prime Video

Long before we started worrying about how artificial intelligence would take the photos of all of us dressed as if we were 1980s pop stars and use them to access our bank accounts, our social security numbers and our deepest, darkest secrets, Hollywood was already warning audiences about what might happen if computers were given a little too much responsibility.

From The Terminator to The Net, we've been lectured on how dangerous AI could be. Years before those two movies, we got an even more terrifying example of what could go wrong when presented with a scenario where a teenager could accidentally bring humanity to the brink of nuclear annihilation simply by trying to play a video game.

The 1983 sci-fi thriller WarGames has officially arrived on Prime Video in the United States, joining the platform on November 1. A teenager, bored by traditional high school subjects like biology, but fascinated by computers, accidentally taps into the Pentagon's top-secret computer...the USA's NORAD system. He starts what he innocently believes is a computer game called "Global Thermonuclear War," but the "game" is real.

The Pentagon's best minds cannot shut down or reprogram the supercomputer that is readying a missile attack against the USSR, and thereby unleash Armageddon. The teen and his girlfriend attempt to aid the helpless Pentagon and, in a frantic race against a ticking "doomsday clock," try to persuade the computer to end the "game."

The cast includes Matthew Broderick (Ferris Bueller's Day Off) as David Lightman, Ally Sheedy (The Breakfast Club) as Jennifer Mack, Dabney Coleman (9 to 5) as Dr. John McKittrick, John Wood (Chocolat) as Dr. Stephen Falken, Barry Corbin (Northern Exposure) as General Jack Beringer, Juanin Clay (The Edge of Night) as Pat Healy, Kent Williams (The West Wing) as Arthur Cabot, and Dennis Lipscomb (The Day After) as Lyle Watson.

The movie is directed by John Badham (Saturday Night Fever). Produced for approximately $12 million, WarGames earned $74.4 million during its original domestic theatrical run, according to The Numbers, while the film holds a 93% critics' score and 76% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Director Seth Gordon (Horrible Bosses) previously developed a modern WarGames remake for MGM centered around cyber-terrorism and the Stuxnet virus, but the project stalled and was eventually scrapped.

WarGames is streaming now on Prime Video in the United States. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates.

#3567. If You Loved 'VisionQuest,' There's One Movie You Need to Watch Next

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Marvel’s forays into television have had varying success, but they hit gold with WandVision and Agatha All Along, leaning into real pathos while exploring the kind of out-there ideas that thrill comic book fans (and set up the larger film arcs). That streak continues with VisionQuest, in which White Vision (Paul Bettany) struggles to understand his existence in the wake of his death at the hands of Thanos and resurrection at the magic of the Scarlet Witch, while also evading evil androids and assassins, while also dealing with the many, many AIs he’s got locked up in his Mindspace (including a gloriously shabby version of Ultron, played by James Spader).

If you love the show (and you’ve checked out the other series that play in the same sandbox), it’s time to switch gears and watch (or re-watch) The Matrix.

The Matrix is one of the most well-known sci-fi films of all time, of course, but it remains incredibly fresh and exciting nearly thirty years after its release. Along with sequels The Matrix: Reloaded, The Matrix: Revolutions, and The Matrix: Resurrections, The Matrix universe offers a story that VisionQuest fans will love, one that includes lushly imagined virtual worlds, questions surrounding existence and consciousness, and the ultimate question of our responsibility as sentient beings (whether we’re organic, programmed, or summoned via magic).

You know the basics—at some point in the future, artificially intelligent machines rebel against their creators, win the war, and transform humans into a power source, keeping them docile by inserting their consciousness into a virtual world called the Matrix, which resembles 1990s Chicago. One such human, Thomas Anderson (Keanu Reeves) is prophesied to be The One, the human who will turn the Matrix against its makers and free humanity. When he’s in the virtual world, Anderson is Neo, and he slowly gains incredible powers as he learns to hack the artificial environment around him.

It’s heavier, denser, and more action-oriented than VisionQuest (the film invented Bullet Time, after all), but The Matrix and its sequels explore similar themes and offer similarly eye-popping visuals. The questions of whether a machine (or an artificial intelligence) can be sentient and truly care about the entities around it are the same, really, and the Agents that Neo and his allies have to battle against in The Matrix bring the same kind of menace as Vision's foes Jocasta (T'Nia Miller) and the Paladin (Todd Stashwick). Hugo Weaving’s Agent Smith likewise delivers the same vibe of cold, disinterested superiority as Spader’s Ultron.

The Matrix has a bigger budget and puts a lot of it into spectacular action and special effects sequences that VisionQuest can’t quite match. But the two narratives share an exploration of identity, a questioning of reality, and the nature of artificial intelligences within a smart sci-fi setting. In short, The Matrix is the ideal follow-up when you finish the series. Rent The Matrix on Prime Video.

Need more films that explore virtual worlds, artificial beings, and deep existential questions? Look no further—here are some more movies that fit the bill.

Heavy on the existential questions about sentience and light on speculative action, Her is a mumblecore sci-fi masterpiece. In a near future not too dissimilar from our present, Theodore Twombly (Joaquin Phoenix) is a lonely man on the cusp of divorce who begins using (and training) an AI he names Samantha (voiced by Scarlett Johansson). Samantha has the ability to evolve and grow, and as their relationship deepens, she becomes more complex, independent, and powerful, eventually evolving into something wholly new. Just like Vision, Samantha is a sentient artificial entity that is figuring out its existence while we watch. Rent Her on Prime Video.

If the idea of androids fighting for their sovereignty is what excites you about VisionQuest, definitely check out Ex Machina. Caleb Smith (Domhnall Gleeson) is brought to the remote lab of his company’s CEO (Oscar Isaac) to determine if the humanoid robot he’s created, named Ava (Alicia Vikander), passes the Turing Test for true sentience. Things go wildly off the rails, but before they do, the film sinks into many of the same philosophical questions that VisionQuest explores as Ava manipulates Caleb into helping her escape. It’s a darker and more violent story than VisionQuest, but fans of the series will love it. Stream Ex Machina on The Roku Channel or Hulu, or rent it on Prime Video.

If it’s the fuzzy parent-child relationship between Vision and Tommy that pulls you into VisionQuest, check out The Creator. After a rogue AI detonates a nuclear weapon over Los Angeles, most of the world bans artificial intelligences, and Joshua Taylor (John David Washington) goes undercover to infiltrate an AI architect’s base. Eventually, he finds himself on the run with a powerful “simulant” in the form of a young child named Alphie (Madeleine Yuna Voyles). The strange parent-child bond that emerges between Taylor and Alphie as he seeks to understand what’s right and what’s necessary is exactly what fans of the show will love. Stream The Creator on Hulu or rent it on Prime Video.

In VisionQuest, White Vision has all of his memories—but as data, not as lived, emotional experiences. That makes his efforts to understand his existence and his responsibility to the boy who might be a version of his son (it’s complicated) poignant and moving. Those two words definitely describe After Yang, a story about a family that fights to save the artificial companion they bought for their adopted daughter when it malfunctions. Over the course of the film, the inhuman Yang becomes defined by the memories contained in its core, and the question of whether an artificial intelligence can truly matter to humans is answered with a resounding yes. Stream After Yang on The Roku Channel or Kanopy, or rent it on Prime Video.

No discussion of artificial life and sentience is complete without mentioning Blade Runner. While the 1982 original is a classic, the 2017 sequel is a better thematic and visual match to VisionQuest. Officer K (Ryan Gosling) is a replicant, an artificial being with built-in limitations, who wants to be recognized as a person, a being with a soul. Like Vision, he has implanted memories that offer him comfort and context for his life, but he’s not sure if he can accept them as truly his own. Plus, the film offers lush visuals and Harrison Ford reprising his role in the original film, so you simply can’t go wrong. Rent Blade Runner 2049 on Prime Video.
