#3566. The Johnny Depp Comeback Hits Judgment Day with ‘Ebenezer’: How Paramount Is Carefully Reintroducing the Controversial Star

Hollywood studios turned away Johnny Depp eight years ago. With “Ebenezer,” Paramount Pictures is betting that audiences have not rejected him too. The “A Christmas Carol” adaptation, out November 13, marks a decisive moment for the studio, as it was one of the first films boarded by the company after its 2025 acquisition by Skydance.

Depp got some positive social media attention Monday evening when he was filmed “wyling out” and “wreaking havoc” in the Christmas Market of New York’s Bryant Park — as Scrooge, of course. In his first major pre-release promotional stop for “Ebenezer,” Depp donned a fright wig and make-up to enact some staged bah-humbugging, which included popping balloons, knocking over a Christmas tree, and playfully antagonizing an on-site Santa Claus. The stunt was Depp’s second in-character appearance as Scrooge, coming three months after a similarly interactive appearance at San Diego Comic-Con that also generated mounds of social media content from passerby. Later on at the event, Scrooge appeared onstage during Collider’s Directors on Directing panel to debut the first “Ebenezer” trailer. Related Stories Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money The Bay Theater in Palisades Village, Closed Since the LA Wildfires, Will Reopen Thanks to Paramount and Rick Caruso

The approach leans into how audiences know Depp, who became one of the industry’s biggest stars in the aughts with his quirked-up performances in the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise and various Tim Burton joints. But several publicity veterans note that it’s also a strategy that helps the star skirt addressing himself: a typical component to the modern promotional gauntlet of podcast appearances and junketing. Paramount and representatives for Depp declined to comment for this story.

Indeed, the last time Depp was promoting a blockbuster in character was at Warner Bros.’ San Diego Comic-Con panel in 2018, where he appeared as Gellert Grindelwald, the seductively authoritarian wizard within J.K. Rowling’s world of “Harry Potter,” to promote the second “Fantastic Beasts” prequel. Depp was mired in controversy at the time, as his ex-wife, Amber Heard, alleged that he had been “physically abusive” in court documents filed in their divorce case. Depp denied the claims. Making things more awkward — Heard appeared at the same studio presentation, popping up an hour later for a panel hyping “Aquaman.”

Two years later, Depp departed from a third (and what ended up to be the final) “Fantastic Beasts” entry. On Instagram, the actor posted that he had been “asked to resign” by the studio. Depp had just lost a U.K. libel trial against The Sun, in which a judge ruled that an article reporting that the actor was a “wife beater” was found to be “substantially true.”

But Depp later claimed victory in a U.S. defamation trial against Heard herself. Heard had written a Washington Post op-ed in which she described herself as a survivor of domestic abuse. Depp claimed the article damaged his reputation and career; both parties argued the other was the aggressor through the grueling six-week spectacle. An initial jury ruling sided with Depp on three separate claims of defamation, ordering Heard pay him $10.35 million in damages. Heard won on one of her three counterclaims of defamation, ordering Depp to pay her $2 million. A later appeal by Heard ended with a settlement in which she agreed to pay $1 million to Depp.

The highly-gawked-at and internet-scrutinized trial reignited his fame and infamy, depending on your perspective. Once a big-screen titan, he was now ubiquitous on social media, particularly TikTok, emerging with an ardent online fanbase forged by a conviction that he was a man who had been rashly cast aside during the #MeToo movement’s prominence in the late 2010’s.

With “Ebenezer,” Paramount has the unique assignment of capitalizing on that celebrity, without inviting relitigation of an ugly legal battle that would cloud the sunny promotion of a family feature. Hence, the in-character appearances, along with underlining Depp’s penchant for transformative turns (though no further ones are planned). A promotional video featuring snippets of cast interviews, including the likes of Ian McKellen, Daisy Ridley, and Tramell Tillman, praise the actor as giving “a performance the likes of which you’ve never seen before.”

“A less clever route would be turning the release into a ‘comeback’ victory lap. The result could be an unnecessary and noisy polarization of views, reviving the very controversy the studio would prefer to move beyond,” says media lawyer and crisis manager Amber Melville-Brown, who heads the media and reputation team at the law firm Withers. “A campaign built around vindication invites an argument about who, precisely, has been vindicated and for what — starting the debate over again. A campaign built around the performance sparks a different conversation.”

Meanwhile, Paramount has been careful to show “Ebenezer” to select audiences so far. The film was unveiled Sunday in New York City with a “special screening” at the Whitby Hotel’s 147-seat screening room — an intimate venue for the first unveiling of a studio feature. A handful of press outlets and more influencers were invited to a small carpet. One front-facing video posted by a guest featured her meeting Depp and calling the occasion “my sign from God that I chose the right path today.” A London premiere will take place at Odeon Luxe Leicester Square on Monday.

In another shrewd booking, Depp made a surprise onstage appearance during Aerosmith’s Hollywood Bowl concert on October 29. While other actors may tap in for a late-night spot or “Hot Ones” interview to mark the home stretch of film promotion, Depp instead let a guitar solo on “Train Kept A-Rollin'” do the talking.

Down the line, the “Ebenezer” review embargo will lift November 12, mere hours before public screenings begin — almost always a sign that a studio has little confidence in finding good PR from the critic class. The film’s director, Ti West, has usually drawn positive reviews through his career, mostly known as an indie horror darling until this first studio feature.

But most importantly for Paramount, “Ebenezer” doesn’t need to be a blockbuster to find success. The film’s production budget netted out to a rather modest $38 million, giving it a much easier pathway to theatrical profitability than Depp’s previous mega-budget tentpoles. Along with that comes hopes to leg out through the holiday season and a bank on grosses from overseas territories, where other older male movie stars like Brad Pitt and Tom Cruise have better retained their ability to sell tickets.

Rival studios are looking closely at whether audiences still see Depp as a big screen draw. Lionsgate is already in the Depp business for the revenge thriller “Day Drinker,” releasing in March. And at Disney’s D23 Expo in August, “Pirates of the Caribbean” producer Jerry Bruckheimer floated hopes to get the star on board for a sixth installment. That franchise has laid dormant for nearly a decade, despite numerous reports of development teams tinkering on a Depp-less take. In one of the more interesting quotes from the “Ebenezer” event in New York, Depp spoke with Entertainment Tonight and slid in a dig at the 2017 entry “Dead Men Tell No Tales,” saying he’d be open to a franchise return but noting that “the only involvement I really want to have, truly, is just to send them off on a better note.”

But when Depp was first jettisoned from Hollywood’s A-list, major studios had begun to tire of his antics. There were reports of erratic on-set behavior, sky-high salary demands, and — in the true offender for studios — diminishing box office returns. The “Pirates” films still made money, but Depp headlined several costly bombs, including “Alice Through the Looking Glass” and “Mortdecai,” which had left companies less eager to write big checks, particularly given his public relations scandals.

But Depp’s absence may have not curbed his following. A National Research Group study from earlier this year found that he was the seventh-most cited name by people, especially in Europe, when they wre asked to name five actors or actresses that would motivate them to see “a new movie in a cinema,” even though he’s been away from the big screen for nearly a decade. Over those years, a growing refrain in the business has been that some movie stars have kneecapped their ability to open films by signing on to streaming productions, curbing consumers’ association of them with theaters. In that context, Depp may prove to be a unicorn, having essentially sat out years of the industry chasing Netflix — even if it wasn’t his choice to.

#3564. The No. 1 Horror Movie of 2026 Is Officially Leaving Peacock

Unless you have a One Wish Willow, you'll want to get your final watch in

Not many directors can say their debut film was a blockbuster hit, let alone a cultural phenomenon. But newcomer Curry Barker, who wrote and directed Obsession, the No. 1 horror movie of 2026, can say he's accomplished both. The film takes a look at the dangers of getting exactly what you wish for when Bear (Michael Johnston) makes a wish that his friend Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette) would love him more than anyone else in the world. Despite being made on only a $750,000 budget, the film dominated the box office when it hit theaters, earning $17.2 million in its first week and a staggering $23.9 million in its second week.

To date, Obsession remains the tenth most profitable film of 2026 at the worldwide box office according to data from Box Office Mojo, earning a gross total of $523 million during its theatrical run. It's no surprise that when Obsession moved to streaming, it continued finding success on Peacock, but going into November, the end of Obsession's victory lap is officially drawing near.

Obsession is leaving Peacock on Nov. 17, 2026, the same date that the film is expected to launch on Netflix in the United States. The film first hit Peacock on July 17, 2026, and drew in 456 million minutes streamed in just its first two days on the service, according to data from Nielsen. It went on to spend more than 150 days on JustWatch’s U.S. streaming Top 10 list, further cementing its domination in the industry.

Obsession was more than just a blockbuster and streaming hit. It became a cultural phenomenon in the months that followed its release, with fans drawn into conversations online about the film's themes surrounding bodily autonomy and consent. A Nikki Freeman actor drew thousands of visitors to California's Halloween Horror Nights this fall, including Inde Navarette herself, and Obsession reached as far as Fortnite, where a Nikki Freeman skin was released for the game in November 2026 (complete with a "No, No, No..." emote).

Even Barker, who first built a following for himself making sketches and short films on YouTube, didn't expect the success that came with Obsession. In a June 2026 interview with the Associated Press, he said, "“That’s when you start to feel this impostor syndrome of like: What? It’s not that good. All I see when I watch ‘Obsession’ is the problems.”

The film follows Bear (Michael Johnston), a lonely, awkward man with strong, unrequited feelings for his friend Nikki Freeman (Inde Navarrette). After failing to confess his feelings, Bear stumbles upon a One Wish Willow in a novelty shop. The instructions seem simple enough: make a wish, break the willow stick, and watch your deepest desires come true, but when Bear wishes for Nikki to love him more than anyone else in the entire world, his dream quickly turns into a nightmare. The film has received plenty of praise from critics and audience members, including Polygon writer Jesse Hassenger, who wrote, "Navarrette gets plenty of time to believably and charmingly establish who Nikki is before the wish takes her true self away. Once that happens, she does bravura work as this imitation version, regularly flying off the handle with panicked eagerness or cackling mania, creating an unusual combination of fear and pity — a true movie monster crossing possession with a Bride of Frankenstein figure."

It's worth noting that Obsession's move to Netflix this month comes as awards season nears, and it could very well be a strategic decision to keep the film in the spotlight. Focus Features, the production company behind Obsession, is definitely pushing for consideration in the forthcoming Academy Awards. The company's website suggests Obsession for Best Picture, Inde Navarrette for Best Actress, and Curry Barker for Best Original Screenplay, among other categories.

Obsession is about to get another boom in viewership

#3563. Sebastián Lelio, Chilean Director of Oscar-Winning ‘A Fantastic Woman,’ Dead at 52

Sebastián Lelio, the humanistic Chilean filmmaker whose trans drama “A Fantastic Woman” won the Best International Feature Film Oscar in 2018, has died at age 52.

The Chilean publication Emol first revealed the news that he was found dead in his home in Santiago on Friday, November 6, amid an undisclosed health issue. His body was discovered by his partner, the actress/director Amalia Kassai, who starred in his final film, the protest musical “The Wave” from Cannes 2025. Kassai also posted a statement in Spanish on her Instagram account.

Lelio was reportedly mid-production on the feature “Chilean Poet,” adapted from Alejandro Zambra’s Viking-published 2022 novel. Along with “A Fantastic Woman,” he also directed the Hasidic lesbian romance “Disobedience” in the same year, 2017; it starred Rachel McAdams and Rachel Weisz, and helped bring the filmmaker to international prominence. In 2013, he directed Paulina García to a Berlinale Silver Bear Best Actress win with “Gloria,” a late-in-life romantic comedy about a 58-year-old divorcee starting over again. He remade his own film in 2018 in English as “Gloria Bell,” released by A24 and starring Julianne Moore in the role García originated, opposite John Turturro.

Lelio regularly collaborated with the Chilean brothers Pablo Larraín and Juan de Dios Larraín, who served as producers on nearly all of his films. They were also collaborating with Lelio on his ongoing, now-final feature. Born in Argentina, he emigrated to Chile at age two with his mother and later graduated from Chilean Film School, after which he launched his career with short films and music videos. His debut narrative feature, “The Sacred Family,” premiered at the San Sebastián International Film Festival in Spain before his follow-up, “Navidad,” premiered at Cannes in 2009. The post-Chilean-earthquake drama “The Year of the Tiger,” starring beloved Chilean actor Luis Dubó, debuted at Locarno in 2011.

His fourth feature, “Gloria,” shot digitally and with a script and dialogue developed in part with his actors, including García, received U.S. distribution from Roadside Attractions and was widely regarded as one of the best films of 2013.

Lelio directed the first Best International Feature Oscar entry to win the Academy Award with 2017’s Golden Bear-nominated “A Fantastic Woman,” an exuberantly styled drama that put trans actress Daniela Vega on the international map. As Vega consulted on the script, it’s widely seen as a groundbreaker of trans portrayals onscreen in the 21st century. And it helped reform the perception and attitudes toward transness in Lelio and Vega’s home of Chile — and inevitably, within the Academy.

Lelio’s favorite films on the 2022 Sight & Sound poll included “La Dolce Vita,” “Playtime,” “The 400 Blows,” and “Singin’ in the Rain,” and you can feel their impact across his often irreverent, at times burstingly colorful, playful body of work.

His 2017 TIFF premiere “Disobedience” received U.S. distribution from Bleecker Street, and told the story of a forbidden, transgressive romance between two Orthodox Jewish women (McAdams and Weisz) in North London. The tender, taboo drama performed well in North America, grossing nearly $3.5 million domestic during a spring-through-summer 2018 run.

Lelio, that year, deftly remade “Gloria” as “Gloria Bell” with Julianne Moore as the free-spirited divorcee being wooed by John Turturro, and weighing choices in her next chapter living as a yoga instructor in Los Angeles. Returning to filming after the pandemic, Lelio broadened his collaborative scope to adapt “Room” author Emma Donoghue’s “The Wonder,” with Donoghue and Alice Birch co-writing the script with him. Florence Pugh starred as a British nurse sent to Ireland to observe a miraculous “fasting girl,” in a film that played Telluride and streamed on Netflix to strong reviews.

His last film, “The Wave,” took a minute to get off the ground after playing out of competition in Cannes 2025. The story of an introverted music student whose passion for protest is awakened amid a growing feminist movement on campus, “The Wave” received a small release from Wolfe Video earlier this year and received positive response throughout its festival run.

The status of Lelio’s final film isn’t known right now, but we can imagine that Lelio’s sensitive approach to character — and unstable identities finding their footing, their purest expression — will carry into the new work. The Larraín brothers were also producing the film, with Lelio’s regular cinematographer Benjamín Echazarreta on board as DP.

Amazon has dropped the Bose Smart Ultra Soundbar to $649 from its usual $999, taking $350 off and bringing it to the lowest price we've seen so far, according to price trackers. PCMag rated the Smart Ultra "outstanding," highlighting its ability to deliver surprisingly immersive Dolby Atmos audio without requiring a room full of additional speakers. If you don't need Bose's top-tier model, there's a less expensive option as well: the Bose Smart Dolby Atmos Soundbar ($399, down from $429), which sits below the Smart Ultra in the lineup.

The Smart Ultra uses a 5.1.2-channel design with nine drivers, including two upward-firing drivers that bounce sound off the ceiling to create height effects. In practice, that means movies, TV shows, and games feel larger and more spacious than they do through most single-bar setups. Bose also includes its AdaptiQ room-calibration system, which measures your room's acoustics and adjusts the sound accordingly. The soundbar also works as a smart speaker, with Amazon Alexa built in and support for Apple AirPlay 2, Google Cast, Spotify Connect, Bluetooth, and multi-room audio through the Bose app.

The good news is that Bose allows you to expand the system later with compatible wireless subwoofers and surround speakers if you decide you want more impact. For anyone looking for a premium one-piece soundbar that delivers convincing Dolby Atmos effects, clear dialogue, built-in smart features, and a much larger soundstage than TV speakers can provide, the Smart Ultra remains one of the strongest standalone options available, especially at this price.

#3561. 13 Darkest Fantasy Books Of All Time

It's safe to say that fantasy books aren't just cozy novels to curl up with or snuggly works that touch upon beautiful, safe magic. There's a complex, dark side of fantasy that's just as compelling as the softer version of the genre, and it's these gripping works that have pushed fantastical storytelling to its limits.

Even the most fun fantasy books have elements of violence, cruelty, and danger, as this is part of the texture of any great work of speculative fiction. However, these works of fiction raise the bar, digging into devastating plots and shocking battles that push the characters and readers to their limits. Despite their intensity, what makes grimdark fantasy books is their cathartic stories and emotional moments that parallel our reality.

Godblind by Anna Stephens is not for the faint of heart, but for readers looking for a cruel and brutal world to spend some time in, it scratches the itch. The dual protagonists, Dom and Rillirin, must use their combined powers and knowledge of the terrifying Mireces​​​​​​, who worship the bloodthirsty Red Gods, to stop an invasion and save the kingdom of Rilpor​​​​​​. However, things aren't as they seem for Dom and Rillirin, and audiences should buckle in for epic battles and crushing plot twists that make Godblind a true work of grimdark fantasy.

The First Law series by Joe Abercrombie begins with The Blade Itself, and the trilogy remains one of the best dark fantasy trilogies for readers looking for their first foray into the grimdark side of speculative fiction. The Blade Itself uses multiple POVs to capture the breadth of the fantastical world where it's set, slowly pushing the characters closer as war brews and individuals must put aside the lives they thought they would have. The first book sets the stage for the final two novels, digging into the texture and character of the world.

The Blade Itself is available for purchase here.

The book that started it all, A Game of Thrones, successfully launched the A Song of Ice and Fire series and led to the creation of the enormous multimedia franchise that is Game of Thrones​​​​​​. However, in 1996, George R.R. Martin's novel was a stunning work of dark fantasy that told the story of the sprawling Seven Kingdoms and the many houses vying for control. From the first chapters of the book, it's clear that Martin will pull no punches when it comes to death and violence, and this holds true throughout every installment.

A Game of Thrones is available for purchase here.

Medieval fantasy meets sci-fi futurism in Xiran Jay Zhao's Iron Widow. Though the book is officially classified as YA, it's still a dark, complex work of speculative fiction that works perfectly as an entry point to the darker, more intense side of the genre. Set in a future society where young women are constantly sacrificed in the battle against an invading alien species, Iron Widow is told through the protagonist, Zetian, who questions the system and wishes to avenge the death of her sister. Socially relevant and brilliantly paced, Iron Widow is a dark and wild ride.

Iron Widow is available for purchase here.

Nothing says dark fantasy like necromancy, and Gideon the Ninth has no shortage of the dark art. Though Tamyn Muir's novel isn't afraid to make jokes and infuse some fun topical references into the text, that doesn't mean the novel won't leave you heartbroken. The novel follows Gideon and Harrowhawk, two young women selected to participate in a cruel and vicious series of trials for the mysterious Emperor. As the pair grow closer and secrets about the Empire are revealed, the women face greater challenges and bloody tests.

Gideon the Ninth is available for purchase here.

Prince of Thorns takes the structure of a traditional Bildungsroman and turns it on its head throughout the gripping, bloody novel. The titular prince, Jorg, begins his journey in the wake of his family's death and his ascension to the top of a band of thieves, only to eventually return to the very castle and throne where he lost everything. In Prince of Thorns, Jorg infiltrates the kingdom with the intention of taking back what was once his, but his quest for power is full of betrayals and secrets.

Prince of Thorns is available for purchase here.

It's impossible not to bring up N.K. Jemisin's award-winning fantasy trilogy, The Broken Earth series, when discussing the best of dark fantasy. The collection begins with The Fifth Season, introducing readers to a world where a deadly apocalyptic weather event known as the Fifth Season destroys the world and leaves the gifted members of society persecuted. In The Fifth Season, Essun searches for her daughter while navigating the forbidding environment and the dangers that lurk around every corner in the stratified culture.

The Fifth Season is available for purchase here.

It's important that a dark fantasy book retains a sense of humor throughout the pages, or it would be nearly impossible to get through the grim events of the story. The Library at Mount Char strikes a good balance between its biting humor and the epic scale of its fantasy world, with some horror elements and demons thrown in. Following Carolyn, a young woman with mystical powers who grew up in an infinite library, the book features some sadistic characters vying for control of the universe and an epic conclusion that sticks with you.

The Library at Mount Char is available for purchase here.

Science fiction, fantasy, and the post-apocalyptic genre come together to form Who Fears Death, an emotionally intense and resonant work by Nnedi Okorafor. Born amid violence and raised knowing that she has a greater destiny than those around her, Onyesonwu develops her magic and connection to her culture while bearing the weight of her people's survival on her shoulders. It's up to Onyesonwu to stop the genocide of her community in Who Fears Death, and that's only the beginning of what she must conquer.

Who Fears Death is available for purchase here.

Forcing the reader and characters to confront what it means to take orders and fight back against the status quo, Glen Cook's The Black Company examines the titular band of mercenaries as they abandon their allegiance to the Lady and try to do what's right. The first in a series of 12 mainline novels, The Black Company throws the audience into a high fantasy world of violence and bloodshed. Though it's a lengthy commitment to take on The Black Company collection, the payoff of Cook's work is worth the time spent reading.

The Black Company is available for purchase here.

#3560. ’Saturday Night Live’s Famous Formula Has 1 Unfixable Problem

Greer Riddell is a London-based film and television journalist writing about comedy, streaming and the evolving media industry in the UK and USA. She works at Collider, covering the latest in film, television and entertainment through interviews, features, reviews and industry coverage.

Her recent brand collaborations include HBO, Warner Bros., Netflix, Hulu, Sky, Disney+ and DC Studios. She has covered titles including Saturday Night Live UK, Rivals, Scrubs, Stuart Fails to Save the Universe, Ludwig, Supergirl and Stranger Things.

Her recent interviews include Florence Pugh, Mike Faist and Christopher Abbott for Netflix's East of Eden, Taika Waititi and Jenna Ortega for Klara and the Sun.

Saturday Night Live has spent 5 decades establishing a format that is instantly recognizable and runs like clockwork. Bringing the show to the UK meant deciding which of those traditions were worth keeping and which could be left behind. At the Edinburgh TV Festival 2026, SNL UK director Liz Clare and cast member Emma Sidi discussed two elements of the original that prompted very different reactions — the famous crane shot and the end-of-show credits.

While Clare rejected the crane because of the practical demands of the British production, Sidi admitted that the cast initially found the closing tradition unbearably "naff." SNL UK could not reproduce the American original and expect every production choice or cultural convention to translate, but neither could it reinvent everything without losing elements that make the format successful. So before any episode aired, the crew behind SNL UK had the mammoth task of working out what it could change and what it needed to keep, and while one problem solved itself, another remains unfixable.

One of the defining features of Saturday Night Live is its production setup, which allows the show to move between the monologue and sketches while maintaining the pace and energy of a live performance. SNL UK has adopted much of the American show's approach, but director Clare decided against using its famous crane shot. Speaking at the Edinburgh TV Festival's The SNL Masterclass, director Clare explained, “The camera setup is probably pretty standard. In fact, it's based on the American show, bar the fact that we don't use the Americans have got this big old bit of kit, big crane that's become a feature of the show,” Clare said. “We decided not to employ that camera because it takes up an awful lot of space.”

Britain makes more detective television than any country has any business making, and somehow almost all of it is good. Here is the one you belong in, what it says about you, and the case for it being the best of the four.

You want the tea, the gossip and the vicar behaving oddly. Midsomer is a county where the scenery is beautiful, the fete is on Saturday and the murder rate is roughly that of a small war, and absolutely nobody involved thinks this is strange.

You feel other people's grief as if it were handed to you personally. Broadchurch is less a whodunnit than a study of what a small town does to itself when it finds out that the answer was always going to be somebody everybody already knew.

You go through things rather than around them. John Luther is the best detective in London and a liability to everybody who works with him, and the show is completely honest that those two facts are the same fact.

You say the thing and you do not dress it up. Vera Stanhope turns up in a hat and a mac, is rude to almost everybody, and is the only person in the room prepared to ask the question that the family has been waiting years for somebody to ask.

The decision makes sense for a show that has to accommodate multiple sets, rapid changes and performances staged in the round. A large crane might be a recognizable part of the American production, but that does not mean it is essential to the format. Instead, the British production has adapted its equipment to suit the way the show operates. “But we do have a jib, and we've got some pads,” Clare explained, describing some of the alternatives available to her team. Her approach is less about reproducing the American show's visual identity exactly and more about understanding what its camera work is trying to achieve. As she put it, “It's really just about making sure that what is interesting about the show is that it's played in the round in a way that then helps all of those resets.”

Jamie Dornan’s turn as host in Season 1, Episode 2, offers a good example of how the money saved on the crane allows the series to follow the technical needs of each joke. Dornan played a criminal taking Annabel Marlow hostage, a role that required the production to recreate the appearance of a video recorded on a camcorder. Rather than relying on a conventional studio camera to capture the scene, Clare's team found a more specific solution. “We knew that we needed some kind of camera that he could look like he was recording a sort of hostage video,” she explained. “So we actually got a live really lovely sort of digicam that was a live picture, live feed that we were able to take out of the camera and put in and used to make it look as authentic as possible.”

'SNL UK' Head Writer Jonno Johnson lifts the curtain on the UK’s buzziest comedy.

The closing sequence of Saturday Night Live is one of its most familiar traditions. As the credits roll, the cast gathers around the host, exchanging hugs and saying goodbye to the audience. For Sidi, however, the practice initially seemed awkward and unnecessary. Her reaction highlights a different challenge for SNL UK. Technical decisions can be made according to the needs of the production, but cultural traditions can be harder to assess up front. Sidi admitted that she had never been particularly fond of the American show's endings. “That's something with the American show... the ending, the goodbyes bit. I would just see it and go, ‘This is just so naff. I can't bear to see this,’” she said at the Edinburgh TV Festival. From the viewer's perspective, the sequence can look like an overly sentimental ritual, particularly when performers who have spent the episode confidently delivering jokes suddenly show their relief that it is over in the farewell.

However, making SNL UK changed Sidi's perspective. The cast were experiencing the pressure of putting together a live show, working through rehearsals, changes, and the demands of performing. Sidi explained that she understood the tradition differently once she had experienced that process, “And when we're doing it now, I get it because we have done the heist during the week, you know?... So we're hugging and crying... fuck it, we're luvvies now,” she joked. “You are just like, thank god we did it. It's so real that hugging at the end.”

SNL UK could have dropped the closing sequence to avoid something the cast found embarrassing, just as Clare dropped the crane. Removing them would not change the quality of the series or make a sketch easier to stage. Yet it would have removed a moment that the people making the show have come to value. Sidi even acknowledged that viewers might still find the sequence uncomfortable: “So sorry you have to watch that, but we're gonna keep doing it!” Now halfway through its second season, Saturday Night Live UK is still developing its own identity away from the American original, but some things stay essential to the show regardless of where it is being made.

Saturday Night Live UK Season 2 Part 2 returns on Sky One in the UK in January 2027 and streams the next day on Peacock in the U.S.

#3559. The Top 10 Movies Right Now, According to Streaming Data

The most streamed movie in October was Steven Spielberg's Disclosure Day, but half of the month's top ten is made up of season-appropriate horror movies. This year's two most successful horror movies, Backrooms and Obsession, made the list; so did a classic (Halloween from 1978) and an art movie about the genre that Halloween created,Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma. Perfect double feature. Rounding out the list is the all-around-excellent Hokum. If you're not into horror, you might like Golden Arm, a comedy that refused to die, star-studded comedy The Invite, or ultimate crowd-pleaser Project Hail Mary.

Legendary director Steven Spielberg returns to the extraterrestrials he loves so much with a thriller that's a spiritual sequel to Close Encounters of the Third Kind. Disclosure Day details the events that lead up to the revelation that aliens are among us. Josh O’Connor plays Dr. Daniel Kellner, a cybersecurity expert for a government contractor who uncovers explosive evidence that his employers would kill to keep secret. Meanwhile, a TV meteorologist (Emily Blunt) begins speaking in an alien language. It all sets the stage for a series of set pieces and chases leading to the biggest revelation in human history. Stream Disclosure Day on Peacock.

Director Kane Parsons' analog horror breakthrough is proof that atmosphere, mood, and a fascinating story is scarier than CGI monsters every time. Based on the viral YouTube series of the same name, Backrooms tells the story of Clark (Chiwetel Ejiofor), a store owner who discovers a labyrinthian liminal space in his furniture shop's basement. Renate Reinsve plays his therapist, who goes downstairs for a visit and does not find it easy to return. A hit with critics—Backrooms is sitting at 86% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes—and audiences, Backrooms is a delicious Halloween treat for horror fans. Stream Backrooms on HBO Max.

Director Curry Barker is still in his 20s, but his debut theatrical feature is the kind of horror film that changes the entire genre. Obsession is a classic "be careful what you wish for" story that feels fresh thanks to its talented young cast, unpredictable plot, and careful pace. Michael Johnston plays a young man too scared to tell his crush how he feels, so he wishes she'd fall in love with him instead. The result is a nightmare embodied by Inde Navarrette, whose portrayal of the villain/victim is at once harrowing, terrifying, and heartbreaking. Obsession is the best horror movie I've seen in years. Stream Obsession on Peacock.

This comedy-drama from A24 is packed with heavy-hitting actors. Olivia Wilde, who also directed the film, plays Angela, and Seth Rogen plays her husband, Joe. With the straight-laced couple's marriage on thin ice, Angela and Joe invite their more, uh, open-minded neighbors Piña, played by Penélope Cruz, and Hawk, played by Edward Norton, over for dinner. The evening unravels in hilarious ways, changing everyone's life. If you're a fan of smart, honest comedy, you will really like The Invite. Stream The Invite on HBO Max.

With Hokum, Director Damian McCarthy (Oddity, Caveat) carefully builds a suffocatingly creepy story around Adam Scott's portrayal of Ohm Bauman, a celebrity novelist and unmitigated jerk who travels to the isolated Bilberry Woods Hotel in Ireland to scatter the ashes of his parents and finish his book. Bauman soon learns that the lore of the hotel includes an ancient witch who feeds her victims to the creatures of hell, and she might be more than just a local legend. Hokum is a horror movie for fans of dreadful atmosphere and careful pacing instead of gore or jump-scares. Stream Hokum on Hulu.

With a title like this, it's not going to be a normal movie. Director Jane Schoenbrun’s I Saw the TV Glow and We're All Going to the World's Fair are two of the most fascinating, fiercely original horror movies of the last decade, and their third film follows in those strange footfalls. While it's technically a meta re-imagining of the slasher genre, Miasma goes way deeper than Scream ever could. It's a postmodern exploration of why the slasher genre's cocktail of sex, death, and subversion casts such a strong spell on interesting, weird people. Definitely see this movie. Stream Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma on Mubi.

When Golden Arm was released in 2021, not many people paid attention—with the pandemic in full swing, people didn't seem to have room for a quirky, indie comedy about a woman's quest to win the ladies' arm-wrestling championship—but it's a new age, and you should stream Golden Arm. It's sitting on a perfect score at Rotten Tomatoes, the movie's stars, Mary Holland and Betsy Sodaro, are charming and hilarious, and you can catch Golden Arm on Fandango, a free streaming service. What's not to love? Stream Golden Arm on Fandango or Prime Video.

In this crowd-pleasing sci-fi flick, Ryan Gosling stars as Ryland Grace, a middle school science teacher who is blasted into the firmament in a last-ditch effort to save the world. Grace is the only person on Earth who might know how to protect the sun from a cosmic infection that threatens all life, but he's definitely not an astronaut and doesn't see himself as a hero either. Will he rise to the occasion and learn something about his inner strength and resilience while saving us all from death? My money is on, "yeah, probably." Stream Project Hail Mary on MGM+, Prime Video, and Philo.

Hundreds of slasher movies have been released since Halloween came out in 1978, but none have surpassed the original. Michael Myers' expressionless visage and the synthesizer theme have become universally recognized cultural signifiers for "horror movie," and every shot in Halloween has been stolen countless times, but the movie is so good, it's still scary. Watch or re-watch Halloween now! Stream Halloween on Philo, AMC+, and Prime Video.

Directed by and starring Ben Affleck, Animals is a thriller that tells the story of Mark Kimball, a Los Angeles mayoral candidate whose son is kidnapped and held for ransom. Having spent every dime on his outsider campaign, Kimball is forced to turn to extreme methods to guarantee his son's safe return, even if it conflicts with his public persona as a man of the people. Animals is a taut, expertly directed movie that should more than satisfy fans of political thrillers. Stream Animals on Netflix.

#3558. Could ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ Re-Ignite Quentin Tarantino’s Bruce Lee Controversy?

It does not take long for the new trailer for “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” to invoke the most discourse-inducing scene from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” In fact, the very first words we hear are “You heard the story about Bruce Lee getting his ass kicked by a stuntman?” Another reference to the Bruce Lee scene follows soon after, long before we hear any mention of Rick Dalton or any of the more consequential events of the first film..

The Netflix pseudo-sequel, directed by David Fincher and written by Quentin Tarantino, sees Brad Pitt reprising his Oscar-winning role as Cliff Booth. It’s billed as a separate adventure that happens to feature one of the film’s main characters — Leonardo DiCaprio is either completely absent or an incredibly well-kept secret, and Tarantino has said the film shares more DNA with Elmore Leonard’s paperback crime novels than the hangout movie style that defined the first film. But the marketing had to remind audiences who Cliff Booth is, and it’s curious that the second trailer’s primary reference point is a scene that is more memorable for the controversies it sparked than its role in the film’s plot. No mention is made, for instance, of the part Cliff played in dispatching several members of the Manson Family. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

A brief recap for those lucky enough to have been offline during the original saga. “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” features a scene in which Cliff is left to hang around a TV set while DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton shoots an episode. While killing time, he ends up in a fight with Bruce Lee (played by Mike Moh). Neither man is particularly polite to the other, with Cliff appearing more interested in Lee’s sidekick role on “The Green Hornet” than his higher profile movie roles, and Lee quickly challenges him to a fight. Each man wins one round of the fight before it’s broken up, ensuring there’s no clear winner — but the mere fact that Cliff was able to throw a martial arts legend into the side of a car is a feather in his cap.

Following the film’s release, Bruce Lee’s daughter Shannon publicly objected to the way the film portrayed her father.

“It’s unfortunate because it has started this narrative in some places where some people are saying, ‘Oh, Bruce Lee was an asshole,’” Shannon Lee said in 2020. “Look, everybody can be an asshole sometimes. I can be arrogant and angry in my life — is that something I would say I am like generally? No, my father was not generally like that. He was extremely passionate and driven.”

She continued, “He could have a temper sometimes, but he did not go around challenging people to fights. Certainly not after he was a teenager. Anyway, he didn’t behave or boast in that way…My father worked extremely hard and directly toward the idea of authentic representation in Hollywood for an Asian man, so I don’t think he would’ve gone around beating up stunt people and that kind of stuff as a way of furthering his cause.”

Tarantino frequently defended the scene, saying that he based his fictional portrayal on real anecdotes about Lee from people who knew the actor.

“Bruce Lee was kind of an arrogant guy,” Tarantino said in a 2019 press conference. “The way he was talking, I didn’t just make a lot of that up. I heard him say things like that to that effect. If people are saying, ‘Well he never said he could beat up Mohammad Ali,’ well yeah he did. Alright? Not only did he say that but his wife, Linda Lee, said that in her first biography I ever read. She absolutely said that.”

The controversy still rears its head sporadically. During a 2021 appearance on “The Joe Rogan Experience,” Tarantino told critics of the scene to “suck a dick,” with the caveat that he understood why a daughter would object to any negative portrayal of her father.

By the time “The Futher Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth” hits select theaters this month (and expands to Netflix in December), more than seven years will have passed since “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood” premiered. Perhaps all parties have said everything there is to say about the Bruce Lee scene. But given how much the trailer leans into the matter, we could be in for another round of arguments about the portrayal.

#3557. Commander Shepard’s Actor Accidentally Immortalized One Mass Effect Race as Steve Buscemi

Mark Meer thought he'd just make alien noises for Mass Effect before he was cast as Shepard

Mark Meer never planned on saving the universe, but the universe had other plans.

You know Meer from a lengthy association with BioWare’s most popular RPGs. He’s lent his voice to several of the studio’s games, from Neverwinter Nights to Jade Empire. Most famously, he voiced the male version of Mass Effect’s Commander Shepard, but his work with BioWare dates back to one of the studio’s earliest breakout hits.

“I did one line in Baldur's Gate 2, and then subsequently, BioWare just kept hiring me for every subsequent project leading up to the Mass Effect trilogy,” Meer said.

In the wake of EA shutting down BioWare, laying off its remaining staff, and canceling Mass Effect: Universe, Polygon spoke with Jennifer Hale and Meer, the voices of Mass Effect’s Commander Shepard. They talked about their hopes for the future of Mass Effect, but also looked backward. Both actors recorded for the studio’s Baldur’s Gate games. Meer would play “monsters and antagonists and that sort of thing.”

They also both had roles in BioWare’s Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. Hale notably played Bastila Shan, while Meer voiced Carth Onasi, but only in KOTOR’s demo. The role in the full game eventually went to Raphael Sbarge, who, as it happens, ended up playing Kaidan Alenko in Mass Effect. (“Because he replaced me, that's why I killed Kaiden on Virmire,” Meer likes to joke.)

While Mass Effect was still in its concept art stage, he was brought in to aid in a presentation for the developers about how the aliens they were creating might sound. “I don't know if people realize how instrumental Mark was in defining the sound of every single species in this game,” Hale said, shouting out her friend and fellow Shepard.

“So what does a typical salarian sound like? What does a typical krogan sound like? That kind of thing,” Meer said. “It was nice to see some of the advice that I gave or some of the suggestions I made get implemented.

“I do take credit for the salarians all having the cadence of Steve Buscemi,” Meer added with a laugh. The first salarian he did was essentially a Buscemi impression for a demo, and it stuck.

While recording all those aliens, BioWare asked Meer if he’d audition for Shepard. “I thought there was absolutely no way I would get it,” Meer said, “which is probably good because I was not nervous at all.” He thought it would be “impossible” for him to land the role, and after auditioning he could “go back to doing my alien stuff.”

Of course, that wasn’t the case. He still did record “a bunch of aliens” for Mass Effect, like the vorcha, but that work was secondary to his role as Shepard. He was thrilled, but also somewhat shocked — and that shock doubled when he learned he’d be doing the same role as Hale, a titan of the industry. “It was sort of like being told, ‘You've been cast in this movie in the lead, and Meryl Streep will be playing opposite you playing the same character.’”

“Getting to be the lead in one of these was really a dream come true.”

Hale noted that Meer “set the tone” for Shepard by recording the initial couple sessions first. He was in Edmonton with BioWare while Hale recorded her lines in Los Angeles. In the early going, Hale’s LA team would play for her whatever Meer had recorded before she’d tackle her lines. His performance would influence the direction Hale took. She’d record a line multiple ways, including imitating Meer’s performance and then giving her own spin on a line read.

Eventually they got into a groove and, because of the way schedules work out, Meer wouldn’t always record first. Regardless of who was up, however, BioWare did have a specific request: “The one thing that they did really stress was you have to take the exact same amount of time to say the line,” Meer said with a laugh.

While Hale isn’t a gamer herself (“I suck at it,” she joked), Meer is a big fan of choice-based RPGs. “Getting to be the lead in one of these was really a dream come true,” he said.

The player is given a lot of flexibility in customizing Shepard, and Mass Effect’s Paragon and Renegade morality system allows them even more freedom in creating the hero. “So we really had to find the core of Shepard. What is the same between Renegade and Paragon?” Meer said.

He compared a Paragon Shepard to an upstanding Paladin in Dungeons & Dragons, and a Renegade Shepard to a “sociopath [who’s] still saving the galaxy, but not being polite or empathetic about it in any way whatsoever.” No matter what, Meer, Hale, and their directors settled on Shepard being a “military officer that's used to giving commands under pressure and is very professional in that sense,” Meer said.

Both Paragon and Renegade are worth playing, and both have their moments to shine. However, the freedom of a Renegade Shepard strikes a certain cord with both actors. “I always joke that Paragon's who I wish I was and Renegade's what I wish I could say,” Hale said. “I think we all aspire to be Paragon, but sometimes wish we could be Renegade,” Meer added.

Because of the Paragon and Renegade system — and because these games are just so damn good — the community loves jumping back into Mass Effect for a new playthrough, regardless of if they make new choices or roll with the same ones as always.

“You know, next year will be the 20th anniversary of the first Mass Effect game,” Meer said. “The fact that we are still talking about it, that we still have fans that are so passionate about that universe — it is impressive and humbling.”

#3556. The Top 10 TV Series Right Now, According to Streaming Data

October's ten most-streamed series are packed with your future favorite shows. There's a couple of modernizations of horror franchises for Halloween (Carrie and Crystal Lake), as well as new horror series Below and Phony. There's an excellent new superhero series Lanterns, sprawling family drama East of Eden, and new seasons of favorites Ted Lasso, Slow Horses, The Diplomat, and Mobland. So don't even try to tell anyone there's nothing on.

Horror master Mike Flanagan (Haunting of Hill House, Midnight Mass) re-imagines Stephen King's tale of teenage telekinesis, taking the story from the 1970s to now, complete with cyber bullying, smart phones, and a modern sensibility. The core of the tale, though, remains the same, as does the titular character's bloody coming-of-age. Powered by a talented young cast that includes Siena Agudong as Susan and Summer H. Howell as the title character, Carrie is a trick-or-treat for horror fans. Stream Carrie on Prime.

Based on John Steinbeck's pillar of Western literature, East of Eden follows three generations of the hardscrabble Hamilton family and the upscale Trask family, farming and ranching clans in California's Salinas Valley. The show's production is a multigenerational story too: It was written and created by Zoe Kazan, whose grandpa Elia directed the 1955 film version of East of Eden. All respect to Elia Kazan, but Steinbeck's story is so massive, it needs a seven-part mini-series. East of Eden is the kind of sprawling, melodramatic story that episodic television was made for. Stream East of Eden on Netflix.

Like Carrie, Crystal Lake reimagines a horror classic—in this case, Friday the 13th—and expands the lore even beyond the 12 films in the franchise. If you've ever wondered how Pamela Voorhees, played here by Linda Cardellini, became a serial murderer, and how her son Jason ended up a relentless, camp-counselor-killing-machine who lives at the bottom of a lake, Crystal Lake has all the answers. In a lot of ways, this show is better than all of the movies. Stream Crystal Lake on Peacock.

Apple TV's Slow Horses delivers a realistic, nuanced take on espionage by detailing the lives of the losers of British Intelligence. Instead of chiseled good guys and gals saving the world, the agents of Slough House are a team of dysfunctional, troubled souls trying to do the right thing (usually) in a morally gray world, just like real agents. Their leader, gruff, obnoxious Jackson Lamb, is played to perfection by Gary Oldman. Slow Horses has an almost perfect Rotten Tomatoes score over its first five seasons, and season 6 is setting new records. Stream Slow Horses on Apple TV+.

DC's TV revamp of Green Lantern details what happens when experienced Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) trains the new guy, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), on how to wield the mysterious and powerful Green Lantern Ring. It's a reserved, neo-noir style take on the comic mythos, as the heroes investigate a series of murders tied to an extraterrestrial threat. Lanterns is pulling in a better than 90% fresh ratings from Rotten Tomatoes, so it's definitely worth a stream. Stream Lanterns on HBO Max.

Created by Jesse McKeown and starring Josh Hartnett, Charlie Heaton, and Mackenzie Davis, Below is set in a Newfoundland fishing village beset with aquatic horror. When the Canadian government offers the residents of Snooks Arm a ton of money to relocate, no one really knows why, but ice fisherman Calvin Penney (Hartnett) suspects it has something to do with the monster he saw under the ice when he was a child. If you like taut creature feature style horror, check out Below. Stream Below on Netflix.

Season four of Ted Lasso sees the title character, played by Jason Sudeikis, returning to the UK to take on a new challenge: coaching the Lady Greyhounds, AFC Richmond's second-division women's football team. This multiple Emmy Award-winning series still has all the heart, humor, and positivity of the original run. Stream Ted Lasso on Apple TV+.

The mystery that drives creepy coming-of-age drama Phony is killer: Sonny Cooke, played by Sam Nivola, is a teenager with a very close relationship to his devoted single mother Ellen, played by Connie Britton. After a freak car accident, he wakes up convinced that his mom is an impostor. She looks the same, but there's something off about her in a way that Sonny can't describe, so he sets out to solve the mystery. Phony is rated over 90% fresh on Rotten Tomatoes. Stream Phony on Hulu.

In season four of political thriller series The Diplomat, the Kate Wyler, played by Keri Russell, finds that diplomatic relations between the U.S. and the UK are starting to crumble, and so is her marriage. Meanwhile, U.S. president Grace Penn, played by Allison Janney, and VP Hal Wyler, played by Rufus Sewell, continue their conspiracy to steal a Russian super-weapon, nudging the nation toward war with our longtime adversary. In other words, it's an international mess, with a few powerful people keeping the world from descending into chaos. If you like political intrigue, this is the series for you. Stream The Diplomat on Netflix.

Who doesn't love a sprawling organized crime drama? In Mobland, the crime is being organized in Great Britain, where two warring London crime families, the Harrigans and Stevensons, are locked in a battle for underworld power. In the middle of the crossfire is Harry Da Souza, a gritty fixer played to gruff perfection by Tom Hardy. Season 2 finds Da Souza in the unenviable position of holding together the Harrigan family on the verge of civil war. If you like backstabbing, scheming, murder, and other tropes of high-stakes crime thrillers, you'll like Mobland. Stream Mobland on Paramount+.

#3555. ‘Soul Patrol’ Review: The Vietnam War’s First Black Special Ops Team Shares Their Stories in An Enlightening Documentary

Editor’s Note: This review was originally published during the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. “Soul Patrol” opens in select theaters from Kino Lorber starting Friday, November 6.

The Vietnam War ended over a half-century ago, but the 20-year war remains a conflict that American artists keep going back to, finding new avenues and perspectives to tackle the many stories of the generation of men who had their lives irrevocably shaped by the conflict. Recent takes have centered the (often-neglected) perspective of the Vietnamese, or — like Spike Lee’s underrated late-career great “Da 5 Bloods” — explored the relatively under-examined service of Black men who served in the war. Related Stories How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Used Real-World Sound to Make Its Monsters More Terrifying ‘Zi’ Review: Kogonada Rediscovers His Voice with a Microbudget Hong Kong Experiment Starring Michelle Mao and Haley Lu Richardson

“Soul Patrol,” a new documentary from director J.M. Harper, looks at the Black soldiers of the war through the perspective of Ed Emanuel, a writer who served as a 17-year-old. In his 2003 memoir of the same title, Emanuel described tracking down and reuniting with the men he served with in the first Black special operations Long-Range Reconnaissance Patrol team, during his short 1968 to 1969 tour.

“Soul Patrol” finds the men in 2024, in what will be the last reunion they hold. Gathering together, the men — Emanuel, Lawton Mackey, Thad Givens, Emerson Branch, Jesse Lewis, Willie T. Brown, Willie Merkerson, and Norman Reid — sit in the conference room of a Florida hotel to discuss the memories of their service that has stuck with them over the decades, in the hope that their discussion can help them move on.

The opening, and Emmanuel’s narration, help bring context to the small stretch of the war that the film explores. In 1968, as the young men went to serve their country, America itself proved more turbulent than ever; Emanuel was on the plane to Vietnam as Robert F. Kennedy’s assassination was first reported. Protests against the war were growing, and the Civil Rights movement opposed the war as well; a speech from Martin Luther King Jr. becomes a crucial emotional turning point for Emanuel later, as he begins to wonder whether the trauma he experienced serving in the war was worth it.

Through the film, Emanuel and the footage of the reunion between the men guide the audience through their experiences, from the trauma they endured to the discrimination and tokenization they faced as Black soldiers fighting for America. One scene peels back at the men’s conflicting feelings around the nickname for their unit, a racialized moniker that’s simultaneously endearing and patronizing. Others focus on formative experiences Emanuel experiences throughout the war, including a hazy night in Bangkok that’s proves formative both sexually and emotionally.

Harper — whose debut feature “As We Speak” also played at Sundance — has a loud, uncompromisingly blunt style, and the film missteps most clearly when his directorial choices verge on heavy-handed. The film makes clumsy use of actor-led reenactments that are a little too slick and generic to slot seamlessly into the Super 8 footage and actor interviews that make up the bulk of the story. This particularly applies to an opening visual metaphor, in which an old veteran is haunted by a vision of his past, which proves more excessive and obvious than enlightening. Other formal choices feel designed to provoke emotional reactions the material can easily do on its own, particularly a loud, string-heavy score that feels overly generic for the material.

It’s when the film mostly gets out of its own way and lets the men’s experiences do the work that “Soul Patrol” really shines. The Super 8 footage collected from their tour in Vietnam, most of which was shot by the men themselves, is visually arresting and intimate, and Harper frequently employs quick cuts and montages of that on-the-ground film and b-roll of newscasts and ads of the time to flesh out the world they once inhabited. The reunion scenes are simply but artfully shot in black and white, including a revealing conversation among the men’s wives and partners about living with them that gently broadens the perspectives in the film’s portrait.

“Soul Patrol” admirably never tries to sum up the full experience of what Vietnam was, rather just trying to sum up what it was for these men. In the film’s closing stretch, it turns its attention to the men’s difficult experiences returning home from the war, with a candor and a vulnerability that’s hard not to tear up from. As one member of Soul Patrol reflects eloquently towards the end of the film, “We need to tell the stories to look at where we were at, where we come from, and where we headed. You need to know your beginning before you can figure out your ending.”

“Soul Patrol” premiered at the 2026 Sundance Film Festival. Kino Lorber opens the film in select theaters starting Friday, November 6.

#3554. DC’s Upcoming Green Lantern Release Is Everything The DCU’s Next Project Should Be

DC reveals the first glimpse at Hal Jordan's next battle, which looks like the ideal basis for the DCU's future Green Lantern movie and show appearances. HBO’s Lanterns marks a remarkable milestone as the first live-action, non-cameo Green Lantern project since the critical and commercial stumble of 2011's Green Lantern movie. The fifteen-year drought feels especially strange given how central the Emerald Knights are to the broader DC Universe and the superhero genre as a whole. Yet, for over a decade following Ryan Reynolds’s polarizing outing, the Lanterns were largely relegated to brief, peripheral nods.

Fortunately, this return is only the beginning, as the Green Lanterns are playing a vital role in the expanding DCU. Following the events of the HBO series' first season, both Aaron Pierre’s John Stewart and Nathan Fillion’s Guy Gardner are confirmed to reunite on the big screen in James Gunn’s upcoming sequel Man of Tomorrow. With the two Lanterns joining Superman and Lex Luthor to confront Brainiac, their presence in the 2027 movie pulls them from grounded terrestrial mysteries to world-scale war. New Lantern heroes and their respective villains could be introduced soon afterward, as their lore seems to be developing faster than that of any other DCU character.

Before Man of Tomorrow adds unbridled sci-fi and fantasy to John Stewart's DCU story, DC Comics shows how visually stunning a full-scale Green Lantern movie or show would look.

Hal Jordan’s clash against the returning Green Lantern villain Krona and the Manhunters in Green Lantern Corps showcases the perfect scale and tone missing from the DCU's Lanterns adaptation. In Green Lantern Corps #22, Hal Jordan teams up Krona, Jayna, and Tobi Y2K to dive deep into the wild Nexus of Emotions, where they meet face to face with the Manhunters. The heroes' varied costumes and powers, the Manhunters' colorful yet intimidating appearance, and the incredibly vibrant landscape of the Nexus of Emotions create a breathtaking visual experience that has never been adapted to live-action in a DC movie or show.

Although the HBO series Lanterns presents a bold and interesting take on the Greek Lantern mythos with its gritty crime-thriller murder mystery, the psychedelic visuals of Green Lantern Corps are something no live-action adaptation has dared to try. Now that Lanterns has introduced a new version of the Corps grounded on Earth, John Stewart's return in James Gunn's bombastic Man of Tomorrow and other future DCU Green Lantern appearances should draw inspiration from the comics and provide an unapologetically hard sci-fi story starring one or more Green Lanterns, especially if Nathan Fillion's scenery-chewing Guy Gardner has a key role in the plot.

Despite the immense popularity of the franchise, the Green Lantern Corps have yet to showcase their full cosmic majesty in live-action. On the big screen, the 2011 Green Lantern movie isolated Hal Jordan on a predictable hero's journey that barely scratched the surface of Oa's vast alien lore, Zack Snyder's Justice League only featured Yalan Gur in a single flashback scene, and James Gunn's Superman only included Guy Gardner in a supporting role. The DCU's Lanterns narrowed its scope and focused entirely on Hal Jordan and John Stewart's grounded mystery bound strictly to Earth.

DC is subtly revolutionizing the Green Lantern mythos, paving the way for the Corps to take a more prominent and completely fresh role.

A new Green Lantern big-screen adaptation could showcase multiple Earth Lanterns fighting side by side, complementing each other's constructs in creative team-up maneuvers with their own unique spin on their weapons. Audiences have yet to witness the sheer thrill of large-scale, live-action space warfare where hundreds of diverse ring-slingers engage in chaotic construct-filled battles against iconic Green Lantern villains such as the Sinestro Corps, the Black Lanterns, and the Manhunters. While the DCU presents a very different perspective, there's still room for a large-scale, colorful take on the Lanterns in the big or the small screen.

He has covered everything from Marvel to the Oscars, and Marvel at the Oscars. In his time at Collider, he has also helped drive diversity by writing stories about the multiple Indian film industries, with a goal of introducing audiences to a whole new world of cinema.

In the run-up to the release of The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, Quentin Tarantino admitted that while the world sees him primarily as a director, he is an equally respected screenwriter. Before he broke out with films such as Reservoir Dogs and Pulp Fiction, Tarantino made a name for himself as the writer of True Romance, directed by the late Tony Scott.

Tarantino always admired Scott deeply, and was a massive fan of several of the late director's hit action movies, which include the Kieran Knightley-led Domino, Tom Cruise's Days of Thunder, and Brad Pitt's Spy Game. Another of Tony Scott's action movies was added to a free streaming platform's library this month.

In a tribute to Scott following his death in 2012, Tarantino screened the film in Los Angeles. He said that he wept throughout the screening because of what Scott meant to him. "He’s like Douglas Sirk, he never got respect, was too commercial, people put him down. Now they teach classes about him,” Tarantino said, adding that the filmmaker's creative partnership with Denzel Washington — including The Taking of Pelham 1 2 3, Crimson Tide, and Unstoppable — was “one of the best actor-director combinations of our time.”

We're talking about Scott's 2004 action-thriller Man on Fire, which was based on a 1980 novel by A.J. Quinnell. Starring Washington, Dakota Fanning, Christopher Walken, and Marc Anthony, the movie grossed $130 million worldwide against a reported budget of $70 million. It now holds a 38% critics' score on the aggregator website Rotten Tomatoes, where the consensus reads, "Man on Fire's solid action and top-shelf cast are undone by a relentlessly grim story that gets harder to take the longer it goes on." The film's 89% audience score, on the other hand, more accurately represents its cult status.

Tarantino has another indirect connection to Man on Fire; when he worked at a video rental store in Los Angeles, he recommended the 1987 adaptation of Quinnell's novel to writer Brian Helgeland, who eventually wrote the Scott movie. Another adaptation, an eight-episode series on Netflix starring Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, was released earlier this year to mostly positive reviews.

You can watch the 2004 cult classic on Pluto TV, and stay tuned to Collider for more updates.

#3552. This New Chrome AI Feature Reads Your Gmail to Make Filling Out Web Forms Easier

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Google Chrome is making it easier to autofill online forms with more than just contact information and credit card numbers. For users with Personal Intelligence enabled, Gemini will now suggest items like order numbers, tracking information, membership IDs, and booking confirmations from Gmail messages when completing forms in Chrome.

Chrome's expanded autofill capabilities use Gemini to read your emails and surface suggestions, meaning you don't have to click back and forth between tabs or manually search for codes or confirmations in your inbox. When you click a form field that has a corresponding piece of data, a pop-up menu appears and indicates that an item is "Suggested by Gemini." You can click this to autofill the suggestion as well as open an additional menu to see the specific source (the original email) or remove the suggestion. The latter doesn't delete anything from Gmail; it simply dismisses the suggestion in Chrome.

As Android Police reports, Google started testing enhanced autofill in Chrome this summer using data from other connected apps like Google Photos. The feature currently rolling out is specific to Gmail and is coming first to U.S. users who have Personal Intelligence enabled on desktop as well as in the Android and iOS apps when using Gemini in Chrome.

In the blog post announcing the enhanced autofill feature, Google states that "sensitive data is encrypted" and that users can manage autofill, including enabling or disabling enhanced suggestions, via Chrome's settings.

#3551. 5 Incredible Anime Arcs That Are 10/10, No Notes

These are some of the very best arcs in the history of anime

An exceptional story arc can elevate even a flawed anime series. Although the mechanics of a great arc vary, the best tend to raise the stakes, test their characters, and build steadily toward a cathartic payoff. The conflict must also feel convincing, with the antagonist’s evolving goals and the heroes’ shifting motivations driving the story forward.

Consider the Chimera Ant arc from Hunter x Hunter, which is nothing short of a rite of passage. It pushes the anime’s deconstruction of shonen conventions to its limits while sending Gon Freecss and Killua Zoldyck down starkly different paths. The Shibuya Incident arc from Jujutsu Kaisen is similarly transformative, shattering the established order of jujutsu society through its intersecting perspectives, major character deaths, and relentless succession of battles.

Perfection is subjective, but the finest anime arcs share a few qualities: They’re memorable, well-paced, emotionally compelling, and resolved in a meaningful way. With those standards in mind, these five story arcs come remarkably close to perfection. We wouldn’t change a thing.

This article contains major spoilers for every story arc discussed below.

What happens when a brilliant story ends with an equally brilliant final arc?

Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood is filled with memorable stretches, from its exploration of the Ishvalan War to the heroes’ hunt for the Homunculi. But the anime saves its best for last with the Promised Day arc, a chaotic culmination of Father’s 400-year plan for Amestris and the intertwined destinies of Edward and Alphonse Elric.

Greed’s rebellion becomes a decisive turning point, while the brothers’ journey ultimately returns them to the Gate of Truth for one final reckoning.

The intricate buildup allows this concluding stretch to operate on an enormous scale. State Alchemists join forces with military defectors, Xingese royalty, and ordinary citizens to form a resistance against Father. The full complexity of Amestrian politics finally comes into play as nearly every faction and character converges upon Central.

Yet the arc never loses sight of the deeply personal story at its center. Amid the battles and political upheaval, the focus remains on Edward and everything he has learned about sacrifice, equivalence, and human connection. The Promised Day arc displays all the strengths of a thoughtful, well-constructed shonen, balancing quieter character moments with spectacular battles without allowing either to overwhelm the other.

Edward’s final sacrifice feels inevitable and surprising at once. His decision completes his development without robbing him of the life he fought so hard to reclaim — a fitting conclusion for someone with a Fullmetal heart.

One could argue that the Berserk: The Golden Age Arc film trilogy, which adapts the corresponding portion of Kentaro Miura’s Berserk, isn’t technically perfect. Despite its stunning hand-drawn artwork, the blend of 2D and 3D animation can feel uneven.

Even so, the trilogy captures the essence of the Golden Age, a breathtaking exploration of ambition, psychological trauma, betrayal, and the tenuous relationships that give people hope. All three films — The Egg of the King, The Battle for Doldrey, and The Advent — carefully portray the deteriorating bond between Guts, Griffith, and Casca, along with how each character responds to grief, desire, and loss.

Griffith and Guts are established as foils from the beginning, but their relationship develops with extraordinary depth and nuance. Guts, shaped by a brutal childhood and hardened by the need to survive, gradually lowers his defenses and learns to trust others. Griffith’s fall from a magnetic leader into a man consumed by pain and ambition destroys that progress, plunging Guts back into a cycle of anguish and revenge.

The Eclipse provides the arc’s unforgettable climax and establishes the horror that will define Guts’ subsequent campaign against the Apostles and the God Hand. Hope and despair are crushed together throughout the Golden Age, forcing its characters to confront the terrible limits of human resilience. It is unforgiving, devastating, and almost impossible to forget.

Mob Psycho 100 is pure shonen excellence. It uses the genre’s familiar framework to tell a radically subversive coming-of-age story about empathy, self-acceptance, and human connection.

Shigeo “Mob” Kageyama spends most of the series trying to control his immense psychic powers. But the emphasis isn’t on physical training or becoming stronger. Mob’s real challenge is developing the emotional intelligence necessary to understand himself and connect honestly with the people around him.

Because Mob’s powers are inextricably linked to his psychological state, the ???% arc serves as the culmination of years of emotional suppression. It answers the question of what happens when an overpowered protagonist finally reaches his breaking point. The ultimate conflict isn’t between Mob and another supernaturally gifted antagonist. It is between Mob and the part of himself he has always refused to accept.

His repressed emotions and unresolved trauma manifest as ???%, also known as the “Unknown.” The resulting conflict cannot be resolved through a conventional power-up or some last-minute supernatural solution. Instead, Reigen Arataka’s unflinching honesty finally allows Mob to confront the truth. Mob accepts the Unknown not as a separate monster that must be defeated, but as an intrinsic part of himself.

Mob Psycho 100 resolves its protagonist’s deepest conflict without offering an easy way out. Mob still has to live with his trauma and continue the difficult work of remaining emotionally open. But judging by his carefree laughter at the end of the anime, he is finally ready to do that work.

A sprawling anime like Naruto is bound to contain more than one standout arc, especially when its central story is interspersed with so many filler episodes. The Chunin Exams and Sasuke Retrieval arcs remain popular for good reason, but the most viscerally uncompromising portion of the series is Pain’s Assault.

Nagato, or Pain, is among the saga’s most compelling antagonists. His attack forces the Hidden Leaf Village to contend with total destruction while compelling Naruto and his allies to confront the ideology behind his violence.

Jiraiya’s death during his infiltration of Amegakure casts a shadow over everything that follows. But Nagato’s motivations extend beyond simple revenge. He believes humanity can achieve peace only after experiencing suffering so catastrophic that people become terrified of repeating it. Because empathy cannot be imposed, Nagato instead attempts to manufacture it through devastation, convincing himself that this atrocity is justified in the pursuit of lasting peace.

Naruto explores that philosophy through both dialogue and combat, using the visual language of a sprawling, devastating battle to deliver the arc’s greatest emotional and dramatic highs. For a time, no character feels safe, and the apparent destruction of the Hidden Leaf fundamentally destabilizes the series’ familiar world.

That sense of danger doesn’t truly lift until Naruto rejects the endless cycle of retaliation. Rather than defeating Nagato through force alone, he chooses empathy, resolving their ideological conflict by demonstrating the very compassion that Nagato believed could exist only through shared suffering.

The Steel Ball Run anime is now taking viewers through the early stages of its cross-country race, but it has not yet reached the Civil War arc. For now, this brilliant segment of JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure: Steel Ball Run remains a manga story waiting to make the leap to animation.

Hirohiko Araki excels at transforming abstract concepts into bizarre, visually inventive conflicts. The entirety of JoJo’s Bizarre Adventure is proof of his profound eccentricity, but the Civil War arc stands out even within a series built upon surreal confrontations.

The arc’s titular Stand belongs to government agent Axl RO and transforms the guilt carried by Johnny Joestar, Hot Pants, and Gyro Zeppeli into physical manifestations. Johnny’s accumulated trauma is laid bare, exposing the defining childhood experiences that continue to haunt him.

These manifestations can assume virtually any form, from a broken knife to a teddy bear. Once touched, they surround their target in a membrane that slowly crushes them to death. The only way to endure this nightmare is to confront the guilt that gave it form.

That forces Johnny to reckon with his past and unlock a new stage of his Spin ability. Jesus Christ himself also appears during the conflict, reinforcing a story already steeped in ideas about faith, personal transformation, and the destructive consequences of unchecked ambition.

The Sugar Mountain and High Voltage/D4C arcs are exceptional in their own right, but Civil War represents a monumental turning point for Johnny. It transforms an inventive Stand battle into something resembling a spiritual rebirth — and proves that even by JoJo standards, Araki is capable of getting profoundly weird.
